activity.cli.interval: Minimum seconds between activity attempts (60–86400; default 60).
activity.cli.max_polls: Stop after this many attempts; otherwise continue until Ctrl+C or a storage or cancellation error.
activity.cli.max_rows: Maximum native session/request rows in one activity observation.
activity.cli.no_window: Current activity has no historical window; omit --from and --until.
activity.cli.output_failed: The activity-monitor output could not be written.
activity.cli.running: Record a request after this many seconds of native elapsed time.

check.big_result.fix.export: If it is an export or ETL job, leave it as it is, and run it on a replica or off-peak if it competes with the application. If the application runs it: Return only what's used: page the results (keyset pagination, or LIMIT / OFFSET … FETCH), filter in SQL rather than in the application, select only the columns you need, and aggregate in the database.
check.big_result.fix.return_used: Return only what's used: page the results (keyset pagination, or LIMIT / OFFSET … FETCH), filter in SQL rather than in the application, select only the columns you need, and aggregate in the database.
check.big_result.impact: {n, plural, one {{rows} row per run} other {{rows} rows per run}}
check.big_result.info.description: Reads that send tens of thousands of rows to the application on every run, with an estimate in bytes from the plan's row width where the engine gives one.
check.big_result.info.title: Queries that return huge results
check.big_result.spill.fix: Where the application doesn't use every row it receives, return only what's used: page the results (keyset pagination, or LIMIT / OFFSET … FETCH), filter in SQL rather than in the application, select only the columns you need, and aggregate in the database.
check.big_result.spill.fix_export: If it is an export or an ETL job, the memory is the fix; run it on a replica or off-peak if it competes with the application.
check.big_result.spill.summary: Each run also sends {sends} to the application, and few screens or jobs need that many at once: returning fewer can keep the sort in memory too.
check.big_result.spill.summary_export: Each run also sends {sends} to the application, the whole table: an export, a dump or an ETL job looks like this, and for those the rows are the point.
check.big_result.spill.verify_between_sc: If it now returns fewer rows, the rows it returns per run between those two scans should drop to what a page or a job actually uses.
check.big_result.spill.verify_rescan: If it now returns fewer rows, re-scan: rows per run should drop to what a page or a job actually uses.
check.big_result.summary.export: It reads the whole table {how_often}: an export, a dump or an ETL job looks like this, and for those the rows are the point. It needs work only if a screen or a request runs it.
check.big_result.summary.sends: Each run sends {n, plural, one {{rows} row} other {{rows} rows}} to the application; its {runs_n, plural, one {{runs} run} other {{runs} runs}} {ran} moved {total_n, plural, one {{total} row} other {{total} rows}}.
check.big_result.summary.sends_bytes: Each run sends {n, plural, one {{rows} row} other {{rows} rows}} to the application, about {bytes} at the plan's estimated {width} per row; its {runs_n, plural, one {{runs} run} other {{runs} runs}} {ran} moved {total_n, plural, one {{total} row} other {{total} rows}}.
check.big_result.summary.too_many: Few screens or jobs need that many at once: the database reads them, the network carries them and the application holds them in memory.
check.big_result.title: {handle} {tense, select, past {returned} other {returns}} {sends} per run
check.big_result.verify.between_scans: Between two scans, the rows it returns per run should drop to what a page or a job actually uses: {source} keeps running totals, so compare its rows and runs in a scan taken once the change is live and one a day or more later ({now} in this scan).
check.big_result.verify.now: {n, plural, one {{rows} row} other {{rows} rows}} in {runs_n, plural, one {{runs} run} other {{runs} runs}}
check.big_result.verify.rescan: Re-scan: rows per run should drop to what a page or a job actually uses.
check.chatty_query.between.counter: compare total time and any avoidable calls, while checking that numbering, metadata updates and returned values remain correct
check.chatty_query.between.fewer: it should run fewer times and take less time in all while the useful work stays the same
check.chatty_query.between.finds_nothing: unnecessary calls and total database time should fall while the useful work stays the same
check.chatty_query.between.read: it should run fewer times and take less time in all
check.chatty_query.caveat.counter: A sequence can have gaps, allocates outside transaction commit order and does not provide per-parent numbering. Check the application's numbering and atomicity requirements before considering one.
check.chatty_query.caveat.delete: Some frequent single-row deletes are legitimate (a row removed as its work completes). Check the calling code before batching.
check.chatty_query.caveat.finds_nothing: Some frequent checks are legitimate (a lease or a lock checked on every request). Check the calling code before changing how often it asks.
check.chatty_query.caveat.insert: Some frequent single-row writes are legitimate (each event recorded as it happens). Check the calling code before batching.
check.chatty_query.caveat.read: Some high-frequency single-row lookups are legitimate (for example, by primary key on a hot path). Check the calling code before batching.
check.chatty_query.caveat.update: Some frequent single-row updates are legitimate (a status that changes as its work progresses). Check the calling code before batching.
check.chatty_query.fix.counter: If the caller confirms that this is solely a number allocator, consider {sequence} only if a database-wide allocator, gaps and allocation order satisfy the application's requirements. It does not preserve gapless or per-parent numbering or commit order. Otherwise keep the atomic UPDATE. Check whether the caller can combine work without losing filters, returned values or transaction guarantees; the SQL alone does not establish a removable call.
check.chatty_query.fix.counter_compound: The SQL does not establish an isolated counter-only operation: preserve every assignment, returned value, row filter and transaction guarantee. Check the caller before changing it. If it already has independent work that can safely share a call, consider batching that work; per-parent numbering and metadata updates may require this atomic UPDATE. A sequence is not a replacement for the whole statement.
check.chatty_query.fix.delete: If the caller already has independent removals that can safely be grouped, delete many rows per statement ({keys}, or by a condition the rows share) inside one transaction.
check.chatty_query.fix.finds_nothing: Check the caller first. If it polls for work, back off after empty results, coordinate pollers, or have the writer wake them (a queue or notification). For request-driven checks, reuse an answer only while it remains valid. Keep necessary checks and their correctness guarantees.
check.chatty_query.fix.insert: If the caller already has independent rows that can safely be grouped, write many rows per statement ({bulk}) inside one transaction; for a heartbeat or lease, renew less often.
check.chatty_query.fix.read: Reuse a result the application already has, or cache it for as long as it remains valid; access checks must still reflect permission changes. If the caller loops over items, load their rows in one query (WHERE key IN (…) or a join) before the loop; ORMs usually have an eager-loading option for this.
check.chatty_query.fix.update: Where the application changes many rows the same way, update them in one statement ({keys}) inside one transaction; for a heartbeat or lease, renew less often.
check.chatty_query.info.description: Tiny queries executed so often that the round trips cost more than the work, typically a loop in application code.
check.chatty_query.info.title: Chatty queries
check.chatty_query.locks.counted: {server} counted {waits} of lock waits out of its {total}
check.chatty_query.locks.query_store: Query Store recorded {waits} of lock waits out of its {total}
check.chatty_query.metric.runs_per_day_s: Runs per day over Culprit's scans
check.chatty_query.metric.share_scans: Share of executions over Culprit's scans
check.chatty_query.sequence.mariadb: a SEQUENCE (`NEXT VALUE FOR`) or an AUTO_INCREMENT column
check.chatty_query.sequence.postgres: a sequence (`nextval()`, or an identity column)
check.chatty_query.summary.counter: Each run adds to {column} in one row of {table} and returns the new value. It may allocate numbers or maintain other application state; the SQL alone does not establish its business purpose or a removable call. Each call can add a round trip, and the row stays locked until its transaction commits, so callers that need the next number of the same row can wait for each other.
check.chatty_query.summary.delete: Frequent small deletes can be independent removals or a row-by-row loop; each call can add a round trip, and each committing transaction can flush the log ({share} in all). The counters do not show whether calls already share a transaction.
check.chatty_query.summary.finds_nothing: Empty results can come from polling, request-driven checks or legitimate misses; the counters do not identify the caller or prove a timer. Each run {tense, select, past {was} other {is}} cheap ({share} in all), but unnecessary calls still add round trips.
check.chatty_query.summary.insert: Frequent small writes can be individual events, heartbeats or a row-by-row loop; each call can add a round trip, and each committing transaction can flush the log ({share} in all). The counters do not show whether calls already share a transaction.
check.chatty_query.summary.read: Repeated lookups can be per-request checks or a loop in application code (N+1). Each run {tense, select, past {was} other {is}} cheap ({share} in all), but each call can add a network round trip.
check.chatty_query.summary.share.changes: Its runs {tense, select, past {were} other {are}} {share} of all statement runs, and each run {tense, select, past {changed} other {changes}} about {rows}.
Its runs {tense, select, past {were} other {are}} {share} of all statement runs over {over}, and each run {tense, select, past {changed} other {changes}} about {rows}.
check.chatty_query.summary.share.poll_ch: Its runs {tense, select, past {were} other {are}} {share} of all statement runs, and on average a run {tense, select, past {changed} other {changes}} {rows}.
Its runs {tense, select, past {were} other {are}} {share} of all statement runs over {over}, and on average a run {tense, select, past {changed} other {changes}} {rows}.
check.chatty_query.summary.share.poll_re: Its runs {tense, select, past {were} other {are}} {share} of all statement runs, and on average a run {tense, select, past {returned} other {returns}} {rows}.
Its runs {tense, select, past {were} other {are}} {share} of all statement runs over {over}, and on average a run {tense, select, past {returned} other {returns}} {rows}.
check.chatty_query.summary.share.returns: Its runs {tense, select, past {were} other {are}} {share} of all statement runs, and each run {tense, select, past {returned} other {returns}} about {rows}.
Its runs {tense, select, past {were} other {are}} {share} of all statement runs over {over}, and each run {tense, select, past {returned} other {returns}} about {rows}.
check.chatty_query.summary.share.runs: Its runs {tense, select, past {were} other {are}} {share} of all statement runs.
check.chatty_query.summary.share.runs_ov: Its runs {tense, select, past {were} other {are}} {share} of all statement runs over {over}.
check.chatty_query.summary.update: Frequent small updates can be independent requests, row-by-row loops, heartbeats or status changes; each call can add a round trip, and each committing transaction can flush the log ({share} in all). The counters do not show whether calls already share a transaction.
check.chatty_query.title.finds_nothing: {query} {tense, select, past {ran} other {runs}} {runs} and most runs {tense, select, past {found} other {find}} nothing
check.chatty_query.title.one_row: {query} {tense, select, past {ran} other {runs}} {runs}, one row each time
check.chatty_query.title.read: {query} {tense, select, past {ran} other {runs}} {runs}, one key at a time
check.chatty_query.title.rows: {query} {tense, select, past {ran} other {runs}} {runs}, about {rows} each time
check.checkpoint_pressure.fix: Inspect the checkpoint log (log_checkpoints) during normal load before changing anything. If it confirms frequent checkpoints caused by WAL filling max_wal_size, check free disk space and consider giving WAL more room: {how} Backups and manual checkpoints need no WAL-size fix.
check.checkpoint_pressure.fix_cost: WAL takes more disk, and crash recovery can take a little longer.
check.checkpoint_pressure.info.descripti: The server's requested checkpoints, with the possible causes and the evidence needed before changing WAL settings.
check.checkpoint_pressure.info.title: Requested checkpoints
check.checkpoint_pressure.summary.causes: Requests can come from WAL reaching max_wal_size, a manual CHECKPOINT, a base backup or CREATE DATABASE.
Requests can come from WAL reaching max_wal_size ({size}), a manual CHECKPOINT, a base backup or CREATE DATABASE.
check.checkpoint_pressure.summary.not_pr: This counter does not distinguish their causes or measure write latency, so it does not establish that WAL is too small or that this database has write pressure.
check.checkpoint_pressure.summary.reques: {requested} of {total} checkpoints across the whole server were requested rather than timed since the checkpoint counters were reset.
check.checkpoint_pressure.title: {percent}% of the server's recorded checkpoints were requested rather than timed
check.checkpoint_pressure.verify: Check checkpoint reasons and write latency during comparable load. After a confirmed WAL-size change, WAL-triggered checkpoints should be less frequent; the requested-checkpoint ratio alone is not a health target.
check.cluster_health.fix: Inspect cluster membership, node logs and state transfer with the cluster owner. Check network and capacity, and route traffic only to suitable nodes. Do not bootstrap a component, disable flow control or force quorum from this observation alone.
check.cluster_health.info.description: The current readiness, connectivity and primary-component verdict reported by a Galera node; its historical flow-control fraction is context, not database-specific pressure.
check.cluster_health.info.title: Galera node readiness and flow control
check.cluster_health.summary.flow_contro: Donor or desynchronized states can be deliberate. The retained flow-control ratio does not establish pressure or delays in this database now.
check.cluster_health.summary.status: Measured node status: ready {ready, select, yes {yes} no {no} other {unknown}}, connected {connected, select, yes {yes} no {no} other {unknown}}, primary component {primary, select, yes {yes} no {no} other {unknown}}.
check.cluster_health.summary.unavailable: This is the node's own availability verdict; it can reject application operations. Check whether it is intentionally being maintained before intervening.
check.cluster_health.title.flow_control: Galera recorded time paused for flow control (whole cluster context)
check.cluster_health.title.unavailable: This Galera node reports that it is not ready, disconnected or outside the primary component
check.cluster_health.verify: Verify the intended node rejoins the primary component, reports ready and connected, and serves application operations. Compare flow control over a fresh known interval before diagnosing sustained pressure.
check.compile_pressure.fix: Inspect this database's Query Store compile counts and durations and its query-family findings. If those measurements show costly repeated compilation, parameterize the affected statements. Do not change database-wide parameterization from the instance's ratio alone.
check.compile_pressure.info.description: Shared compilation counters provide context for this database's literal query families; measured Query Store costs establish its compilation impact.
check.compile_pressure.info.title: Instance compilation context
check.compile_pressure.summary: {since}, the instance averaged {batches}/s batches across all its databases and compiled a new plan for {percent}% of them, recompiles not counted. This ratio does not identify this database's compiles or measure its CPU pressure. This database has statements with different literal values; its own Query Store compile costs can show whether they warrant work.
check.compile_pressure.title: The SQL Server instance recorded compilation for {percent}% of batches (about {per_minute} a minute)
check.compile_pressure.verify: Compare this database's measured compilation costs under comparable load before and after the change. The instance-wide ratio alone cannot verify a fix in this database.
check.config.auto_statistics.caveat.vend: Some products require it off and maintain statistics themselves (SharePoint content databases do): check the vendor's guidance before turning it on.
check.config.auto_statistics.summary: The optimizer relies on statistics to estimate row counts. With this off, estimates go stale or missing and plans degrade over time.
check.config.auto_statistics.title: {setting} is off
check.config.autovacuum.fix: Turn it back on; tune it per table instead of disabling it.
check.config.autovacuum.summary: Dead rows from updates and deletes are never cleaned up automatically, tables and indexes keep growing, planner statistics go stale, and transaction-ID wraparound becomes a real risk.
check.config.autovacuum.title: Autovacuum is off
check.config.autovacuum_scale.fix: Lower it for the big tables only.
check.config.autovacuum_scale.summary: autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor is {factor}: {table} ({rows} rows, with updates and deletes) is only vacuumed after about {changed} rows change, so dead rows pile up between runs and each run is long.
check.config.autovacuum_scale.title: Autovacuum waits for {share} of {table} to change before cleaning it
check.config.autovacuum_scale.verify.gon: Re-scan: the tables have their own scale factor and this finding is gone.
check.config.autovacuum_scale.verify.mor: Re-scan: the tables the SQL changed have their own scale factor and drop out of this finding; the next ones it names need the same change.
check.config.buffer_pool.fix: Check measured read latency and this database's workload before resizing the server's buffer pool. If they confirm a memory shortage, allow more memory for the pool while leaving room for connections and the operating system; it can be resized online with SET GLOBAL innodb_buffer_pool_size.
check.config.buffer_pool.fix_cost: Uses that much RAM; a pool larger than the free memory makes the server swap or be killed.
check.config.buffer_pool.fix_managed: If measured read latency and this database's workload confirm a memory shortage, consider giving the buffer pool more of the instance's memory{controlled, select, yes { in {control}} other {}} ({platform} sizes it from the instance's memory), or move to an instance with more memory. Leave room for connections and the operating system.
check.config.buffer_pool.metric.from_dis: Pages read from disk per second
check.config.buffer_pool.summary: innodb_buffer_pool_size is {pool}, and this database has {data} of InnoDB tables and indexes. Since {server} started, {hit} of page reads across the whole server were served from its buffer pool{measured, select, yes { (about {reads} pages a second from disk)} other {}}. The rest may have been served by the operating system cache; this does not establish slow reads in this database.
check.config.buffer_pool.title: The server's InnoDB buffer pool records {share} of reads missing memory
check.config.buffer_pool.verify: Re-scan after a day of normal load: reads served from memory should be at 99% or more ({hit} now). The share counts since {server} started, so after an online resize it rises slowly; after a restart it counts afresh.
check.config.buffer_pool_wait_free.fix: If the buffer pool is undersized for the working set, grow innodb_buffer_pool_size; if write bursts dirty pages faster than background flushing cleans them, raise innodb_io_capacity (and innodb_io_capacity_max) to match the storage's IOPS.
check.config.buffer_pool_wait_free.summa: Innodb_buffer_pool_wait_free is {count} {since}: foreground threads needed a free page in the InnoDB buffer pool when none was clean, and had to wait for dirty pages to be flushed first.
check.config.buffer_pool_wait_free.title: Queries waited {n, plural, one {once} other {{count} times}} for a clean buffer-pool page
check.config.buffer_pool_wait_free.verif: Compare Innodb_buffer_pool_wait_free between two scans under normal write load: it should stop growing.
check.config.compatibility_level.fix: Raise it after testing; Query Store makes this safe because you can force the old plans for any query that regresses.
check.config.compatibility_level.summary: The server supports level {latest}, but the optimizer behaves as it did at {level}. Newer levels bring adaptive joins, memory grant feedback and parameter-sensitive plans.
{service} supports level {latest}, but the optimizer behaves as it did at {level}. Newer levels bring adaptive joins, memory grant feedback and parameter-sensitive plans.
check.config.compatibility_level.title: The database runs at compatibility level {level}
check.config.cost_threshold.fix: A common starting point is 50; adjust with your workload.
check.config.cost_threshold.summary: Even cheap queries go parallel, which wastes CPU on coordination and shows up as CXPACKET/CXCONSUMER waits.
check.config.cost_threshold.title: Cost threshold for parallelism is still the 1990s default of 5
check.config.digest_length.fix_cost: A little more memory per digest.
check.config.digest_length.summary: Long statements are truncated in performance_schema, so statements that differ only after the cut are merged into one digest, and Culprit can't explain them.
check.config.digest_length.title: {count} statements are cut off at 1,024 characters
check.config.digest_length.verify: Re-scan after the server has restarted with the change and the statements have run again: they are no longer cut off, and this finding is gone.
check.config.digests_lost.fix: Raise the table size and truncate the summary to start fresh.
check.config.digests_lost.summary: Its digest table holds {size} statements and is full: {lost} new statements were lumped into one anonymous row{untracked, select, yes {, which holds {share} of statement time} other {}}. Those statements are invisible to per-query analysis. It usually means the app sends many distinct statements (generated SQL, unparameterized literals).
check.config.digests_lost.title: performance_schema ran out of room for statement digests
check.config.digests_lost.verify: Re-scan after the restart: no digests lost, and no statement time left in the anonymous row. After a truncate alone, compare the lost count between two scans: it should stop growing.
check.config.info.description: Database and server settings that commonly hurt performance or hide the data needed to diagnose it.
check.config.info.title: Configuration
check.config.legacy_cardinality_estimati: Turn it off after testing, and use Query Store to force the old plan for any query that regresses (or a per-query hint).
LEGACY_CARDINALITY_ESTIMATION is on, so the optimizer uses the old estimator regardless of the compatibility level. It was often set as a quick fix after an upgrade and then forgotten.
The database estimates row counts the pre-2014 way
check.config.maxdop.fix_database: Cap it for this database (or for the whole server).
check.config.maxdop.fix_server: Cap it for the server: this version has no per-database setting (SQL Server 2016 added it).
check.config.maxdop.summary: With no limit on parallelism, a single large query can occupy all {count} schedulers and make everything else queue behind it. Microsoft's guidance is at most 8, and no more than the processors in one NUMA node{nodes, select, many { ({per_node} here)} other {}}.
check.config.maxdop.title: One query may use all {count} processors (MAXDOP 0)
check.config.my_cnf_and_restart: Set it in the server configuration (my.cnf) and restart.
check.config.performance_schema.fix.at_n: Turn performance_schema on at the next restart for statistics on every statement: set performance_schema to ON in {control}.
Turn performance_schema on at the next restart for statistics on every statement: set it in the server configuration (my.cnf) and restart.
check.config.performance_schema.fix.slow: Start with the slow query log, which needs no restart: Culprit reads it from the mysql.slow_log table.
check.config.performance_schema.fix.turn: Turn it on (it can't be changed at runtime).
check.config.performance_schema.fix_cost: A few hundred MB of memory and a small CPU overhead.
check.config.performance_schema.summary: Without it {server} keeps no statement digests, index usage or wait statistics: there is nothing to tell which queries are slow or which indexes are used.
check.config.performance_schema.summary_: Culprit reads the slow query log, so statements slower than long_query_time are covered. Without performance_schema, {server} keeps no statistics for faster statements and no wait statistics.
check.config.performance_schema.title: performance_schema is off
check.config.query_store.fix: Turn it on with automatic capture so ad-hoc noise isn't recorded.
check.config.query_store.fix_cost: Uses some space in the database (default cap 1 GB) and a little CPU.
check.config.query_store.summary: Without Query Store, Culprit (and you) only see what is still in the plan cache: no history, no plan regressions, no per-query waits. It costs little and is on by default in Azure SQL and SQL Server 2022.
check.config.query_store.title: Query Store is off, so query history is lost on every restart
check.config.query_store_capture.summary: Capture mode ALL keeps statements that ran once or cost nothing ({count} statements in {window}). They crowd the store, shorten how far back it can look and add overhead; AUTO keeps what matters.

Capture mode ALL keeps statements that ran once or cost nothing. With {count} {n, plural, one {statement} other {statements}} in {window} it costs little now; once one-off statements arrive (ad-hoc queries, generated SQL), they crowd the store, shorten how far back it can look and add overhead. AUTO keeps what matters.
Capture mode ALL keeps statements that ran once or cost nothing. On a busy database they crowd the store, shorten how far back it can look and add overhead; AUTO keeps what matters.
check.config.query_store_capture.title: Query Store records every statement, including one-off ones
check.config.query_store_read_only.fix.c: Record only statements that matter (automatic capture), then turn recording back on.
check.config.query_store_read_only.fix.d: Free or add space in the database's data files, then turn recording back on.
check.config.query_store_read_only.fix.r: Give it more room and let it clean up old data by itself, then turn recording back on.
check.config.query_store_read_only.fix.w: It usually returns to recording once the data is written; if it stays read-only, turn recording back on.
check.config.query_store_read_only.reaso: the database is out of disk space
the database is in emergency mode
data waiting to be written to disk reached its memory limit
the database is in single-user mode
it holds as many different statements as its memory allows
check.config.query_store_read_only.summa: Query Store is read-only because {why}. New queries and plan changes aren't being captured.
check.config.query_store_read_only.title: Query Store stopped recording
check.config.query_store_size.fix: Raise the limit and let it clean up old data on its own.
check.config.query_store_size.summary: It holds {used} MB of its {max} MB limit. At the limit it turns read-only: new queries, plan changes and regressions stop being captured until someone makes room.
check.config.query_store_size.title: Query Store is {share} full and stops recording when it fills
check.config.query_store_waits.fix: Turn wait capture on; the overhead is small.
check.config.query_store_waits.summary: With wait capture off, Culprit can say the server waits on locks or disk but not which queries do the waiting.
check.config.query_store_waits.title: Query Store isn't recording waits, so waits can't be tied to queries
check.config.read_committed_snapshot.cav: Readers then see the last committed version instead of waiting. Code that relies on blocking reads for correctness (rare) must use locking hints.
ALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION is on: code can already opt into SNAPSHOT isolation per transaction; RCSI makes every read-committed read use versions.
check.config.read_committed_snapshot.fix: Turn on row versioning for read committed. It needs a moment with no other connections, so schedule it.
Row versions live in tempdb (or the database with ADR), which adds some write overhead.
ALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION is already on, so SQL Server already keeps row versions for this database: little extra overhead.
check.config.read_committed_snapshot.sum: In {window}, reads waited {duration} on locks held by writes ({share} of database time){came, select, when {, all of it {when}} when_stopped {, all of it {when}, and {reads, plural, one {that read hasn't} other {those reads haven't}} run since} stopped {, and {reads, plural, one {that read hasn't} other {those reads haven't}} run since} other {}}.

In {window} reads waited {duration} on locks ({share} of database time){came, select, when {, all of it {when}} when_stopped {, all of it {when}, and {reads, plural, one {that read hasn't} other {those reads haven't}} run since} stopped {, and {reads, plural, one {that read hasn't} other {those reads haven't}} run since} other {}}, so it costs little now.
{n, plural, one {{count} deadlock in this database had a read in it.} other {{count} deadlocks in this database had a read in them.}}
With row versioning off for read committed, a SELECT waits for any write holding a lock on the rows it reads, and vice versa.

check.heap_table.fix: Add a clustered index, usually on the primary key or an ever-increasing column such as an identity or creation time. Plan it as a maintenance operation: it rewrites the table.

check.heavy_query.fix.fewer_runs.cheap_p: Each run is fast and its plan is already cheap; the cost is in how often it runs.
check.heavy_query.fix.fewer_runs.fast: Each run is fast; the cost is in how often it runs.
check.heavy_query.fix.finds_nothing.no_u: Most of its runs find nothing. If it checks whether a row exists before writing one (a duplicate or idempotency check), let the write do the check instead: with a unique index on those columns, an insert that handles the duplicate-key error (or an upsert) needs no read first. If it polls for work, ask less often when it finds none, or have the writer notify the poller.
check.heavy_query.fix.finds_nothing.uniq: Most of its runs find nothing. If it checks whether a row exists before writing one (a duplicate or idempotency check), let the write do the check instead: this plan seeks {index} on {table}{filtered, select, yes { (unique for the rows where `{filter}`)} other {}}, a unique index that exists already, so an insert that handles its duplicate-key error (or an upsert) needs no read first. If it polls for work, ask less often when it finds none, or have the writer notify the poller.
check.heavy_query.fix.idle.app_lock: Shorten the work done while the lock is held, or take the lock without waiting (a try-lock, or a lock timeout) and retry later.
check.heavy_query.fix.idle.client: The application reads the results slowly, or row by row while it does other work. Read all rows first and process them afterwards, or fetch fewer.
check.heavy_query.fix.idle.latch: Sessions queue for the same pages: typically inserts at the end of an index on an increasing key, or tempdb allocation. See the hot-rows and last-page findings, and Live while it happens.
check.heavy_query.fix.idle.locks: Keep those transactions short: commit sooner, and don't wait for a user or another service inside a transaction. An index or a rewrite of this statement won't shorten the wait.
check.heavy_query.fix.idle.memory: It waits for a memory grant while other queries hold the memory: find the queries with the largest grants ({health}) and reduce them, usually with better estimates or an index that avoids a big sort or hash.
check.heavy_query.fix.idle.sleep: Find who sends it (a health check, a test, a retry loop with a back-off) and whether the pause belongs in the database at all: while it sleeps it holds a connection, and any locks its transaction took.
check.heavy_query.fix.idle.unknown: Find what it waits for while it runs: Live shows each session's wait and any blocking chain. Typical causes are locks other transactions hold, a slow client reading the results, or a call outside the database.
check.heavy_query.fix.kind.aggregate: Find this statement in the application and check whether it aggregates more rows than it needs.
check.heavy_query.fix.kind.aggregate_kep: Find this statement in the application and check whether it aggregates more rows than it needs, or whether the result could be kept up to date instead of recomputed on every run.
check.heavy_query.fix.kind.locking: Find this statement in the application: it locks the rows it finds until its transaction ends. Check that it locks only the rows the transaction goes on to change, and that the transaction commits soon after.
check.heavy_query.fix.kind.read: Find this statement in the application and check whether it reads more rows or columns than it needs.
check.heavy_query.fix.kind.write: Find this statement in the application and check that it finds the rows it changes through an index, and changes no more rows per run than it needs (split large updates into batches).
check.heavy_query.fix.measure.capture_pl: Capture an actual execution plan for a representative run in a test environment.
check.heavy_query.fix.measure.locate: Check how many rows each step reads and keeps, and collect IO measurements for the same run to locate the reads on {table}. Use that evidence to decide whether a change to statistics or the access path is justified.
check.heavy_query.fix.measure.retained_p: Read a retained actual plan when the server has one; otherwise capture a representative actual plan in a test environment.
check.heavy_query.fix.scan.index: The plan scans {table} and filters afterwards. An index on the filtered columns turns that into a seek; open the plan to see the predicate.
check.heavy_query.fix.scan.read_less: The plan reads all of {table} and keeps about {kept} of the rows, too many for an index to help. Read only the rows and columns the caller needs, or page through them.

check.heavy_query.fix.session.settings: The driver or the connection pool sends this around the application's statements, not the application's own code: look at what the pool runs each time it hands out a connection (session settings, a reset), and set what the application needs once instead: in the connection string, or as the role's or the server's defaults.
check.heavy_query.fix.session.transactio: The driver or the connection pool sends this around the application's statements, not the application's own code: check whether it wraps every statement in a transaction of its own (each commit waits for the log to reach disk), and run the statements that belong together in one transaction.
check.heavy_query.fix.statistics_mainten: Check whether this was an automatic refresh or scheduled maintenance. Keep necessary statistics current; review an unnecessarily frequent schedule or full scan only with evidence of its cost.
check.heavy_query.fix.storage.compare: Compare physical reads and storage latency under representative load to distinguish slow I/O, a cold cache and repeated cache misses. The wait share alone does not establish eviction or insufficient memory. Check independent cache-pressure evidence before considering a memory or service-tier change.

check.last_actual_plans.info.description: SQL Server 2019+ can keep each query's last actual plan (LAST_QUERY_PLAN_STATS) and report live per-operator progress (LIGHTWEIGHT_QUERY_PROFILING).
check.last_actual_plans.info.title: Actual plans without re-running queries
check.last_actual_plans.last_query_plan_: Turn it on for this database.
Uses SQL Server's lightweight profiling to keep a little runtime data per cached plan: a small CPU overhead on very busy servers.

With LAST_QUERY_PLAN_STATS on, SQL Server can keep the real row counts and timings of an eligible cached query's most recent run. Complex or resource-intensive queries can then show where they actually spent their time, operator by operator, without running them again. Simple transactional queries may retain only the root operator; plans that aren't cached or have been evicted retain no last-run data. Without retained runtime data, the saved estimated plan cannot confirm a row misestimate.
LAST_QUERY_PLAN_STATS is off for this database
(Trace flag 2451 turns the same on for the whole server; if it is set, actual plans are kept already.)

Let the workload run, re-scan, then open a complex or resource-intensive query in {queries} and pick "{last_run}" when available: the diagram shows the rows and timings SQL Server retained. A simple query may have only a root operator, and an uncached or evicted plan has no last-run data.

check.lock_escalations.caveat.counted_si: SQL Server counts escalations over each index metadata entry’s lifetime, which can end without a server restart. Individual escalations are not dated.
check.lock_escalations.caveat.no_new_inc: These totals do not establish a new increase or continuing blocking in the selected window. Capture dated events or compare counters wholly within that period before treating this as current pressure.
check.lock_escalations.fix.loop_bulk: Change the statement that touches thousands of rows of {table} into smaller batches, for example up to 1,000 changed rows per statement, after checking its access path and lock footprint. A row limit does not bound all locks acquired or prevent escalation under lock-memory pressure. Use smaller transactions only where partial commits preserve the application's required atomicity. An UPDATE loop's filter must leave out rows already changed. A single enclosing transaction can retain locks until commit, so batching is no guarantee against a table lock. To be sure it is the one, start the event session below ({session}): it keeps each escalation with its statement, in memory, at almost no cost.
check.lock_escalations.fix.loop_history: If a statement still changes thousands of rows of {table} at once, change it into smaller batches, for example up to 1,000 changed rows per statement, after checking its access path and lock footprint. A row limit does not bound all locks acquired or prevent escalation under lock-memory pressure. Use smaller transactions only where partial commits preserve the application's required atomicity. An UPDATE loop's filter must leave out rows already changed. A single enclosing transaction can retain locks until commit, so batching is no guarantee against a table lock. To learn which statement it is, start the event session below ({session}): it keeps each escalation with its statement, in memory, at almost no cost.
check.lock_escalations.fix.loop_unknown: None of the statements in the query history changes thousands of rows of {table} at once, so the one that escalated is likely a job, a migration or maintenance. Once the event session below has caught it, change it into smaller batches, for example up to 1,000 changed rows per statement, after checking its access path and lock footprint. A row limit does not bound all locks acquired or prevent escalation under lock-memory pressure. Use smaller transactions only where partial commits preserve the application's required atomicity. An UPDATE loop's filter must leave out rows already changed. A single enclosing transaction can retain locks until commit, so batching is no guarantee against a table lock. check.log_volume.fix.batch_pages: Touch each page once per checkpoint: batch the changes (one statement for many rows, sorted by key) rather than many scattered single-row writes.
check.log_volume.fix.compress_images: Full-page images dominate and wal_compression is off: turning it on shrinks them (lz4 or zstd on PostgreSQL 15+). {how}
check.log_volume.fix.drop_unread: Every index on the table adds its own {log, select, wal {WAL} other {transaction log}}, and {table} has one nobody reads: drop it (see Indexes).
check.log_volume.fix.images_compressed: wal_compression already shrinks full-page images; a longer checkpoint interval (checkpoint_timeout, max_wal_size) logs fewer of them.
check.log_volume.fix.images_unknown: If full-page images dominate, a longer checkpoint interval (checkpoint_timeout, max_wal_size) logs fewer of them, and wal_compression shrinks them if it is off.
check.log_volume.fix.insert: An insert logs every row it adds in full, with an entry in each index: this much {log, select, wal {WAL} other {transaction log}} is this much data. Store less per row (large values compressed as they're written, or kept in object storage with a reference in the row), and commit many rows per transaction rather than one.

check.log_volume.fix.rewrite: Log this heavy usually means wide rows rewritten whole, many indexes updated, or one transaction per row. Batch writes into transactions of about a thousand rows, and update only the columns that change.
check.log_volume.info.description: Statements that write a large share of the WAL (PostgreSQL 13+) or transaction log (SQL Server 2017+), or many kilobytes of it per row changed. Log volume drives replication lag, backup size and checkpoints. MySQL keeps no redo bytes per statement.

check.logged_errors.fix.busy: Inspect transaction duration and retry outcomes on the application's own connections. Keep write transactions short and serialize writers where appropriate. Set a suitable busy handler on each application connection; changing Culprit's connection does not change the app.
check.logged_errors.fix.busy_snapshot: Roll back and retry the complete transaction with a fresh snapshot. If appropriate for its semantics, obtain the write transaction before reading (BEGIN IMMEDIATE). Do not retry only the failed statement inside the same obsolete snapshot.
check.logged_errors.fix.constraint: Check the constraint and caller's intended conflict behavior. Keep integrity checks; verify the application handles expected conflicts correctly before changing SQL or the schema.
check.logged_errors.fix.full: Check current filesystem headroom, database page limits and the application's storage quota. Restore capacity with the owner while preserving the database, WAL and a valid backup.
check.logged_errors.fix.locked: Inspect open statements and cursors on the application's connection, schema changes and any shared-cache use. Finalize or reset the conflicting statement when correct. A longer busy timeout does not resolve SQLITE_LOCKED; preserve transaction semantics when retrying.
check.logged_errors.fix.readonly: Check the application's open mode, filesystem access and WAL/sidecar access using its own process identity. Preserve intended read-only deployments.
check.logged_errors.fix.storage: Preserve the original files and logs. Investigate storage and restore/recovery options with the owner before any repair; use an appropriate backup and offline integrity investigation rather than rewriting the live file.
check.logged_errors.fix.unrecognized: Inspect the original error in the application's log, its transaction context and retry outcome. Measure a representative successful execution separately when timing is missing.
check.logged_errors.info.description: Recognized error codes in structured query logs, including errors with no duration. Counts describe log records, not failed business requests or zero-cost executions.
check.logged_errors.info.title: SQL errors recorded by the application
check.logged_errors.summary.durations: Missing durations are not counted as instant executions.
check.logged_errors.summary.records: These are records in the supplied log, which can include retries or duplicate logging.
check.logged_errors.title: {code} appears in {count} application log records
check.logged_errors.verify: Compare a fresh, dated log interval and application request/retry outcomes. Confirm the operation succeeds with its intended transaction semantics; old log records need not disappear.
check.logged_errors.why.busy: SQLite reported a conflicting connection or transaction. The caller may already retry successfully; these records do not establish failed user requests.
check.logged_errors.why.busy_snapshot: A read transaction could not upgrade its older WAL snapshot to a writer. Waiting longer cannot make that snapshot current.
check.logged_errors.why.constraint: A constraint rejected an operation. Some applications deliberately use this for uniqueness or conflict handling.
check.logged_errors.why.full: SQLite could not extend storage because a database or filesystem limit was reached. This is an observed error, not a claim that the limit is still reached now.
check.logged_errors.why.locked: SQLite reported a conflict within the connection or a shared-cache connection. This differs from ordinary cross-connection SQLITE_BUSY and can require finishing an outstanding statement.
check.logged_errors.why.readonly: The application's connection could not perform a write. Culprit's own read-only connection is separate.
check.logged_errors.why.storage: The application recorded a storage or database-integrity error. The log alone cannot establish its extent or whether recovery succeeded.
check.logged_errors.why.unrecognized: The log records a SQL error whose detailed code is not recognized. Its raw message and values were not retained.
check.memory_grant.fix: Fix the row estimate that sizes the grant: refresh statistics on the tables it reads and look in its plan for estimates far above actual rows. On SQL Server 2019+ (compatibility level 150+) memory grant feedback shrinks repeated grants by itself. As a stopgap, cap the grant on this statement.
check.memory_grant.info.description: Statements whose memory grant (reserved before they run, for sorts and hashes) is many times what they use, so other queries queue for memory.
check.memory_grant.info.title: Queries that reserve far more memory than they use
check.memory_grant.summary: Before each run SQL Server sets aside {granted} to sort and hash, sized by how many rows it expects; runs use {used} ({share}). While a run holds memory it doesn't use, other queries can queue for it (RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE). It ran {runs} times since its plan was cached; the largest grant was {largest}.

check.memory_grant.title.stopped: {query} reserved {granted} of memory per run and used {used}

check.memory_queue.fix.grants: Shrink the biggest over-sized grants first (see the memory-grant findings), then look at plans that sort or hash large scans. Raising max server memory, or the tier, treats the symptom.
check.memory_queue.fix.sample: Sample {waits} → {now} while it happens to see which wait it is. For grant waits (RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE), shrink the biggest over-sized grants (the memory-grant findings); for allocation waits (CMEMTHREAD), parameterize one-off statements so fewer compile, and keep parallelism in check.

check.memory_queue.summary.allocations: Grant waits (RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE) mean queries queue for memory to sort or hash; allocation waits (CMEMTHREAD) mean many sessions contend for one of the server's memory objects, often while compiling.
check.memory_queue.summary.grant_story: A query needs its memory grant to sort or hash before it starts; when the pool is spoken for, the rest wait. The usual cause is a few queries that reserve far more than they use.
check.memory_queue.summary.grants: {since}, this database's queries waited {time} for memory grants (RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE), about {per_hour} an hour on average; when isn't recorded.

check.memory_queue.summary.history_insta: Waits for memory are {share} of all waiting in {window}, about {per_hour} an hour, across every database on the instance. They include memory grants and memory allocations inside the server; the totals don't say which.

check.memory_queue.title.history: Waiting for memory takes {share} of all waiting (about {per_hour} an hour)
check.memory_queue.title.pending: {n, plural, one {{count} query in this database was} other {{count} queries in this database were}} waiting for a memory grant when the scan ran
check.memory_queue.verify: Re-scan, or sample {now} in {waits}: memory waits should fall under a minute an hour and nothing should be waiting for a grant.
