check.missing_index.fix.too_small_create: Create one only if the table grows past {rows} rows or these lookups come to take real time.
check.missing_index.fix.too_small_recons: Reconsider it only if the statements return and the optimizer asks again, and the table grows past {rows} rows or those lookups come to take real time.
check.missing_index.fix.too_small_servin: {index} already leads with {seeks}{filtered, select, yes {, for the rows where {filter}} other {}}.
check.missing_index.fix.widen_checks: {index} already finds these rows by {seeks}{filtered, select, yes {, in the rows where {filter}} other {}}: all the request asks for but {missing}. Widen it rather than add an index: with {add} included, it checks {missing} on the rows it finds without going back to the table, and there is one index fewer to maintain.
check.missing_index.fix.widen_covers: {index} already finds these rows by {seeks}{filtered, select, yes {, in the rows where {filter}} other {}}. Rebuild it with {add} included rather than add an index, so it covers {n, plural, one {the query below} other {the queries below}} without going back to the table.
check.missing_index.info.description: Index suggestions recorded by SQL Server's optimizer, merged with each other and checked against existing indexes.
check.missing_index.info.title: Missing indexes
check.missing_index.lately: None of {window} statements asked for it: SQL Server's optimizer last did {when}, {silence} before this scan's data ends, too short a time to say the statements that wanted it stopped.
check.missing_index.query_note.previous: Associated with a request made before the selected window; current query activity does not date that request.
check.missing_index.summary.asked: SQL Server's optimizer asked for an index on {table} ({keys}) {lookups} times {since}.
check.missing_index.summary.azure: Azure SQL's automatic tuning recommends the same index{scored, select, yes {, scoring it {score} out of 100} other {}}.
check.missing_index.summary.estimate: It {tense, select, past {estimated} other {estimates}} the index would make them about {percent}% cheaper.
check.missing_index.summary.literal_filt: It's a filtered index, and SQL Server uses one only for a query whose filter matches it as written: {n, plural, one {the query below compares} other {the queries below compare}} {columns} to a parameter, which could hold any value, so the optimizer can't use the index and asks for a new one instead.
check.missing_index.summary.literal_find: SQL Server's optimizer asked for an index on {table} ({keys}) {lookups} times {since}, but {index} ({index_keys}) already finds these rows where {literals} by {equality}, though not by {range}.
check.missing_index.summary.literal_serv: SQL Server's optimizer asked for an index on {table} ({keys}) {lookups} times {since}, but {index} ({index_keys}) already serves these lookups where {literals}.
check.missing_index.summary.no_query: None of the queries in this scan asked for it: the requests came from plans that ran before the scan's window, or that Query Store no longer keeps.
check.missing_index.summary.previous: SQL Server last requested this index {when}, before {window}. The {lookups} requests are cumulative {since}. Associated statements may still run, but their activity does not establish that this historical request is still needed in the selected period.
check.missing_index.summary.reads_more: Without it, each of those lookups {tense, select, past {read} other {reads}} more of {table}{counted, select, yes { ({rows} rows)} other {}} than it {tense, select, past {needed} other {needs}} to.
check.missing_index.summary.share: {n, plural, one {The query that asked for it {tense, select, past {accounted} other {accounts}}} other {The {n} queries that asked for it {tense, select, past {accounted} other {account}}}} for {share} of database time.
check.missing_index.title: {table} {tense, select, past {was} other {is}} searched by {keys} without a supporting index
check.missing_index.title.literal: {n, plural, one {A query on {table} passes {columns} as a parameter, so {index} can't serve it} other {{n} queries on {table} pass {columns} as a parameter, so {index} can't serve them}}
check.missing_index.title.previous: SQL Server previously requested an index on {table} ({keys})
check.missing_index.title.too_small: SQL Server {tense, select, past {asked} other {asks}} for an index on {table}, which is too small for one to pay off
check.missing_index.verify.candidate: Test the candidate index with representative parameters and load, then capture a newly compiled plan. Old stored suggestions need not disappear.
check.missing_index.verify.existing: Check whether newly compiled plans use {index}; an old stored suggestion alone does not establish a current gap.
check.missing_index.verify.literal: Change the query, let the workload run, then re-scan: this request disappears, and the query's plan seeks {index}.
check.missing_index.verify.literal_parti: Change the query, let the workload run, then re-scan: the query's plan seeks {index}, and if the optimizer still asks for an index, it's the one above.
check.missing_index.verify.previous: A later scan must show a new request inside its workload window and enough measured work before this becomes an index recommendation.
check.missing_index.verify.queries_use: Check whether the queries listed here use {index} and compare reads and execution time under equivalent parameters and load, including index storage and write cost.
check.missing_index.verify.queries_use_n: Check whether the queries listed here use the new index and compare reads and execution time under equivalent parameters and load, including index storage and write cost.
check.missing_index.verify.rebuilt: After testing the rebuild of {index}, capture a newly compiled plan under representative load. A stored suggestion can remain in old plan XML.
check.missing_index.verify.stopped: Nothing to check unless they come back: if the optimizer asks for this index again within a scan's window, this finding names the queries behind it and gives the index to create.
check.missing_index.verify.too_small: Nothing to check while it stays this small: once {table} holds {rows} rows or more, a scan says whether the index is worth creating.
check.multixact_age.fix: Inspect aggressive vacuum progress and transactions holding row locks, then vacuum the oldest affected tables under an operational plan. MultiXact cleanup differs from XID cleanup: replication slots do not directly retain MultiXacts, so removing slots is not a fix for this age.
check.multixact_age.fix_cost: Aggressive vacuum adds I/O and must finish to advance the oldest age; inspect locks and capacity before scheduling it.
check.multixact_age.info.description: The independent PostgreSQL MultiXact age limit, which can reject row-locking writes even when ordinary transaction ID age is healthy.
check.multixact_age.info.title: MultiXact wraparound risk
check.multixact_age.summary: MultiXact IDs track shared row locks and have their own wraparound limit, independent of ordinary transaction IDs. If vacuum cannot advance them, PostgreSQL eventually rejects writes that require a new MultiXact. A healthy XID-age result does not rule this out. This observation is the current age, not a forecast of time remaining.
check.multixact_age.title: MultiXact IDs are {age} old in {subject}
check.multixact_age.verify: Re-scan and confirm mxid_age(datminmxid) and the oldest tables' mxid_age(relminmxid) fall. Verify row-locking writes proceed and later vacuum cycles keep age controlled.
check.network_wait.fix: Return fewer rows (filter, or page with OFFSET/FETCH or keyset pagination), or read them faster: stream the results and do per-row work after the read, not while the result set is open.
check.network_wait.info.description: Queries that spend much of their time waiting for the application to take results (ASYNC_NETWORK_IO), usually because they return large result sets.
check.network_wait.info.title: Results the application reads slowly
check.network_wait.summary: SQL Server had its results ready but the application took them slowly (ASYNC_NETWORK_IO), so each run holds its locks and memory longer. That is {share} of this query's time. Usually the result set is bigger than needed, or the application does work for each row before reading the next.
check.network_wait.title.rows: {query} waits on the application {share} of its time while sending {rows} rows per call
check.network_wait.title.rows_stopped: {query} waited on the application {share} of its time while sending {rows} rows per call
check.network_wait.title.waited: {query} waited on the application {share} of its time
check.network_wait.title.waits: {query} waits on the application {share} of its time
check.network_wait.verify: Re-scan: this query's {results} (network) share should drop.
check.operational_errors.fix.archive: Check current archiver progress and server logs for the failure, archive destination capacity and access. Confirm retained WAL and backup/recovery requirements; never remove WAL files to clear the counter.
check.operational_errors.fix.checksum_fa: Inspect the server error log immediately to identify the affected relation or file, verify recent backups, and check underlying storage health before running repair or restore procedures.
check.operational_errors.fix.connection_: Inspect server connection logs and client configuration for bad credentials, TLS mismatches, connect_timeout settings, or health checks that close TCP sockets without completing the handshake.
check.operational_errors.fix.redo_waits: Compare counter growth, redo write/flush latency and representative write activity across the server. Inspect transaction size, log-buffer capacity and storage before testing a setting change; preserve durability requirements.
check.operational_errors.fix.standby_con: Correlate cancelled requests with recovery-conflict logs and query duration. Consider shorter reads or a suitable reporting replica; feedback and longer replay delays trade cancellations for primary bloat, retained WAL or replica lag.
check.operational_errors.fix.subscriptio: Inspect the subscription worker state and server log. Resolve the reported schema, constraint or data conflict with the replication owner, then verify apply resumes. Do not skip transactions without proving correctness.
Inspect subscription relation states and the worker's server-log error. Repair permissions, schema or capacity as indicated, then verify affected tables finish synchronization.
check.operational_errors.info.descriptio: WAL archive failures, logical subscription errors, standby recovery cancellations, InnoDB redo buffer waits, connection handshake failures, and storage page checksum or I/O corruption errors. Counter history is kept separate from newly observed errors.
check.operational_errors.info.title: Archive, replication and redo failures
check.operational_errors.label.checksum_: Data page checksum or I/O corruption
check.operational_errors.summary.corrupt: Any recorded page checksum or I/O corruption in this database warrants immediate investigation of the server error log and backups.
check.operational_errors.summary.history: No comparable counter interval inside the requested period establishes new failures; this is historical information.
check.operational_errors.summary.new: These are newly recorded events over the stated interval, not proof that the cause persists now.
check.operational_errors.summary.shared: It is context for the whole server and is not graded as a problem in this database.
check.operational_errors.verify: Compare two scans over a stated interval: new errors or waits should stop increasing, and the relevant worker/archive or application operations should succeed. Lifetime totals need not return to zero.
check.operational_errors.why.archive: {subject}: the archive command or library failed. This is a shared server counter, and a later successful archive may have resolved the incident.
check.operational_errors.why.checksum_fa: {subject}: the storage engine recorded data pages that failed checksum verification or suffered a torn-page / I/O read error in this database.
check.operational_errors.why.connection_: {subject}: clients attempted to connect to the server and failed during authentication, TLS negotiation or packet read (Aborted_connects). This is a shared server counter.
check.operational_errors.why.redo_waits: {subject}: InnoDB waited for redo buffer space to become available. This counter does not measure wait duration or prove that this database's requests were delayed.
check.operational_errors.why.standby_con: {subject}: recovery cancelled queries whose snapshots, locks or buffers conflicted with replay. This records actual cancellations, not ordinary replica lag or a claim that every read failed.
check.operational_errors.why.subscriptio: {subject}: the subscriber could not apply some incoming changes. Counters do not identify the conflicting row or establish that replication is still stopped.
{subject}: initial table synchronization failed. A retained error count does not establish that the table is still unsynchronized.
check.over_indexed.fix.drop_hidden: Drop the hidden or invalid indexes that writes still maintain.
check.over_indexed.fix.hide: Hide the indexes nothing reads first (reversible), then drop them after a business cycle.
check.over_indexed.fix.review: Review which queries need each index; fold indexes that share a leading column into one.
check.over_indexed.info.description: Tables with many secondary indexes that are written a lot: every insert updates each index.
check.over_indexed.info.title: Many indexes on write-heavy tables
check.over_indexed.summary.all_read: All of them are read, so trim only after checking which queries rely on each.
check.over_indexed.summary.idle: {count} of them ({indexes}) are never read or duplicated by another; start there.
check.over_indexed.summary.one_idle: {index} of them is never read or duplicated by another; start there.
check.over_indexed.summary.upkeep_change: Every insert into {table} updates all {count} secondary indexes, and every update touching their columns updates them too: up to {how_many}.
check.over_indexed.summary.upkeep_entrie: Every insert into {table} adds an entry to all {count} secondary indexes, and so does every update that isn't HOT (HOT updates change no indexed column and stay on their page): up to {how_many}.
check.over_indexed.summary.upkeep_statem: Every insert into {table} updates all {count} secondary indexes, and every update touching their columns updates them too: {how_many}, each one doing that for every row it changes.
check.over_indexed.title: {table} has {count} indexes and gets {how_many}
check.over_indexed.verify: Write latency on {table} drops; the reads that used the hidden indexes stay as fast.
check.overlapping_index.caveat.covers: {index} may cover columns {wider} lacks; a query that only reads it for those columns would need a key lookup instead.
check.overlapping_index.fix: Find the queries that read {index} and check their plans against {wider}; if they seek it just as well, hide {index} first and drop it after a business cycle.
check.overlapping_index.fix_cost: Frees {size} and one index's worth of work on every write.
check.overlapping_index.info.description: Two indexes that lead with the same column where one is barely read and the other holds all its key columns: queries that use the first can seek the second and filter the rest there.
check.overlapping_index.info.title: Overlapping indexes
check.overlapping_index.summary.keys: {index} ({keys}) and {wider} ({wider_keys}) both lead with {lead} on {table}, and the second has every key column of the first among its keys.
check.overlapping_index.summary.reads: {index} was read {n, plural, one {once} other {{reads} times}} {since}, {wider} {wider_n, plural, one {once} other {{wider_reads} times}}.
check.overlapping_index.summary.seek: Queries that use the first can seek the second on {lead} and filter the rest inside it, while every write to {table} keeps both up to date.
check.overlapping_index.title: {index} is barely read next to {wider}, which also starts with {lead}
check.overlapping_index.verify: After hiding {index}, the queries on {table} keep their speed and {wider}'s reads grow by about {reads}.
check.parameter_sensitive.cost.force: Forcing a plan pins it for every value until you unforce it: try a value from a slow call under it first.
check.parameter_sensitive.cost.recompile: RECOMPILE spends a compile on every call.
RECOMPILE spends a compile on every call (about {each} each).
RECOMPILE spends a compile on every call: about {each} each, {total} over its {runs} runs in {window}, more than the {slow} its slow calls cost, so it comes last.
check.parameter_sensitive.fix.ladder: Pick the lightest option that works: {options}. Each is reversible.
check.parameter_sensitive.fix.locks: The slow runs mostly wait for row locks.
check.parameter_sensitive.fix.locks_shor: Keep the transactions that touch these rows short.
check.parameter_sensitive.fix.mariadb: Compare a slow and a fast value with ANALYZE (outside production). If some values match far more rows, an index that narrows them, or a histogram on the uneven column, lets MariaDB choose a better plan for each.
check.parameter_sensitive.fix.mysql: Compare a slow and a fast value with EXPLAIN ANALYZE (outside production). If some values match far more rows, an index that narrows them, or a histogram on the uneven column, lets MySQL choose a better plan for each.
check.parameter_sensitive.fix.postgres: First see what differs: plan the statement with a value from a slow call and one from a fast call. If a generic plan is reused for very different values, plan per call for the application's role; if one column's values are very uneven, give the planner finer statistics for it.
check.parameter_sensitive.info.descripti: Statements whose run time depends heavily on the values they run with: two plans used side by side, one fast and one slow (SQL Server Query Store), or a long tail in the run-time histogram (MySQL). Single-plan variance on any engine is `unstable-query`.
check.parameter_sensitive.info.title: Queries that are fast for most calls and slow for some
check.parameter_sensitive.option.force: force the plan most calls run fast with
check.parameter_sensitive.option.psp: let SQL Server keep several plans
check.parameter_sensitive.option.recompi: plan per call for this statement only
check.parameter_sensitive.source.log_eve: The slow query log's runs of this statement (it keeps every run)
check.parameter_sensitive.source.log_kep: Of the runs of this statement the slow query log kept (only those over long_query_time, so faster runs aren't counted)
Of the runs of this statement the slow query log kept (only those over long_query_time, {threshold}, so faster runs aren't counted)
check.parameter_sensitive.summary.plans: SQL Server runs this statement with {plans} plans side by side. Plan {fast} handles {fast_calls} of the calls and averages {fast_ms}{fast_compiled}; plan {slow} averages {slow_ms}{slow_compiled} and handled {slow_calls} calls.
check.parameter_sensitive.summary.plans_: SQL Server runs this statement with {plans} plans side by side. {fast_plans} plans that average {fast_ms} or less handle {fast_calls} of the calls (plan {busiest} the most, {busiest_calls} of them at {busiest_ms}{busiest_compiled}); plan {slow} averages {slow_ms}{slow_compiled} and handled {slow_calls} calls.
A plan is compiled for the parameter values of the call that happened to compile it, then reused for every other value, so values that need a different strategy get the wrong one.
check.parameter_sensitive.summary.tail: {source}: half finished within {typical}, the slowest took {slowest}.
check.parameter_sensitive.summary.tail_l: {share} of its time is spent waiting for locks, so start with what holds them (the fix says how to find it).
check.parameter_sensitive.summary.tail_p: {source}: half finished within {typical}, 99 in 100 within {p99}, the slowest took {slowest}.
check.parameter_sensitive.summary.tail_w: {server} plans every call afresh, so slow calls usually touch far more rows for some values (skewed data) or wait for locks.
check.parameter_sensitive.title.plans: {query} {tense, select, past {ran} other {runs}} in {fast} for most calls but {slow} for {share} of them
check.parameter_sensitive.title.plans_or: {query} {tense, select, past {ran} other {runs}} in {fast} or less for most calls but {slow} for {share} of them
check.parameter_sensitive.title.tail: {query} {tense, select, past {usually took} other {usually takes}} {typical} but {share} of its runs {tense, select, past {took} other {take}} over {slow}
check.parameter_sensitive.title.tail_log: Logged runs of {query} {tense, select, past {usually took} other {usually take}} {typical} but {share} of them {tense, select, past {took} other {take}} over {slow}
check.parameter_sensitive.title.tail_p99: {query} {tense, select, past {usually took} other {usually takes}} {typical} but 1 in 100 {tense, select, past {took} other {takes}} over {p99}
Logged runs of {query} {tense, select, past {usually took} other {usually take}} {typical} but 1 in 100 {tense, select, past {took} other {takes}} over {p99}
check.parameter_sensitive.verify.compare: Run the statement with a value from a slow call and one from a fast call and compare the plans (Editor → Explain, or Analyze outside production).
check.parameter_sensitive.verify.rescan: Re-scan after the change: {queries} → {spread} should show the slow lane gone or close to the fast one.
check.plan_insights.caveat.estimated: Based on the estimated plan; actual row counts can tell a different story.
check.plan_insights.info.description: Key lookups, functions on filtered columns, leading wildcards, NOT IN, scalar functions, eager spools, misestimates and repeated loops in the plans of queries that matter.
check.plan_insights.info.title: Plan insights
check.plan_insights.summary.shared: The same problem shows up in {count} queries that together take {share} of database time.
check.plan_regression.caveat.force_failu: A forced plan can fail to apply after schema changes; Query Store reports that in sys.query_store_plan.last_force_failure_reason_desc.
check.plan_regression.fix.force: Force the fast plan now to stop the bleeding, then find out why the optimizer changed its mind (statistics, parameter values, schema). Unforce once the cause is fixed.
check.plan_regression.fix.not_forced_yet: It hasn't forced plan {plan} for this one so far.
check.plan_regression.fix.table_gone: {table} is no longer in the catalog, so the statement can't run as it was, and plan {plan} can't be forced onto it: a forced plan that names a table or an index that is gone fails to apply. Nothing to force; if a statement on the table that replaced it is slow, its own findings say so.
check.plan_regression.info.description: Queries whose current plan is much slower than a plan they used before.
check.plan_regression.info.title: Plan regressions
check.plan_regression.summary.running: Query Store saw this query run with plan {fast} at {fast_ms} on average until {until}, and with plan {slow} at {slow_ms} since {since} ({runs} runs). The plan choice changed, typically after a statistics update, a schema change or a recompile with unusual parameter values.
check.plan_regression.summary.stopped: Query Store saw this query run with plan {fast} at {fast_ms} on average until {until}, and with plan {slow} at {slow_ms} {span} ({runs} runs). The plan choice changed, typically after a statistics update, a schema change or a recompile with unusual parameter values.
check.plan_regression.timeline.running: Query Store saw {named, select, yes {query {query}} other {this query}} run with plan {fast} at {fast_ms} on average until {until}, and with plan {slow} at {slow_ms} since {since} ({runs} runs).
check.plan_regression.timeline.stopped: Query Store saw {named, select, yes {query {query}} other {this query}} run with plan {fast} at {fast_ms} on average until {until}, and with plan {slow} at {slow_ms} {span} ({runs} runs).
check.plan_regression.title: {query} got {factor} slower after its plan changed
check.plan_regression.verify.force: The query's average duration in Query Store should return to the fast plan's level within an interval or two.
check.plan_regression.verify.table_gone: Nothing to check unless the statement runs again.
check.plan_warnings.fix.cross_join: Make sure the cross join is intended and both inputs stay small.
check.plan_warnings.fix.join_dropped: Nothing to change while both inputs keep few rows. If the plan multiplies many rows, check the join columns and the filters on them in the plan.
check.plan_warnings.fix.join_missing: Check the query's joins and add the missing condition.
check.plan_warnings.fix.spill.mssql: Update statistics on the tables involved; if the estimate is still far off, add an index that delivers rows in the needed order so the sort disappears.
check.plan_warnings.fix.spill.mysql: Raise tmp_table_size and max_heap_table_size for this workload so the temporary table stays in memory, or add an index that returns rows already ordered or grouped.
check.plan_warnings.fix.spill.postgres: Raise work_mem for this workload (per role or per session), or add an index that delivers rows in the needed order so the sort disappears.
check.plan_warnings.fix.spill.sqlite: Give the sort an index that returns rows in the order asked for; otherwise PRAGMA temp_store = MEMORY keeps temporary b-trees in memory, and a larger cache_size helps them fit.
check.plan_warnings.fix.statistics: Inspect current column statistics and automatic statistics settings, then compare a newly compiled plan before choosing a statistics change.
check.plan_warnings.info.description: Implicit conversions, spills, missing join predicates and missing statistics in the plans of heavy queries.
check.plan_warnings.info.title: Plan warnings
check.plan_warnings.statistics.table_the: The table held {then} when this plan was compiled.
The table held {then} when this plan was compiled, and holds {now} now.
check.plan_warnings.statistics.updated: The statistics of {index} were last updated on {date}.
check.plan_warnings.statistics.updated_c: The statistics of {index} were last updated on {date}, and have counted {changes} since.
check.plan_warnings.statistics.updated_r: The statistics of {index} were last updated on {date}, when the table had {rows}.
The statistics of {index} were last updated on {date}, when the table had {rows}, and have counted {changes} since.
The statistics of {index} were last updated on {date}, when the table had {rows}, with no changes counted since.
check.plan_warnings.statistics.updated_u: The statistics of {index} were last updated on {date}, with no changes counted since.
check.plan_warnings.summary.blocks_seek: SQL Server warns that the conversion keeps it from searching an index, so it reads every row instead.
check.plan_warnings.summary.convert: The database has to convert {column} before comparing it with a parameter of a different type.
check.plan_warnings.summary.convert_expr: The database has to convert {column} before comparing it with a parameter of a different type (`{expression}`).
check.plan_warnings.summary.cross_join: Part of this plan combines every row of one input with every row of another, and the statement asks for it (CROSS JOIN or CROSS APPLY). That multiplies rows: fine for a small list of values, costly for two large tables.
check.plan_warnings.summary.estimates: SQL Server warns that the conversion may affect its row estimates, which can lead it to a poorer plan; it doesn't say an index can't be used.
check.plan_warnings.summary.join_dropped: Part of this plan combines every row of one input with every row of another, though the statement does join them. {engine} does this when both join columns are compared with the same value (a.x = @v AND a.x = b.x): it filters each side by the value and drops the join condition as redundant. That is harmless while both sides keep few rows.
check.plan_warnings.summary.join_missing: Part of this plan combines every row of one input with every row of another (a cross join), and the statement has no condition joining them: no ON clause and no comparison of one table's column with another's. A missing join condition multiplies the rows the query reads and returns.
check.plan_warnings.summary.parameters: The application declares its parameters as `{parameters}`.
check.plan_warnings.summary.parameters_u: The application declares its parameters as `{parameters}`: Unicode strings compared with a non-Unicode column.
check.plan_warnings.summary.shared: The same mismatch appears in {count} queries that together take {share} of database time.
check.plan_warnings.summary.spill: A sort or hash in this plan needed more memory than it was granted and wrote the overflow to disk (tempdb or temp files). Spills usually come from a row estimate that was far too low, or a sort the index could have avoided.
check.plan_warnings.summary.statistics: SQL Server reported unavailable statistics at compilation time. The saved warning alone does not establish missing or stale statistics now, or a slow plan.
check.plan_warnings.summary.unicode: This often happens when an application sends strings as nvarchar (Unicode) to a varchar column.
check.plan_warnings.title.conversion: A type mismatch on {column} {tense, select, past {slowed} other {slows}} down {query}
check.plan_warnings.title.conversion_sto: A type mismatch on {column} {tense, select, past {stopped} other {stops}} {query} from seeking an index
check.plan_warnings.title.conversion_unk: A type mismatch {tense, select, past {slowed} other {slows}} down {query}
check.plan_warnings.title.cross_join: {query} {tense, select, past {asked} other {asks}} for a cross join
check.plan_warnings.title.join_dropped: {query}'s plan {tense, select, past {joined} other {joins}} two inputs without a join condition
check.plan_warnings.title.join_missing: {query} {tense, select, past {joined} other {joins}} tables without a join condition
check.plan_warnings.title.shared: A type mismatch on {column} {tense, select, past {slowed} other {slows}} down {count} queries
check.plan_warnings.title.shared_stops_s: A type mismatch on {column} {tense, select, past {stopped} other {stops}} {count} queries from seeking an index
check.plan_warnings.title.spill: {query} {tense, select, past {ran out of memory and spilled} other {runs out of memory and spills}} to disk
check.plan_warnings.title.statistics: The captured plan for {query} reported a statistics warning
check.plan_warnings.title.statistics_on: The captured plan for {query} reported a statistics warning on {columns}
check.plan_warnings.verify.rescan: Re-scan after the change; the warning should be gone from this query's plan.
check.plan_warnings.verify.statistics: Capture a newly compiled plan after any justified statistics change and compare its warning and estimates with representative runs. Query Store may retain the original XML, so a re-scan of that saved plan alone cannot verify the change.
check.planning_time.caveat.query_store: This Query Store entry's first compile falls within the selected period, so its compile totals can be compared with its runs in that period. Older entries' compile totals are shown separately as retained query history.
check.planning_time.fix.every_run: It compiles on every run: look for OPTION (RECOMPILE), a procedure created WITH RECOMPILE, or literal values in the text instead of parameters (sp_executesql with parameters reuses one plan). Forced parameterization reuses plans for statements that differ only in literals, for the whole database: test it first.
check.planning_time.fix.prepare: Prepare it once and reuse it: most drivers do when you bind parameters (pgjdbc prepareThreshold, Npgsql Max Auto Prepare, psycopg prepare=True). Behind PgBouncer in transaction mode, prepared statements need 1.21+ with max_prepared_statements set. If planning stays slow when reused, look at the number of joins and partitions it touches.
check.planning_time.fix.recompile_hint: Test removing OPTION (RECOMPILE) from this statement so SQL Server can reuse a plan. Compare representative parameter values, including those that need different plans: keep the hint if the extra runtime from reuse costs more than the compiles it saves. Forced parameterization does not override this hint.
check.planning_time.fix.slow_compiles: Plans are reused but each compile is slow: simplify the statement (fewer joins and views), or keep its plan with a Query Store hint or plan forcing so it isn't recompiled after statistics change.
check.planning_time.info.description: Statements where planning (PostgreSQL, with pg_stat_statements.track_planning on) or compiling (SQL Server Query Store) takes a large part of their time, usually because the plan isn't reused.
check.planning_time.info.title: Queries that spend their time being planned
check.planning_time.summary.every_run: Each {work, select, plan {plan} other {compile}} takes {per_plan} and the statement then runs for {run}: {share} of its time goes to {work, select, plan {planning} other {compiling}}, {plan_ms} {ran} (a new plan for every run). Planning gets expensive with many joins, partitions or large statistics targets, and it repeats when the plan isn't reused.
check.planning_time.summary.recompile_hi: Its OPTION (RECOMPILE) hint explicitly asks SQL Server for a new plan on every run.
check.planning_time.summary.reused: Each {work, select, plan {plan} other {compile}} takes {per_plan} and the statement then runs for {run}: {share} of its time goes to {work, select, plan {planning} other {compiling}}, {plan_ms} {ran} (a plan reused about {reuses} times). Planning gets expensive with many joins, partitions or large statistics targets, and it repeats when the plan isn't reused.
check.planning_time.title: {work, select, plan {Planning} other {Compiling}} {tense, select, past {took} other {takes}} {share} of the time of {handle}
check.planning_time.verify.between_scans: Between two scans, its planning time per run should drop: {source} keeps running totals, so compare its planning time and runs in a scan taken once the change is live and one a day or more later ({now} in this scan).
check.planning_time.verify.now: {plan_ms} over {n, plural, one {{runs} run} other {{runs} runs}}
check.planning_time.verify.recompile_hin: Compare compiles per run and planning time per run before and after, and check that time per run stays acceptable across representative parameter values. The rewritten statement has a new entry.
check.planning_time.verify.rescan: Re-scan: planning should be a small part of its time.
check.query_family.caveat.inferred: Culprit sees one of these statements' text, so what the others differ in is inferred from it.
check.query_family.fix.declarations: Declare each string parameter with a fixed size, the column's length, instead of letting the driver size it from the value (in ADO.NET, set SqlParameter.Size or use Add with a SqlDbType and size rather than AddWithValue; other drivers have a similar setting). Then one plan serves every value. Forced parameterization can't help: these statements are already parameterized.
check.query_family.fix.declarations_quot: In the code that sends this statement (one copy is quoted below, as recorded), declare each string parameter with a fixed size, the column's length, instead of letting the driver size it from the value (in ADO.NET, set SqlParameter.Size or use Add with a SqlDbType and size rather than AddWithValue; other drivers have a similar setting). Then one plan serves every value. Forced parameterization can't help: these statements are already parameterized.
check.query_family.fix.literals: Send values as parameters (sp_executesql, or your driver's parameterized queries) so one plan serves every value. If you can't change the app, forced parameterization does it for the whole database.
check.query_family.fix.literals_quoted: In the code that sends this statement (one copy is quoted below, as recorded), send values as parameters (sp_executesql, or your driver's parameterized queries) so one plan serves every value. If you can't change the app, forced parameterization does it for the whole database.
check.query_family.fix.value_lists: Pass value lists as one array parameter (`= ANY($1)` in Postgres) instead of a growing IN list, and batch multi-row inserts with UNNEST or COPY.
check.query_family.fix.value_lists_quote: In the code that sends this statement (one copy is quoted below, as recorded), pass value lists as one array parameter (`= ANY($1)` in Postgres) instead of a growing IN list, and batch multi-row inserts with UNNEST or COPY.
check.query_family.fix_cost.literals: Forced parameterization can make some queries pick a plan that suits one value badly (parameter sensitivity); watch the regression findings after switching.
check.query_family.info.description: The same statement sent many times with different literal values (or value-list lengths), so the database compiles and tracks each copy separately; and plan caches filled with single-use plans.
check.query_family.info.title: Statements with literals baked in
check.query_family.plan_cache.fix.parame: Parameterize the statements behind it (see the families above).
check.query_family.plan_cache.fix.stub: Keep only a stub for a plan's first use, and parameterize the statements behind it.
check.query_family.plan_cache.metric.sin: Ad hoc entries with one lookup
check.query_family.plan_cache.summary: {plans} ad hoc cache entries have one recorded lookup and occupy memory that could hold data pages or reusable plans.
check.query_family.plan_cache.summary_ad: 'Optimize for ad hoc workloads' is off. Enabling it stores a small stub on a plan's first use.
check.query_family.plan_cache.title: Ad hoc plans with one lookup fill {share} of the cache ({size})
check.query_family.plan_cache.verify: Re-scan after a day: ad hoc entries with one lookup take a smaller share of the cache.
check.query_family.summary.declarations: {variants} variants of the same statement ran {executions} times{timed, select, yes { for {share} of database time} other {}}, because their parameters are declared differently from call to call ({declarations}): drivers do this when a string parameter's size comes from each value (ADO.NET's AddWithValue, for one). SQL Server compiles and keeps a plan for each declaration{cached, select, yes { ({cache} of plan cache)} other {}}.
check.query_family.summary.literals: {variants} variants of the same statement ran {executions} times{timed, select, yes { for {share} of database time} other {}}, so SQL Server compiles each one separately and keeps a plan for each{cached, select, yes { ({cache} of plan cache)} other {}}.
check.query_family.summary.statistics_sp: Statistics split across the copies too, so none of them looks as heavy as the statement really is.
check.query_family.summary.value_lists: {variants} variants of the same statement ran {executions} times{timed, select, yes { for {share} of database time} other {}}, because its value lists (IN lists, multi-row VALUES) have different lengths; each length is planned and counted on its own{cached, select, yes { ({cache} of plan cache)} other {}}.
check.query_family.title.declarations: The app sends {count} versions of {statement} that differ only in how their parameters are declared
check.query_family.title.literals: The app sends {count} versions of {statement} that differ only in literal values
check.query_family.verify.entries_kept: After a deploy, no new copies should appear: pg_stat_statements keeps an entry for each copy until it evicts it or its statistics are reset, so compare the family's copies in a scan taken when the change ships and one a day or more later ({count} in this scan): the count should stay as it is, or fall.
check.query_family.verify.shrinks: Re-scan after a deploy: this family shrinks to one or a few statements.
check.regression.caveat.restarted: {server} started {when}, just before it got slower: the first hours after a start read from disk what was in memory before. If it stays slow once the cache is warm, it's a real change.
check.regression.caveat.scans: Culprit built this trend from its own scans. Each point covers the time between two scans, so the start time is only as precise as how often you scan.
check.regression.fix.compare_plans: The plan changed when it got slower. Compare the two plans (Queries → Plans), refresh statistics on the tables it reads, and check the parameter values the slow runs use.
check.regression.fix.find_change: Find what changed {when}: a deploy touching this statement, its parameters or its indexes; data growth in the tables it reads; a statistics update; or blocking (Live shows current waits). Open the query to compare its plan with what you expect.
check.regression.fix.force: Force plan {plan} to stop the bleeding, then find out why the optimizer switched (statistics, parameter values, schema). Unforce once the cause is fixed.
check.regression.info.description: Queries whose runs became much slower at some point in the window, with when it started and whether a plan change coincides. Needs Query Store history or a few earlier scans.
check.regression.info.title: Queries that got slower
check.regression.summary.no_new_plan: No new plan started when it got slower, so look at what else changed then: a deploy that changed this statement or its parameters, a jump in data volume, a statistics update, or new blocking.
check.regression.summary.per_day: Until {until} it averaged {before} per run; since then {after}, over {runs} runs: about {extra} of extra {time} a day.
check.regression.summary.plan_change: Plan {new} first ran {first} and averages {new_ms}; plan {old} averaged {old_ms}.
check.regression.summary.plan_unknown: This scan does not establish which plan the earlier and later runs used, so a plan change remains possible. Compare plans and parameter values, and check for changed data volume, statistics, blocking or application code around that time.
check.regression.summary.total: Until {until} it averaged {before} per run; since then {after}, over {runs} runs: {extra} of extra {time} in {span}.
check.regression.timeline.per_day: Query Store's timeline: until {until} it averaged {before} per run; since then {after}, over {runs} runs: about {extra} of extra {time} a day.
check.regression.timeline.total: Query Store's timeline: until {until} it averaged {before} per run; since then {after}, over {runs} runs: {extra} of extra {time} in {span}.
check.regression.title: {query} got {factor} slower {when}
check.regression.title.plan_changed: {query} got {factor} slower {when}, when its plan changed
check.regression.verify: Re-scan after the fix: this query's trend in Queries should drop back to about {before} per run.
check.repeated_request.fix: Inspect the caller for the correlated request groups. If it loads one object at a time unnecessarily, test a set-based query or appropriate eager loading while preserving ordering, permissions, limits and result semantics. Keep required batches and retries; SQLite's embedded calls have no server network round trip.
check.repeated_request.info.description: Repeated SQL shapes correlated by explicit request_id in structured logs. Repetition identifies a caller to inspect; it does not prove an N+1 bug or removable work.
check.repeated_request.info.title: Repeated statements within logged requests
check.repeated_request.summary.correlate: Explicit request_id values correlate this statement with {requests} recorded requests; one contains {calls} timed SQL records.
check.repeated_request.summary.hashed: Request identifiers are hashed during reading and are not stored in the report.
check.repeated_request.summary.not_proof: Repeated per-object loads, intentional batches or retries can explain this. The log does not prove an N+1 bug, network round trips or redundant work.
check.repeated_request.summary.truncated: Request counting reached its bounded sample limit; these counts are a lower bound.
check.repeated_request.title: The same statement repeats at least 10 times in {requests} logged requests
check.repeated_request.verify: Compare equivalent request groups before and after: unnecessary SQL records and total time should fall while results, permission boundaries and retry correctness remain the same.
check.replica_lag.fix.behind: Split large write transactions into batches, check the replica's storage and CPU, and move long reports off it or let them run against a snapshot.
check.replica_lag.fix.cap: To keep any slot from filling the disk, cap what slots may keep: {how}
check.replica_lag.fix.cap_from_13: PostgreSQL 13 and later can cap what slots keep (max_slot_wal_keep_size).
check.replica_lag.fix.cap_if_unset: If max_slot_wal_keep_size isn't set, cap what slots may keep so none can fill the disk: {how}
check.replica_lag.fix.consumer_behind: Look at the consumer, not this server: the subscriber's apply worker (pg_stat_subscription and its log) or the CDC connector's lag and errors. Split very large transactions so changes flow in smaller pieces.
check.replica_lag.fix.left_configured: If it is no longer a replica, remove the configuration with RESET REPLICA ALL (RESET SLAVE ALL before MySQL 8.0.22 and MariaDB 10.5.1). If it should replicate, make it read-only and START REPLICA.
check.replica_lag.fix.logical_slot: Find its consumer first: the slot's name and plugin usually say which subscription or connector it is. If it still syncs, leave the slot: it catches up when the consumer connects. If the consumer is gone for good, drop it.
check.replica_lag.fix.physical_slot: If nothing will stream through this slot again (a standby that was removed), drop it.
check.replica_lag.fix.stopped: Find why it stopped (the replica's error log, network, disk space), fix it, and let it catch up before relying on it.
check.replica_lag.fix.stopped_by_hand: If it should replicate, START REPLICA and let it catch up before relying on it; if it is no longer a replica, RESET REPLICA ALL removes the configuration.
check.replica_lag.fix.stopped_mysql: Read the full error with SHOW REPLICA STATUS on the replica, fix its cause, then START REPLICA.
check.replica_lag.info.description: Replicas far behind the primary or stopped, and PostgreSQL replication slots that keep WAL for a consumer that's gone: pg_stat_replication, availability group replica states, SHOW REPLICA STATUS.
check.replica_lag.info.title: Replicas that fall behind
check.replica_lag.metric.wal_left: WAL left before it is given up
check.replica_lag.summary.behind: Reads from the replica return data {lag} old, and failing over now would lose or wait for that much. Lag grows when the replica applies changes slower than the primary writes them: large transactions, long queries on the replica, or slower storage.
check.replica_lag.summary.behind_replay: Reads from the replica return data {lag} old, and failing over now would lose or wait for that much. Lag grows when the replica applies changes slower than the primary writes them: large transactions, long queries on the replica (which can pause replay), or slower storage.
check.replica_lag.summary.consumer_behin: {name} receives this database's changes through logical decoding: a subscription, or a CDC tool such as Debezium. It has confirmed changes only up to {lag} ago, so whatever it feeds sees data that old, and its slot keeps the WAL since then on this server. A consumer falls behind when it applies changes slower than this server writes them: one very large transaction, a slow destination, or a connector that is throttled or failing.
check.replica_lag.summary.delayed: It is also set up to apply changes {delay} late on purpose ({setting}); that part isn't counted.
check.replica_lag.summary.left_configure: Both replication threads are off and no error is recorded, so someone stopped them, and this server takes writes (read_only is off). A former replica promoted to primary looks like this: its old replication settings stay behind, and starting them by mistake would apply another server's changes on top of this one's.
check.replica_lag.summary.no_receiver: This standby is set up to stream from its primary (primary_conninfo is set) but no WAL receiver is running, so it isn't getting changes: its data is getting older by the minute and failing over to it now would lose them.
check.replica_lag.summary.slot_cannot_ca: Before PostgreSQL 13 nothing can cap it: it grows until the disk fills and the server stops accepting writes.
check.replica_lag.summary.slot_cap_unkno: Unless max_slot_wal_keep_size caps what slots keep, it grows until the disk fills and the server stops accepting writes.
check.replica_lag.summary.slot_capped: max_slot_wal_keep_size caps what it can keep: {left} more WAL and PostgreSQL gives the slot up, so the disk is safe, but its consumer then has to start over.
check.replica_lag.summary.slot_idle_for: A replication slot keeps every WAL file its consumer hasn't confirmed. {name} has had no consumer for {idle}, so the WAL it holds keeps growing.
check.replica_lag.summary.slot_logical: It is a logical slot: a subscription or a CDC tool (Debezium, Fivetran, Airbyte…) reads changes through it, and many connect only between syncs. Dropping it makes that consumer copy everything again.
check.replica_lag.summary.slot_no_consum: A replication slot keeps every WAL file its consumer hasn't confirmed. {name} has no consumer connected, so the WAL it holds keeps growing.
check.replica_lag.summary.slot_physical: It is a physical slot: a standby or a backup tool streams WAL through it.
check.replica_lag.summary.slot_uncapped: Nothing caps what it keeps (max_slot_wal_keep_size is -1), so it grows until the disk fills and the server stops accepting writes.
check.replica_lag.summary.stopped: The copy no longer keeps up, so its data is getting older by the minute and failing over to it now would lose changes.
check.replica_lag.summary.stopped_by_han: Both replication threads are off and no error is recorded: someone ran STOP REPLICA, for a backup or maintenance perhaps. While it stays stopped the copy gets older by the minute, and failing over to it would lose the changes since.
check.replica_lag.title.left_configured: This server is still set up as a replica, but replication isn't running
check.replica_lag.title.logical_slot: The logical slot {name} keeps {kept} of WAL while its consumer is away
check.replica_lag.title.physical_slot: The inactive replication slot {name} keeps {kept} of WAL
check.replica_lag.title.stopped_by_hand: Replication to this server was stopped by hand
check.replica_lag.title.stopped_consumer: The logical consumer {name} isn't receiving changes ({state})
check.replica_lag.title.stopped_this_ser: Replication to this server has stopped ({state})
check.replica_lag.title.this_server_behi: This server is {lag} behind its primary
check.replica_lag.verify.lag: Re-scan: the lag should be seconds.
check.replica_lag.verify.left_configured: Re-scan: the leftover replication configuration should be gone.
check.replica_lag.verify.logical_slot: Re-scan once the consumer has synced: the WAL kept should drop, or the slot be gone.
check.replica_lag.verify.physical_slot: Re-scan: the slot should be gone, or active again.
check.row_lock_waits.caveat.server_wide: {engine} counts row-lock waits for the whole server, so other databases' waits are in these numbers.
check.row_lock_waits.fix: Keep transactions short (no user input or slow calls inside them), make UPDATE and DELETE filter on indexed columns, and touch tables in the same order everywhere. Live shows who blocks whom right now.
check.row_lock_waits.info.description: InnoDB row-lock waits add up to real time (a minute an hour or more across the server), from long transactions or updates that scan instead of using an index.
check.row_lock_waits.info.title: Transactions waiting for row locks
check.row_lock_waits.summary.causes: Lock waits grow with long transactions, and with UPDATE or DELETE statements whose filter isn't indexed: they lock every row they scan.
check.row_lock_waits.summary.longest: In this database, {query} waited longest on locks ({time} in total).
check.row_lock_waits.summary.waits: {since}, InnoDB made transactions across the whole server (it counts every database together) wait for row locks {count} times, {total} in all and about {average} each: about {per_hour} an hour on average; the counters don't say when.
check.row_lock_waits.summary.waits_share: {since}, InnoDB made transactions across the whole server (it counts every database together) wait for row locks {count} times, {total} in all and about {average} each: about {per_hour} an hour on average, against {share} of statement time an hour in this database; the counters don't say when.
check.row_lock_waits.title: Transactions on this server waited {total} for row locks {since}, {average} each on average
check.row_lock_waits.verify: Sample {waits} → {now} during normal load: it counts row-lock waits over the sample, which should be rare and short.
check.scan_heavy.caveat.counters: Counters accumulate since statistics were last reset; one nightly report can make up much of them.
check.scan_heavy.fix.listed: Explain the statements listed with this finding{generic, select, yes { (Culprit can show a generic plan, which does not measure actual rows)} other {}} to check their access paths.
check.scan_heavy.fix.measure: To measure each filter, capture an actual plan with representative values in a controlled environment: this runs the statement. Compare rows kept with rows read. If a filter keeps at most {share} of the rows read, consider an index on the columns it searches by; if it keeps more, read fewer rows or columns instead. Small lookup tables are fine to scan.
check.scan_heavy.fix.unlisted: Find the statements that read it in full (they aren't among the heaviest this scan captured), explain them{generic, select, yes { (Culprit can show a generic plan, which does not measure actual rows)} other {}} to check their access paths.
check.scan_heavy.info.description: Large tables that queries read in full many times a day, from the table scan counters.
check.scan_heavy.info.title: Tables read in full over and over
check.scan_heavy.metric.rows_read_per_da: Rows read without an index per day
check.scan_heavy.shown.both: by their plans, or by the rows they examine a run
check.scan_heavy.shown.many_rows: each examines half its rows or more a run
check.scan_heavy.shown.rows: it examines {rows} rows a run, about the whole table
check.scan_heavy.summary.proven: {proven, plural, one {{proven} of the captured statements reads it in full ({shown}); explain it} other {{proven} of the captured statements read it in full ({shown}); explain them}} to check the access path, then measure rows kept in representative runs.
check.scan_heavy.summary.proven_and_unpl: {proven, plural, one {{proven} of the captured statements reads it in full} other {{proven} of the captured statements read it in full}} ({shown}), and {unplanned} more without a captured plan may; explain them to check the access path, then measure rows kept in representative runs.
check.scan_heavy.summary.read: {table} has {rows} rows, and queries have read all of it {how_many}: {rows_read} rows read without an index.
check.scan_heavy.summary.read_per_day: {table} has {rows} rows, and queries have read all of it {how_many} {since}: {rows_read} rows a day read without an index.
check.scan_heavy.summary.rest_elsewhere: The rest come from statements outside the top of the workload.
check.scan_heavy.summary.through_index: The captured statements that name it reach it through an index, so the full reads come from statements outside the top of the workload.
check.scan_heavy.summary.unnamed: None of the captured statements names it, so the scans come from statements outside the top of the workload.
check.scan_heavy.summary.unplanned: {unplanned, plural, one {{unplanned} of the captured statements reads or changes it without a captured plan; explain it to see whether it reads it in full.} other {{unplanned} of the captured statements read or change it without a captured plan; explain them to see whether they read it in full.}}
check.scan_heavy.summary.whole_many: {count} statements with no WHERE clause (queries {ids}) read it in full too, on purpose: no index on a filter changes that.
check.scan_heavy.summary.whole_one: {handle} (query {id}) reads it in full too, on purpose: it has no WHERE clause, so no index on a filter changes that.
check.scan_heavy.title.counted: {table} {tense, select, past {was} other {is}} read in full {how_many} ({rows_read} rows)
check.scan_heavy.title.per_day: {table} {tense, select, past {was} other {is}} read in full {how_many} ({rows_read} rows a day)
check.scan_heavy.verify.cheaper: {n, plural, one {its time per run should drop} other {their time per run should drop}}
check.scan_heavy.verify.counters: After adding an index for a selective filter, the full reads of {table} should grow far slower. Compare how much its scan counters grow between a scan taken once the change is live and one a day or more later ({full_reads} full reads in this scan).
check.scan_heavy.verify.counters_with_in: After adding an index for a selective filter, the full reads of {table} should grow far slower. Compare how much its scan counters grow between a scan taken once the change is live and one a day or more later ({full_reads} full reads and {index_scans} index scans in this scan).
check.scan_heavy.verify.either_fix: Whether the fix adds an index or reads fewer rows or columns: {verify}
check.scan_heavy.verify.rescan: Re-scan after the workload has run: {n, plural, one {its time per run should drop} other {their time per run should drop}}.
check.sequence_capacity.fix: Plan a migration to a larger numeric range, including referencing columns, constraints, indexes and application types. Validate cache/increment behavior and rollout locking first. Do not reseed, restart or enable cycling without proving values cannot collide.
check.sequence_capacity.fix_cost: Changing column types and dependent keys may rewrite data and require locks; plan and test the migration.
check.sequence_capacity.info.description: Non-cycling identities, sequences and auto-increment columns approaching their numeric bounds; cache allocation is not a forecast of remaining requests.
check.sequence_capacity.info.title: Identity and sequence allocation limits
check.sequence_capacity.int32.fix: Plan a multi-step migration of {table}.{column} (and any foreign-key columns referencing it) to 64-bit `bigint` before the 32-bit range is exhausted.
check.sequence_capacity.int32.fix_cost: Widening a primary key column to bigint rewrites the table or requires a dual-column backfill and swap.
check.sequence_capacity.int32.summary: Primary key {table}.{column} is declared as `{data_type}` (signed 32-bit maximum 2,147,483,647) and {table} already holds {rows} live rows. Once the sequence or auto-increment counter reaches 2,147,483,647 — which happens earlier than the live row count when rows have been deleted or sequence caches skipped values — every new INSERT into {table} fails with an integer overflow error.
check.sequence_capacity.int32.title: {table}.{column} is a 32-bit integer primary key on a {rows}-row table
check.sequence_capacity.int32.verify: Re-scan after migrating {table}.{column} to `bigint`: its type is `bigint` and this finding is gone.
check.sequence_capacity.summary.allocate: The source may record reserved cache space or the next auto-increment value rather than the last value returned to a caller.
check.sequence_capacity.summary.not_a_fo: Caching, skipped values and per-connection allocation rules mean this is not the number of application requests left or a time-to-failure estimate. Reaching the bound can reject inserts or allocations; reusing old numbers can violate uniqueness.
check.sequence_capacity.summary.observed: This is the allocation state observed by the source.
check.sequence_capacity.summary.recorded: The recorded value is {current}, increment {increment}, with bounds {minimum} to {maximum} and cycling off.
check.sequence_capacity.title: {name} is near its numeric limit ({steps} recorded steps remain)
check.sequence_capacity.verify: Check the new type and allocation bounds, confirm foreign keys and application values remain compatible, and verify inserts or sequence allocations under representative load.
check.slow_storage.caveat.historical: Historical averages: a slow hour long ago still counts, and a later scan does not isolate new operations without comparing counter differences.
check.slow_storage.caveat.shared: Historical file statistics do not establish that this database's queries are slow now; check the stated source scope and measure recent operations alongside query waits.
check.slow_storage.fix.azure_sql_databas: In Azure SQL Database the service tier decides this: General Purpose reads from remote storage (5 to 10 ms is normal there), Hyperscale serves most reads from a local cache and the rest from page servers, Business Critical uses local SSDs. Check avg_data_io_percent and avg_log_write_percent in sys.dm_db_resource_stats: near 100% means the tier's I/O limit is throttling, so add vCores or move to a faster tier; well below it, cut the reads instead (indexes, fewer full scans). A since-startup average hides bursts: sample {waits} → {now} during the busy hour.
check.slow_storage.fix.managed_instance: On Managed Instance General Purpose each data and log file is a remote disk whose IOPS and throughput come from the file's size (up to 128 GB about 500 IOPS, up to 512 GB about 2,300, up to 1 TB 5,000): growing a busy file past the next size step raises its limit, and the next-gen General Purpose tier sets IOPS apart from size. Business Critical uses local SSDs. Compare each file's latency in sys.dm_io_virtual_file_stats with its size, and cut the reads too (indexes, fewer full scans). A since-startup average hides bursts: sample {waits} → {now} during the busy hour.
check.slow_storage.fix.volume: Check the volume's limits first: cloud disks throttle at their provisioned IOPS and throughput, and burst credits run out. Then look for other load on the same disk and antivirus scanning data files, and give the log its own low-latency volume. A since-startup average hides bursts: sample {waits} → {now} during the busy hour.

check.table_bloat.fix.vacuum: Vacuum it: VACUUM clears the dead rows without blocking reads or writes, and new rows then reuse their space. Make autovacuum visit it sooner so they don't pile up again. Rewrite the table (pg_repack online, VACUUM FULL offline) only if the estimate stays high after a vacuum.

Validation can issue distributed scans and acquire locks. It fails if a row breaks a constraint; fix those rows first. Do not assume PostgreSQL lock or concurrent-write guarantees.
check.untrusted_constraint.impact.not_va: {n, plural, one {{count} not validated} other {{count} not validated}}
check.untrusted_constraint.info.descript: SQL Server foreign keys and check constraints added or re-enabled WITH NOCHECK (or switched off), PostgreSQL CHECK constraints added NOT VALID, and YugabyteDB CHECK or foreign-key constraints awaiting validation.
check.untrusted_constraint.info.title: Unvalidated or disabled constraints
check.untrusted_constraint.summary.data_: {names} {n, plural, one {was} other {were}} added NOT VALID: PostgreSQL checks new and changed rows against {n, plural, one {it} other {them}} but never checked the rows that existed then, so some may break {n, plural, one {it} other {them}}. That is often deliberate: NOT VALID adds a constraint without a long scan under lock. The planner doesn't read it here either way (constraint exclusion looks at CHECK constraints only on inheritance children unless constraint_exclusion is on). Validating proves the old rows, and lets later steps skip their own full scan: SET NOT NULL (12+) and ATTACH PARTITION when the constraint implies them.
check.untrusted_constraint.summary.defer: {names} {n, plural, one {was} other {were}} added NOT VALID. YugabyteDB checks new and changed rows but has not checked the rows that existed when these constraints were added. Some old rows may violate them. Deferred validation can be deliberate during a migration; this catalog state does not establish a query-plan regression.
check.untrusted_constraint.summary.noche: {names} {n, plural, one {was} other {were}} created or re-enabled WITH NOCHECK, so existing rows were never checked against {n, plural, one {it} other {them}}. The optimizer only relies on trusted constraints: it can't remove a join to the referenced table when no columns from it are used, or rule out values a check constraint excludes, so it plans work it could skip.
check.untrusted_constraint.summary.plann: {names} {n, plural, one {was} other {were}} added NOT VALID, so rows that existed then were never checked. Until it is validated the planner can't use it to skip the table when a query's filter contradicts it (constraint exclusion, which it applies to this inheritance child).

{names} {n, plural, one {was} other {were}} added NOT VALID, so rows that existed then were never checked. Until it is validated the planner can't use it to skip the table when a query's filter contradicts it (constraint exclusion, which constraint_exclusion = on applies to every table).
check.untrusted_constraint.summary.switc: A switched-off constraint doesn't check new rows either, so the data may already break it.

check.worker_pressure.fix.mysql: Size the application's connection pools to what the server can run (a few per core), close idle sessions, and use ProxySQL or the cloud proxy if many clients connect. Raise max_connections only with memory to spare.
check.worker_pressure.fix.postgres: Put a connection pooler in front (PgBouncer, or the application's pool with a smaller maximum) and close idle sessions. Raise max_connections only with memory to spare (it needs a restart).
check.worker_pressure.fix.threadpool: Find the head blocker in Live and end the transaction behind the chain; then lower parallelism so each query takes fewer workers (cost threshold for parallelism, MAXDOP). Raising max worker threads only hides it.

common.widen_index.clustered: {index} is the table's clustered index: it already holds every column, so there is nothing to include in it.
common.widen_index.cost: The index grows from {size}; writes that touch the included columns maintain it.
common.widen_index.disabled: {index} has the right keys but is disabled, so SQL Server neither maintains nor reads it. Rebuilding it brings it back, with {columns} included so it covers the query; if it was disabled because nothing read it, the queries below now would.
common.widen_index.held: {index} already has these keys and includes {columns}.
common.widen_index.keeps: The statement keeps its keys, their order, its filter and the columns it already includes; restate DATA_COMPRESSION, FILLFACTOR or its partition scheme in it if the index uses them.
common.widen_index.lookups: {index} already has the right keys but makes every matching row go back to the table for {columns}. Rebuild it with those columns included so it covers the query.
common.widen_index.no_include: {engine} has no included columns: an index there holds only its keys.
common.widen_index.postgres: PostgreSQL can't add included columns to {index} in place; a new index has to be built.
common.widen_index.primary_key: {index} enforces the primary key, and SQL Server won't change a constraint's index to include columns.
common.widen_index.unique: It stays unique. If {index} enforces a UNIQUE constraint rather than being a unique index, SQL Server refuses the rebuild (error 1907): create a separate index with these keys and included columns instead.
common.widen_index.yugabyte: YSQL cannot add included columns to {index} in place; build a separate covering index and verify its distributed cost.
common.write_cost.none: {table} received no writes {since}, so {index} would cost next to nothing to maintain.
common.write_cost.none_maybe_reset: {table} had no writes in what its counters cover, which may be short: performance_schema's counters start over when they are reset, and a weekly job may not have run since; each write it gets will also update {index}.
common.write_cost.none_too_short: {table} had no writes in the {span} its counters cover, too short to say it gets none (a weekly job may not have run yet); each write it gets will also update {index}.
common.write_cost.some: {table} receives {how_many}; each one will also update {index}.
core.blocking.advice.idle: Session {head} isn't running anything but still holds locks, typically from a transaction the client never finished. Ending it releases them.
core.blocking.advice.idle_in_transaction: The application opened a transaction and stopped sending statements: usually a missing COMMIT, an error path that skips the ROLLBACK, or slow work (an HTTP call, a user prompt) done while the transaction is open. Ending session {head} rolls its transaction back and frees everyone behind it.
core.blocking.advice.prevent.mssql: SET XACT_ABORT ON in the application makes an error roll the transaction back instead of leaving it open.
core.blocking.advice.prevent.mysql: Keep transactions short; waiters give up after innodb_lock_wait_timeout (50 s by default).
core.blocking.advice.prevent.postgres: Set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout so the server ends sessions that sit in a transaction.
core.blocking.advice.prevent.sqlite: Keep write transactions short: SQLite allows one writer at a time, and the others wait busy_timeout, then fail with SQLITE_BUSY.
core.blocking.advice.readers_rcsi: The waiters only want to read: with READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT on, readers use row versions and stop waiting on writers.
core.blocking.advice.running: A long statement is holding locks the others need. Look at its plan in Queries, and keep the transaction around it short: do reads and outside calls before it starts.
core.blocking.advice.unknown: The blocker belongs to another database or a login Culprit can't see; ask someone with VIEW SERVER STATE (or pg_read_all_stats / PROCESS) to look.

core.deadlock.explanation.cycle: Each transaction holds a lock the next one needs. Consistent access order and shorter transactions break most cycles.
core.deadlock.explanation.key_lookup: The read finds rows through {index} and then looks each one up in the table's main index; the write changes the main index first and then {index}. Each ends up holding the lock the other needs next. It recurs whenever the two statements touch the same rows at the same time.
core.deadlock.explanation.key_lookup_unn: The read finds rows through a secondary index and then looks each one up in the table's main index; the write changes the main index first and then the secondary index. Each ends up holding the lock the other needs next. It recurs whenever the two statements touch the same rows at the same time.
core.deadlock.explanation.lock_conversio: Both took a shared lock to read, then asked for an exclusive lock to write. A shared lock lets the other reader in, so neither can upgrade: whoever asks second deadlocks. Typical of 'read, check, then update' code.
core.deadlock.explanation.lock_escalatio: SQL Server turned thousands of row locks into one lock on the whole table to save memory. That table lock blocks everyone touching the table, so an otherwise harmless overlap became a cycle.
core.deadlock.explanation.opposite_order: Each transaction locked one thing and then wanted what the other had already locked. With the same order in both, the second would simply wait instead of deadlocking.
{story}. With the same order in both, the second would simply wait instead of deadlocking.
core.deadlock.explanation.parallelism: Threads of the same parallel plan exchange rows and waited on each other. These are usually a symptom of a plan that goes parallel when it shouldn't (a scan that an index would avoid).
core.deadlock.fix.fewer_rows.detail: Modify in batches (for example 2,000 rows at a time) and index the WHERE columns, so SQL Server keeps row locks instead of locking the whole table.
core.deadlock.fix.fewer_rows.title: Change fewer rows per statement
core.deadlock.fix.parallel_plan.detail: Find the query in Queries: usually a scan an index would avoid. As a stopgap, OPTION (MAXDOP 1) on that query, or raise cost threshold for parallelism if it is still 5.
core.deadlock.fix.parallel_plan.title: Fix the plan that goes parallel
core.deadlock.fix.primary_key.detail: Look up the primary key values first, then update or lock by primary key, so both statements lock the main index in the same order.
core.deadlock.fix.primary_key.title: Change rows through the primary key
core.deadlock.fix.rcsi.alternative: let reads stop taking shared locks
core.deadlock.fix.rcsi.detail: With READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT on, reads use row versions instead of shared locks, so a read can't be part of this cycle. It costs some tempdb space for the versions.
core.deadlock.fix.rcsi.title: Let reads stop taking shared locks
core.deadlock.fix.retry.detail_code: A deadlock victim can be retried safely; the application should catch {code} and run the transaction again.
core.deadlock.fix.retry.detail_error: A deadlock victim can be retried safely; the application should catch error {error} and run the transaction again.
core.deadlock.fix.retry.title: Retry the victim
core.deadlock.fix.same_order.detail: Make every code path that changes {tables} do it in one order (for example, always the parent row first, and rows sorted by key). Then the second transaction waits instead of deadlocking.
core.deadlock.fix.same_order.title: Touch tables and rows in the same order everywhere
core.deadlock.fix.short_transactions.det: Do reads, validation and outside calls before the transaction starts; hold locks only for the writes.
core.deadlock.fix.skip_lookup.detail: Add the columns the read needs to {index} (as INCLUDE columns) so it never touches the main index the write locks. The query's plan in Queries shows the Key Lookup and its output columns.
core.deadlock.fix.skip_lookup.detail_unn: Add the columns the read needs to the index it seeks (as INCLUDE columns) so it never touches the main index the write locks. The query's plan in Queries shows the Key Lookup and its output columns.
core.deadlock.fix.skip_lookup.title: Make the read skip the lookup
core.deadlock.fix.write_lock.alternative: take the write lock when you read
core.deadlock.fix.write_lock.detail: Read the rows you are about to change with an update lock, or do the check and the change in one UPDATE … WHERE statement.
core.deadlock.fix.write_lock.title: Take the write lock when you read

core.deadlock.headline.opposite_order_vi: Two transactions locked {tables} in opposite order and waited on each other; {victim}'s transaction was rolled back.
core.deadlock.headline.parallelism: A parallel query deadlocked with its own threads; SQL Server broke the cycle, but the query lost time.
