core.engines.mssql.accepts: An ADO.NET connection string, an mssql:// or JDBC URL, or host,port/database. Azure SQL without a user name signs in with your az login (Entra ID).
core.engines.mssql.errors_note: Query Store counts errors but doesn't keep them; the finding shows how to capture them.
core.engines.mssql.index_advice_sources: This login can't read SQL Server's missing-index requests (VIEW DATABASE STATE), so candidates come from captured plans and foreign keys only.
core.engines.mssql.limitation.estimated_: An estimated or stored compilation plan does not measure the rows, timing or waits of the run you are investigating. Runtime-only problems require recorded runtime evidence or an explicitly measured run.
core.engines.mssql.limitation.host: Host CPU and filesystem capacity need their own measurements, such as connected cloud telemetry. Backup recoverability and database corruption are not checked by the statistics scan; they need backup/recovery validation and an appropriate integrity investigation.
core.engines.mssql.limitation.query_stor: Query Store records aggregate executions and plan history, not an application's request trace or every parameter value. Caller identity and transaction boundaries need application telemetry.
core.engines.mssql.refresh_statistics.co: Reads a sample of the table; run it outside peak hours on very large tables.
core.engines.mssql.refresh_statistics.su: Update the statistics now; if this table changes fast, schedule the update in a maintenance job.
core.engines.mssql.runtime_cache_note: The plan cache keeps the fastest and slowest run of each cached plan since it was cached, not their spread: Query Store would add it.
core.engines.mssql.runtime_note: Query Store keeps the fastest and slowest run and the spread of every plan, and each plan's compiled parameter values.
core.engines.mssql.session_advice: The driver or the connection pool sends this around the application's statements, not the application's own code: a pooled connection returns to the login's defaults each time it is reused (sp_reset_connection), so options set per session are sent again on every checkout. Set them once instead: as the database's or the login's defaults, or in the connection string where the driver allows.
core.engines.mssql.unused_index: Disable first: the definition stays, nothing reads it, and `ALTER INDEX … REBUILD` brings it back. Drop it after a full business cycle without complaints.
core.engines.mssql.wait_not_per_statemen: Query Store didn't record this wait for individual queries in the window.
core.engines.mysql.accepts: A mysql://, mariadb:// or JDBC URL, a .NET connection string (Server=…;Uid=…), or host:port/database.
core.engines.mysql.change_setting.global: Set {name} to {value} now, and in the server's option file (my.cnf) so it survives a restart.
core.engines.mysql.change_setting.persis: Set {name} to {value}; SET PERSIST keeps it across restarts.
core.engines.mysql.deadlocks: InnoDB keeps only its most recent deadlock. Turn on innodb_print_all_deadlocks to write every one to the error log.
{server} doesn't record missing-index requests. Candidates come from the plans of logged statements and foreign keys; performance_schema would add rows read without an index.
{server} doesn't record missing-index requests. Candidates come from captured plans, foreign keys, and rows read without an index (performance_schema).
core.engines.mysql.limitation.digests: Statement digests keep aggregate totals, not an application's request trace, transaction boundaries or the plan of every historical execution. Culprit compares only intervals its scans or the slow log record.
core.engines.mysql.limitation.innodb_sta: InnoDB status keeps only the latest deadlock. A complete incident history requires the error log; an empty or old latest report does not prove that no other deadlocks happened.
core.engines.mysql.limitation.products: MySQL and MariaDB differ in plan details, instrumentation and syntax. Runtime measurements, metadata-lock visibility and replication diagnostics depend on the product, version and permissions.
core.engines.mysql.missing_costs_note: {engine} keeps no planning time or redo bytes per statement.
core.engines.mysql.plan_format: EXPLAIN FORMAT=JSON, EXPLAIN ANALYZE or FORMAT=TREE
core.engines.mysql.refusal.last_actual_p: MySQL and MariaDB don't keep the actual plan of past runs
Measure it instead: Analyze runs the statement's recorded text once inside a read-only transaction.
core.engines.mysql.refusal.operator_prog: MySQL reports a running statement's progress, not each step's
core.engines.mysql.runtime_histogram_not: {engine} keeps a run-time histogram per statement, so the bars show how many runs took how long.
core.engines.mysql.runtime_note: This {engine} scan includes no run-time histogram; the lane shows fastest, average and slowest. Histogram availability depends on the product, server version and collection permissions; the slow query log can add individual logged runs.
core.engines.mysql.unused_index.ignored: Have the optimizer ignore it first: it stays maintained, and `ALTER INDEX … NOT IGNORED` brings it back instantly. Drop it after a full business cycle without complaints.
core.engines.mysql.unused_index.invisibl: Make it invisible first: the optimizer stops using it but it stays maintained, and `ALTER INDEX … VISIBLE` brings it back instantly. Drop it after a full business cycle without complaints.
core.engines.mysql.unused_index.mariadb_: Save its definition, then drop it: this MariaDB version can't hide an index (ignored indexes arrived in 10.6).
core.engines.mysql.unused_index.mysql_ca: Save its definition, then drop it: MySQL 5.7 can't hide an index (invisible indexes arrived in 8.0).
core.engines.mysql.unused_index.unknown_: Save its definition before dropping it. Index-hiding support is not established for this server version.
core.engines.mysql.wait_not_per_statemen: {server} doesn't attribute this wait to statements; it is a server-wide total.
No statement recorded this in performance_schema.
core.engines.pg_stat_statements.missing_: {engine} keeps no error count or lock time per statement; Live shows blocking as it happens.
core.engines.pg_stat_statements.runtime_: {engine} keeps one fastest, average, slowest and spread per statement: enough to see a long tail, not which values caused it.
core.engines.postgres.accepts: A postgres:// or JDBC URL, libpq's key=value pairs, an Npgsql connection string, or host:port/database.
core.engines.postgres.change_setting: Set {name} to {value} and reload the configuration (settings marked as needing a restart take effect after one).
core.engines.postgres.database_setting: Set {name} to {value} for this database only, as its owner: sessions that connect after the change use it, and other databases on the server keep theirs.
core.engines.postgres.deadlocks: PostgreSQL keeps a cumulative deadlock count in SQL, but the graphs and statements are only in the server log. Import the relevant log entries to explain the pattern. Turning on log_lock_waits also logs waits longer than deadlock_timeout.
core.engines.postgres.index_advice_sourc: PostgreSQL doesn't record missing-index requests. Candidates come from captured plans that read whole tables, foreign keys, and the table scan counters.
core.engines.postgres.limitation.generic: A newly obtained generic plan uses this connection's role, settings and search path; it may differ from the application's custom plan. Actual rows, spills and timing require a measured plan.
core.engines.postgres.limitation.logs: Deadlock graphs, statement errors and auto_explain output live in server logs. SQL counters alone cannot reconstruct them; import the relevant logs or correlate application telemetry.
core.engines.postgres.limitation.pg_stat: pg_stat_statements keeps aggregate totals, not per-request traces, historical parameter values or the plan used by each execution. Culprit's scans provide comparisons only over their recorded intervals.
core.engines.postgres.plan_format: EXPLAIN or EXPLAIN ANALYZE, as text or FORMAT JSON
core.engines.postgres.refresh_statistics: ANALYZE reads a sample of the table and does not block reads or writes.
Analyze the table now. If autovacuum falls behind on it regularly, lower its analyze threshold for this table only.
core.engines.postgres.refusal.last_actua: PostgreSQL doesn't keep the actual plan of past runs
auto_explain can write them to the server log, which Culprit can't read over SQL. Open the query in the editor with real values and use Analyze: it runs inside a transaction that is rolled back.
core.engines.postgres.refusal.operator_p: PostgreSQL reports a running statement's progress, not each step's
core.engines.postgres.session_reset: This resets session state and is commonly sent by a driver or connection pool; the statement statistics do not identify its caller or pooling mode. Inspect the application's connection lifecycle and the driver or pool configuration, and benchmark any change against the measured absolute cost shown here. Keep resets that prevent session state leaking between users. Npgsql arranges its reset on close and sends it on reuse; PgBouncer normally resets on release in session pooling, and normally does not in transaction pooling. Consider changing reset behavior only after verifying that every caller safely handles retained session state.
core.engines.postgres.timescale_plan_for: PostgreSQL EXPLAIN, including hypertable and chunk operators
core.engines.postgres.unused_index.concu: Drop it concurrently so writes aren't blocked. Save the definition first so you can recreate it.
core.engines.postgres.unused_index.hyper: Save the definition first so you can recreate it. TimescaleDB does not support dropping hypertable indexes concurrently; schedule the drop for a maintenance window.
core.engines.postgres.wait_not_per_state: PostgreSQL doesn't time this per statement. {now} samples what sessions wait on.
core.engines.refusal.cant: {engine} can't do this ({ability, select, sessions {sessions} wait_sample {wait sample} deadlocks {deadlocks} measures_runs {measures runs} plan_estimates {plan estimates} writes {writes} periods {periods} last_actual_plan {last actual plan} operator_progress {operator progress} sign_in {sign in} other {{ability}}})
core.engines.refusal.operator_progress_h: Its plan doesn't change while it runs: ask for the plan once.
core.engines.runtime_note: The scan includes aggregate run-time statistics rather than individual execution traces.
core.engines.sqlite.accepts: The database file. Culprit opens it read-only and needs nothing from your app.
core.engines.sqlite.change_setting: Set {name} to {value} with PRAGMA. If it is a per-connection pragma, the application has to set it each time it opens the file.
core.engines.sqlite.index_advice_sources: SQLite doesn't record missing-index requests. Candidates come from the indexes it builds for itself on every run of the logged statements, and foreign keys.

SQLite keeps no history of the statements it ran, so candidates come from foreign keys only. With the application's query log on the connection, the indexes SQLite builds for itself on every run join them.
core.engines.sqlite.limitation.access_pa: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN records access paths, not estimated or measured rows, costs or timing. Query durations and errors require a supported application log; request traces need request identifiers in that telemetry.
core.engines.sqlite.limitation.connectio: SQLite file inspection cannot see the application's connections, transaction owners, foreign_keys, busy_timeout or synchronous settings. Configure and inspect those on the application's own connections.
core.engines.sqlite.limitation.library: Plans are obtained with Culprit's SQLite library, which may differ from the application's version, modules or build options. Logged placeholders are planned with NULL values, so value-dependent access paths may differ.
core.engines.sqlite.limitation.wal: A WAL file can retain allocated space after checkpointing. Its size or growth alone does not establish checkpoint starvation or identify a reader holding a snapshot.
core.engines.sqlite.plan_format: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN, as the sqlite3 shell prints it
core.engines.sqlite.refresh_statistics.c: ANALYZE reads the indexes and briefly takes the write lock to store what it found.
core.engines.sqlite.refresh_statistics.s: Run ANALYZE, so the planner knows each table's size and how selective each index is.
core.engines.sqlite.refusal.deadlocks: SQLite records no deadlocks: one writer at a time holds the file
core.engines.sqlite.refusal.deadlocks_hi: A transaction that can't get the write lock waits busy_timeout, then gets SQLITE_BUSY in the application: its logs say when.
core.engines.sqlite.refusal.periods: SQLite keeps no statement history to compare two periods of
core.engines.sqlite.refusal.periods_hint: Add the log your framework writes to the connection, scan before and after the change, and compare the two reports' queries.
core.engines.sqlite.refusal.plans: SQLite's plans have no actual rows or timings: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN shows the access path only
core.engines.sqlite.refusal.plans_hint: Use the estimated plan; time the statement in the application to see how long it takes.
core.engines.sqlite.refusal.sessions: SQLite has no server, so no sessions to show
core.engines.sqlite.refusal.sessions_hin: A writer that has to wait gets SQLITE_BUSY in the application: its logs say when.
core.engines.sqlite.refusal.sign_in: A SQLite file takes no sign-in: Culprit opens it read-only from disk
core.engines.sqlite.refusal.wait_sample: SQLite has no server, so nothing records what it waits on
core.engines.sqlite.refusal.wait_sample_: Time spent waiting for the write lock shows up in the application as SQLITE_BUSY or slow commits.
core.engines.sqlite.refusal.writes: Culprit opens SQLite files read-only, so it never changes one
core.engines.sqlite.refusal.writes_hint: Run it with the sqlite3 shell or from the application, then scan again to see the effect.
core.engines.sqlite.runtime_note: SQLite keeps no run times; these come from the query log Culprit read, one entry per logged run.
core.engines.sqlite.unused_index: Drop it: SQLite can't hide an index first, so keep its CREATE INDEX statement to put it back if a query slows down.
core.engines.yugabyte.accepts: A YSQL postgres:// or yugabyte:// URL, libpq parameters, or host:port/database.
core.engines.yugabyte.change_setting: Configure the supported YSQL or DocDB parameter {name} through YugabyteDB's administration tools; review its scope and restart requirements.
core.engines.yugabyte.database_setting: Set {name} for new YSQL connections to this database.
core.engines.yugabyte.deadlocks: DocDB's distributed deadlock detection is not PostgreSQL's heap lock accounting. A PostgreSQL deadlock counter does not establish this database's distributed deadlocks.
core.engines.yugabyte.index_advice_sourc: Without statement statistics, candidates come from foreign keys and the index catalog.
Candidates come from YSQL plans, the index catalog and foreign keys; DocDB does not publish missing-index requests.
core.engines.yugabyte.limitation.generic: Captured generic plans use this login's current role and settings. Actual DocDB RPCs and rows scanned require EXPLAIN ANALYZE with DIST.
core.engines.yugabyte.limitation.nodes: Local statistics cover the connected YB-TServer. Configured cluster views add other nodes; skipped nodes and independent counter resets prevent complete comparisons.
core.engines.yugabyte.limitation.shardin: An index's sharding keys affect distributed reads and write hotspots. Suggested ordered keys use explicit ASC/DESC; review partitioning before deployment.
core.engines.yugabyte.limitation.storage: YSQL uses DocDB/RocksDB over Raft. PostgreSQL heap pages, buffer-cache ratios, dead tuples, vacuum and XID ages are not storage measurements here.
core.engines.yugabyte.plan_format: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, DIST, FORMAT JSON), including DocDB storage metrics
core.engines.yugabyte.refresh_statistics: ANALYZE samples table data and can issue distributed reads.
Refresh YSQL's optimizer statistics. This does not vacuum or compact DocDB storage.
core.engines.yugabyte.refusal.deadlocks_: Correlate YSQL errors and the YB-TServer logs for the affected transaction.
core.engines.yugabyte.refusal.last_actua: YSQL statement totals do not retain the measured plan of every past execution
Analyze a representative statement to capture its actual DocDB work.
core.engines.yugabyte.refusal.operator_p: YSQL does not expose live row counters for every plan operator
Use a measured plan and native statement/operation progress.
core.engines.yugabyte.refusal.other: {ability, select, sessions {{engine} cannot provide sessions} wait_sample {{engine} cannot provide wait samples} deadlocks {{engine} cannot provide deadlocks} measures_runs {{engine} cannot provide measured runs} plan_estimates {{engine} cannot provide plan estimates} writes {{engine} cannot provide writes} periods {{engine} cannot provide periods} last_actual_plan {{engine} cannot provide the last actual plan} operator_progress {{engine} cannot provide operator progress} sign_in {{engine} cannot provide sign-in} other {{engine} cannot provide this capability}}
core.engines.yugabyte.runtime_note: YSQL keeps aggregate run-time statistics in the recorded node or cluster scope. Their spread does not identify which parameter values, tablets, RPCs or retries caused slow runs.
core.engines.yugabyte.session_target: Select a node-qualified YSQL session from Live
core.engines.yugabyte.unused_index: Save its native definition and sharding keys before dropping it. Check a complete cluster-wide business cycle of usage, and measure the affected queries after the change.
core.engines.yugabyte.wait_not_per_state: DocDB RPC and storage wait timings may overlap; they are not exclusive shares of statement execution time. Use their native metrics or sample active sessions.

core.plan.too_deep: The plan nests its steps more than {depth} deep, deeper than a saved scan can hold
core.plan_compare.conversion.cause: This usually means the application sent the parameter with a different type (e.g. nvarchar for a varchar column).
core.plan_compare.conversion.detail: A converted column can't be searched through its index, so the plan reads every entry instead.
core.plan_compare.conversion.title: {plan} converts a column's type before comparing it; {other} doesn't.
core.plan_compare.estimates.compiled_aro: The two plans may have been compiled before and after an update.
core.plan_compare.estimates.detail: Different row estimates lead the optimizer to different joins and access paths. They come from different parameter values, newer statistics or a different estimator.
core.plan_compare.estimates.misestimate_: Estimates this far off lead to the wrong join type, too little memory or a needless scan.
core.plan_compare.estimates.parameters: The parameter values they were compiled for likely match very different numbers of rows.
core.plan_compare.estimates.title: On {table}, {plan} expects {rows} and {other} expects {other_rows}.
core.plan_compare.estimates.title_per_ex: On {table}, {plan} expects {rows} and {other} expects {other_rows} per execution.
core.plan_compare.estimator.detail: SQL Server estimates rows differently per estimator version. It follows the database's compatibility level unless a hint or LEGACY_CARDINALITY_ESTIMATION overrides it, so a compatibility-level change alone can change the plan.
core.plan_compare.estimator.title: Different cardinality estimators: version {version} in {plan}, {other_version} in {other}.
core.plan_compare.index.detail: If an index was added, dropped or rebuilt between the two plans, that explains it; otherwise the optimizer chose differently because it expected a different number of rows.
core.plan_compare.index.title: Different indexes on {tables}.
core.plan_compare.memory.detail: Sorts and hashes get memory sized from the row estimates. A large grant on a busy server makes other queries wait for memory; a small one spills to tempdb.
core.plan_compare.memory.title: {plan} reserves {memory} of memory per run; {other} {other_memory}.
core.plan_compare.parallelism.detail: Parallelism helps large scans and joins and costs more CPU; the optimizer only chooses it when the estimated cost passes the server's threshold.
core.plan_compare.parallelism.title: {plan} runs in parallel; {other} runs on one thread.
core.plan_compare.parallelism.title_thre: {plan} runs in parallel ({threads} threads); {other} runs on one thread.
core.plan_compare.parameters.detail: A plan is optimized for the values it was first compiled with. When some values match a few rows and others many, the same query gets very different plans (parameter sensitivity).
core.plan_compare.parameters.title: Compiled for different parameter values: {plan} for {values}; {other} for {other_values}.
core.plan_compare.plan_kind.actual: {plan} is an actual plan and {other} isn't.
core.plan_compare.plan_kind.detail: Compare estimates with estimates; actual rows and times only exist on the executed plan.
core.plan_compare.plan_kind.kinds: {plan} is a {kind} plan and {other} a {other_kind} plan.
core.plan_compare.spill.detail: Its sort or hash got less memory than the rows needed, usually because it expected fewer rows than it read.
core.plan_compare.spill.title: {plan} spills to disk; {other} doesn't.
core.plan_compare.stale: Statistics on {table} are stale: {share} of the table changed since they were updated.
core.plan_compare.stale_age: Statistics on {table} are stale: {share} of the table changed since they were updated, {age} before the scan.
core.plan_compare.statement.detail: Some differences may come from the SQL itself (another filter, join or column), not from the optimizer.
core.plan_compare.statement.title: These plans are for different statements.
core.plan_diff.because.access_worse: because it {verb} ({share} of its cost) where {other} {other_verb}
core.plan_diff.branch: {first} and {n, plural, one {{count} operator below it} other {{count} operators below it}}
core.plan_diff.change.share_detail: {a} of the plan's cost in A, {b} in B
core.plan_diff.headline.adds: {initial, select, vowel {{plan} adds an {steps} ({share} of its cost).} other {{plan} adds a {steps} ({share} of its cost).}}
core.plan_diff.headline.engines: These plans come from different engines ({a} and {b}), so their costs aren't comparable.
core.plan_diff.headline.minor_steps: {plan} differs from {other} only in minor steps.
core.plan_diff.headline.warnings: {n, plural, one {{plan} has a plan warning {other} doesn't: {warnings}.} other {{plan} has plan warnings {other} doesn't: {warnings}.}}
core.plan_diff.verb.seeks_and_looks_up: seeks {index} and looks up the rows in {table}
core.redact.plan.index_context: Check this observation against the selected scan's workload and current index definitions before changing an index. Prefer narrow projections and balance saved reads against storage and write cost; a full covering index is not automatically worthwhile.
core.redact.plan.scan_context: Workload priority and SQL restrictions from the selected scan are retained. Historical or cheap statements can still have structural scaling risks; consult the selected scan for catalog-specific advice.
core.redact.plan.verify_context: Compare a newly compiled plan, reads and time under equivalent parameters and load. Stored warnings and a changing share of database time alone do not verify improvement.

core.waits.category.compilation.label: Compiling plans
core.waits.category.compilation.meaning: Building query plans. A lot of it means the application sends one-off statements instead of parameterized ones.
core.waits.category.cpu.gist: Running on a processor, or queued for one.
core.waits.category.cpu.gist_threadpool: Running on a processor, queued for one, or (THREADPOOL) waiting for a worker thread before the request could start at all.
core.waits.category.cpu.label: CPU
core.waits.category.cpu.meaning: Running on a processor, or queued for one. When CPU dominates, queries usually do more work than they need to: scans, conversions, functions evaluated on every row.
core.waits.category.cpu.meaning_threadpo: Running on a processor, queued for one, or (THREADPOOL) waiting for a worker thread before the request could start at all. When CPU dominates, queries usually do more work than they need to: scans, conversions, functions evaluated on every row. Worker waits instead point at blocking chains or heavy parallelism holding the workers.
core.waits.category.io.gist: Waiting for data to come from disk because it wasn't in memory.
core.waits.category.io.label: Disk reads
core.waits.category.io.meaning: Waiting for data to come from disk because it wasn't in memory. Usually scans of large tables, or memory too small for the data the workload keeps touching.
core.waits.category.latch.gist: Short waits on the server's own memory structures (page latches, mutexes).
core.waits.category.latch.label: In-memory contention
core.waits.category.latch.meaning: Short waits on the server's own memory structures (page latches, mutexes). Hot spots such as an ever-increasing key or busy temporary space cause most of it.
core.waits.category.lock.gist: Waiting for another transaction to release a row or table lock.
core.waits.category.lock.label: Locks
core.waits.category.lock.meaning: Waiting for another transaction to release a row or table lock. Long transactions, and missing indexes on the columns updates filter by, make it worse.
core.waits.category.log.gist.mssql: Commits waiting for the transaction log to reach disk (WRITELOG), or a tier's log-rate limit.
core.waits.category.log.gist.mysql: Commits waiting for InnoDB's redo log to reach disk.
core.waits.category.log.gist.postgres: Commits waiting for the write-ahead log (WAL) to reach disk.
core.waits.category.log.gist.sqlite: Commits waiting for the journal or write-ahead log file to reach disk.
core.waits.category.log.gist.yugabyte: Commits waiting on DocDB replication and Raft log durability.
core.waits.category.log.label: Log writes
core.waits.category.log.meaning.mssql: Commits waiting for the transaction log to reach disk (WRITELOG), or a tier's log-rate limit. Many tiny transactions, or slow log storage.
core.waits.category.log.meaning.mysql: Commits waiting for InnoDB's redo log to reach disk. Many tiny transactions, or slow log storage.
core.waits.category.log.meaning.postgres: Commits waiting for the write-ahead log (WAL) to reach disk. Many tiny transactions, or slow log storage.
core.waits.category.log.meaning.sqlite: Commits waiting for the journal or write-ahead log file to reach disk. Many tiny transactions, or slow storage.
core.waits.category.log.meaning.yugabyte: Commits waiting on DocDB replication and Raft log durability. Correlate transaction latency with the affected tablets and replicas.
core.waits.category.memory.gist: Waiting for memory: a grant to sort or hash before a query can start (RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE), or an allocation inside the server (CMEMTHREAD, MEMORY_ALLOCATION_EXT).
core.waits.category.memory.label: Memory
core.waits.category.memory.meaning: Waiting for memory: a grant to sort or hash before a query can start (RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE), or an allocation inside the server (CMEMTHREAD, MEMORY_ALLOCATION_EXT). Grant waits usually mean a few queries reserve far more than they use; allocation waits mean many sessions contend for one of the server's memory objects.
core.waits.category.network.gist: {engine} has results ready but the application reads them slowly.
core.waits.category.network.label: Sending results
core.waits.category.network.meaning: {engine} has results ready but the application reads them slowly. Usually large result sets, or an application that processes each row before asking for the next.
core.waits.category.other.label: Everything else
core.waits.category.other.meaning_postgr: Statement time PostgreSQL doesn't break down: running on CPU, or waiting on locks and events it doesn't time per statement.
core.waits.category.parallelism.gist: Threads of a parallel query waiting for each other.
core.waits.category.parallelism.label: Parallel queries
core.waits.category.parallelism.meaning: Threads of a parallel query waiting for each other. Often a big scan that an index would avoid, or work split unevenly across threads.
core.waits.category.rows.gist: Time inside InnoDB fetching and changing rows.
core.waits.category.rows.label: Row access
core.waits.category.rows.meaning: Time inside InnoDB fetching and changing rows. MySQL's table I/O instrument counts rows served from memory too, so this is storage-engine work, not only disk.
core.waits.category.rpc.gist: Waiting for remote DocDB operations or catalog requests.
core.waits.category.rpc.label: Distributed RPCs
core.waits.category.rpc.meaning: Waiting for remote DocDB operations or catalog requests. Native session events identify these waits; statement RPC timings can overlap and are not exclusive wait shares.
core.waits.category.storage.gist: Waiting for native storage reads or writes, including RocksDB operations.
core.waits.category.storage.label: Storage I/O
core.waits.category.storage.meaning: Waiting for native storage reads or writes, including RocksDB operations. These are session observations, not PostgreSQL heap-page or buffer measurements.

fleet.cli.limit: Stop after this many work items; otherwise continue until shutdown.

health.cleanup_holder: A cleanup holder observed at the scan's instant; no long-held-cleanup finding is supported by this scan.
health.explain.buffer_pool_hit: The share of reads served by InnoDB's buffer pool across the whole server. A miss ratio alone does not establish a memory shortage in this database.
health.explain.cache_hit: Reads served by PostgreSQL's shared_buffers; misses may be served by the operating system cache. The ratio alone does not establish slow storage or a memory shortage.
health.explain.checkpoints_requested: Requested checkpoints include WAL-triggered checkpoints, manual CHECKPOINT, backups and CREATE DATABASE. This shared historical ratio does not identify their cause or establish current write pressure.
health.explain.compiles_per_batch: New plan compilations compared with batches across the server. Compilation is normal; the ratio alone does not establish pressure in this database.
health.explain.deadlocks: A count over the statistics period, not deadlocks happening now. The deadlock finding uses the amount and period recorded.
health.explain.history_length: Committed undo logs awaiting purge across the whole server. This is not a count of rows, and a large value alone does not establish a purge problem in this database.
health.explain.max_used_connections: The busiest moment since these counters started, compared with today's limit. This does not establish a connection shortage now.
health.explain.new_connections: The historical rate of new connections. A busy application can use a pool and still open connections; the rate alone does not prove pooling is missing.
health.explain.page_life: A server cache counter at the scan's instant. There is no universal healthy number of seconds; cache size, workload and measured I/O matter.
health.explain.pooled_reuse: SQL Server's recorded connection resets compared with new logins, across the server. Some pools reuse a connection without resetting it, so this does not prove whether the application pools connections.
health.explain.rollbacks: Rollbacks can be deliberate application behavior. This historical share alone does not establish failed requests.
health.explain.row_lock_avg: An average across the whole server's recorded row-lock waits, not a current wait. The lock findings use the amount of waiting too.
health.explain.session_length: Average session lifetime over the statistics period. Session length alone does not measure connection overhead or request latency.
health.explain.sessions_abandoned: The share of sessions that ended through a lost client connection over the statistics period, not sessions failing now.
health.explain.signal_wait: The share of recorded waiting spent ready to run, before a worker was scheduled. This is not CPU utilization and alone does not establish CPU pressure.
health.explain.temp_bytes: Temporary data written by this database over its statistics period. This amount alone does not establish a performance problem; the findings identify costly spills.
health.explain.thread_cache_misses: The share of connections needing a new server thread across the whole server. This does not measure application connection pooling or its cost.
health.explain.threadpool_waits: Average worker wait time over the counters' history; this does not establish a worker shortage now. The worker finding checks the amount and the database's own evidence.
health.explain.tmp_disk_tables: The share of internal temporary tables written to disk across the whole server. Table sizes and the statements' measured cost determine whether this needs work.
health.explain.version_store: Space occupied by row versions now. Keeping versions is normal; the amount alone does not establish a problem. Long transactions and storage pressure need their own evidence.
health.queue_empty: No requests in this queue when the scan ran. Historical waits are reported separately.
health.queue_now: Requests waiting at the scan's instant. Sample again to establish whether the queue persists before changing settings.
health.resource.at_limit: At or above {limit} of this database's limit in {share} of samples.
health.resource.average: Average over {span} of recorded samples; peak {peak}.
health.resource.coverage: Too little coverage to judge sustained pressure; at least {span} of samples are needed.
health.resource.label.data_io: Storage I/O used against its limit
health.resource.label.log_write_use: Log throughput used against its limit
health.resource.label.workers_use: Worker slots used against their limit
health.resource.memory: Allocated memory includes cache; a full cache is normal and is not graded as memory pressure.
health.resource.warning: A warning needs at least {share} of samples near the limit.

PostgreSQL runs the subquery for every row instead of once for the whole set, reading {table} each time.
insight.correlated_subquery.fix: Rewrite it as a join (or LEFT JOIN … GROUP BY for counts and sums) so it runs once; if it must stay correlated, index the columns it filters on so each run is a quick lookup.

insight.cross_table_or.rule: A filter across tables after a scan; evaluate a semantics-preserving rewrite before indexing
insight.deep_pagination.detail: The statement's literal OFFSET requires skipping the preceding matches before returning a later page. A small table or an early end can make it cheap today; later pages can read much more as matching data grows. This does not establish the cost of other parameter values or every run.
insight.deep_pagination.fix: If the product permits cursor pagination, test continuing from the last ordered key using a deterministic order with a unique tie-breaker. Preserve permissions, filters, NULL ordering and behavior under concurrent changes. Keep OFFSET when arbitrary page jumps are required; an ordered index can help find rows but does not remove the skipped matches.
insight.deep_pagination.rule: A literal OFFSET skips many matches before returning a later page
insight.deep_pagination.title: {n, plural, other {Pagination asks to skip {count} rows before returning this page}}
insight.deep_pagination.verify: Compare identical page results and ordering, then rows read and duration for early and late pages on representative data. Confirm cursor behavior under inserts/deletes and equal sort keys; a changed operator alone is not success.
insight.eager_spool.detail: {n, plural, other {The Index Spool copies {rows} rows of {named, select, true {{table}} other {the table}} into a temporary index in tempdb on each run and drops it afterwards, because no index fits the lookup.}}
insight.eager_spool.detail_keys: {n, plural, other {The Index Spool copies {rows} rows of {named, select, true {{table}} other {the table}} into a temporary index in tempdb on each run and drops it afterwards, because no index fits the lookup on {keys}.}}
insight.eager_spool.fix: Create that index permanently, so the work happens once instead of on every run.
insight.eager_spool.fix_computed: It seeks on a value computed in the plan, not on a column of the table: rewrite the join or subquery above the spool to compare columns, so an index on them can replace the spool.
insight.eager_spool.rule: A temporary index built on every run
insight.eager_spool.title: SQL Server builds a temporary index on {named, select, true {{table}} other {the table}} every time this runs
insight.eager_spool.verify: Explain again: the Index Spool is gone and the lookup seeks the new index.
insight.heap_fetches.detail: PostgreSQL must visit table pages that the visibility map cannot certify as all-visible. Recent writes, an older snapshot or maintenance that has not yet caught up can explain this; heap fetches alone do not establish a vacuum failure.
insight.heap_fetches.fix: Check recent writes, vacuum activity and cleanup holders on {table}. If vacuum can advance visibility and the saved reads justify it, test VACUUM; a frequently updated table can legitimately keep requiring heap fetches.
insight.heap_fetches.rule: An index-only scan that still visits the table
insight.heap_fetches.title: {n, plural, other {The index-only scan on {table} still visits the table {times} times}}
insight.heap_fetches.verify: Compare heap fetches, buffers and execution time with equivalent parameters and write activity after maintenance. Fewer heap fetches may help; zero is not required on a table that keeps changing.
insight.implicit_conversion.detail.block: The value it's compared with has a different type, so SQL Server converts {named, select, true {{column}} other {a column}}{typed, select, true { to {target}} other {}} on every row (`{expression}`) and, by its own warning, can't seek the index.
insight.implicit_conversion.detail.estim: SQL Server converts {named, select, true {{column}} other {a column}}{typed, select, true { to {target}} other {}} before comparing it (`{expression}`), which by its own warning only affects how many rows it expects here; an index can still be used.
insight.implicit_conversion.detail.per_r: SQL Server converts {named, select, true {{column}} other {a column}}{typed, select, true { to {target}} other {}} on every row it reads to compare it with a value of that type (`{expression}`). It didn't warn that this changes the plan, so the cost is the conversion itself.
insight.implicit_conversion.fix: Make the types match: send the value with {named, select, true {{column}} other {the column}}'s own type, or change {named, select, true {{column}} other {the column}} to {typed, select, true {{target}} other {the type the application sends}} if that's what it should hold. Changing a column rewrites it and the indexes on it.
insight.implicit_conversion.fix_unicode: Make the types match: send the value as non-Unicode text (SqlDbType.VarChar in .NET, sql.VarChar in Node's mssql, a non-Unicode mapping in your ORM), or, if your schema keeps text as Unicode, change {named, select, true {{column}} other {the column}} to {target}. Changing a column rewrites it and the indexes on it.
insight.implicit_conversion.rule: A type mismatch that blocks an index seek (CONVERT_IMPLICIT)
insight.implicit_conversion.title.blocks: A type mismatch on {named, select, true {{column}} other {a column}} stops SQL Server from seeking an index
insight.implicit_conversion.title.estima: A type mismatch on {named, select, true {{column}} other {a column}} turns row estimates into guesses
insight.implicit_conversion.title.per_ro: A type mismatch on {named, select, true {{column}} other {a column}} adds a conversion to every row
insight.implicit_conversion.verify: Explain again: no CONVERT_IMPLICIT on {named, select, true {{column}} other {a column}} in the plan.
insight.implicit_conversion.verify_seek: Explain again: no CONVERT_IMPLICIT in the plan, and the scan became a seek.
insight.index_ignored.detail_expected: MySQL expects the filter to keep {kept} of {rows} rows, yet MySQL judged {indexes, plural, one {the index} other {those indexes}} not worth it; that usually means stale statistics or a type mismatch in the comparison.
insight.index_ignored.detail_kept: The filter kept {kept} of {rows} rows, yet MySQL judged {indexes, plural, one {the index} other {those indexes}} not worth it; that usually means stale statistics or a type mismatch in the comparison.
insight.index_ignored.fix: Refresh the table's statistics and compare the column with a value of its own type; if it still scans, compare with FORCE INDEX to see which is really faster.
insight.index_ignored.rule: An index was possible but the whole table was read
insight.index_ignored.title: MySQL could use {keys} but reads all of {table} instead
insight.index_ignored.verify: Explain again: access_type is ref or range on the index.
insight.jit.detail: PostgreSQL compiled parts of this query to machine code because its estimated cost crossed jit_above_cost.
insight.jit.detail_dominates: Compiling took longer than everything else the query did, so it can't have paid for itself here.
insight.jit.detail_may_pay: Compiled code evaluates each row faster, so on a long run it can pay for itself; only a run without it tells.
insight.jit.fix: Compare with JIT off in your session before changing anything.
insight.jit.fix_dominates: Check with JIT off in your session; if it's faster, turn JIT off for this workload's role, or raise jit_above_cost so only long analytical queries use it.
insight.jit.rule: JIT compilation taking a large share of the run
insight.jit.title: JIT compilation took {time}
insight.jit.title_of: JIT compilation took {time} of the {ran} this query ran
insight.jit.verify: Explain analyze again: no JIT section, and a shorter execution time.
insight.join_buffer.detail: {n, plural, other {MySQL has no index to look up matching rows of {table} for each row it joins, so it reads all {rows} rows into a join buffer and matches them there.}}
insight.join_buffer.detail_possible: {n, plural, other {MySQL listed {keys} as possible for {table}, yet reads all {rows} rows into a join buffer and matches them there, rather than looking up each row's matches.}}

insight.join_buffer.title_possible: Joins {table} through a join buffer ({how}) over a full read instead of an index

insight.key_lookups.detail.index: {index} finds the rows but doesn't hold {columns}, so SQL Server goes back to {table} for each one ({op}).
insight.key_lookups.detail.lookup: Each row found by the index needs a second read from {table} ({op}).
insight.key_lookups.fix.cover: Add {named, select, true {{columns}} other {the looked-up columns}} to the index as included columns, or select fewer columns.

insight.key_lookups.fix.heap: {table} has no clustered index, so every lookup follows a row pointer.
insight.key_lookups.fix.heap_cover: Give it a clustered index, or add {named, select, true {{columns}} other {the looked-up columns}} to {indexed, select, true {{index}} other {the index}} as included columns.
insight.key_lookups.rule: Thousands of key or RID lookups back into the table
insight.key_lookups.title.estimated: {n, plural, one {Estimated to look up {count} row in {table} one at a time} other {Estimated to look up {count} rows in {table} one at a time}}
insight.key_lookups.title.measured: {n, plural, one {Looks up {count} row in {table} one at a time} other {Looks up {count} rows in {table} one at a time}}
insight.key_lookups.together: Together that's {share} of this plan's work.

insight.leading_wildcard.detail: {n, plural, other {A pattern that starts with a wildcard can't use an index, so {op} checks every row's {named, select, true {{column}} other {the column}} ({rows} rows) to keep {kept} of them.}}
insight.leading_wildcard.fix.mssql: Use full-text search for word searches, or drop the leading % if a prefix search is enough. For suffix searches, store the reversed value of {named, select, true {{column}} other {the column}} and index it.
insight.leading_wildcard.fix.mysql: Use a FULLTEXT index with MATCH … AGAINST for word searches, or drop the leading % if a prefix search is enough.

insight.leading_wildcard.fix.sqlite: Use an FTS5 virtual table with MATCH for word searches, or drop the leading % if a prefix search is enough.
insight.leading_wildcard.fix.yugabyte: Use a prefix filter when it preserves the intended search. For substring search, evaluate a supported search index or search service; PostgreSQL trigram GIN support is not assumed for DocDB.
insight.leading_wildcard.rule: LIKE '%…' that can't use an index

insight.lossy_bitmap.detail_brin: A bitmap outgrowing work_mem does that, and so does a BRIN index combined into it, which only ever gives pages: check the indexes it combines before raising work_mem.
insight.lossy_bitmap.detail_rechecked: {n, plural, other {For {pages} pages it only remembered the page, not the rows, so every row on them was re-checked ({rechecked} rows thrown away).}}

insight.many_to_many.detail: When neither input is unique on the join columns, SQL Server rewinds the inner side for every duplicate on the outer side.
insight.many_to_many.fix: If one side really is unique on the join columns, declare it (a unique index or constraint); otherwise a hash join is usually cheaper.
