insight.memory_grant.desired.detail: Large grants are reserved for the whole run; a few of these at once make other queries queue for memory.
insight.memory_grant.desired.fix: Check the row estimates of the sorts and hashes; sort fewer rows or columns, or cap it with OPTION (MAX_GRANT_PERCENT = n).
insight.memory_grant.desired.title: Asks for {size} of memory per run
insight.memory_grant.desired.verify: Explain again: the desired memory is lower.
insight.memory_grant.oversized.detail: The grant is sized from row estimates before the query runs; when they're too high, memory sits reserved and other queries wait for it (RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE).
insight.memory_grant.oversized.fix: Fix the estimates (update statistics, avoid functions on filtered columns). SQL Server 2019+ shrinks grants on later runs (memory grant feedback); as a last resort cap it with OPTION (MAX_GRANT_PERCENT = 5).
insight.memory_grant.oversized.title: Reserves {granted} of memory per run and uses {used}
insight.memory_grant.oversized.verify: Run with an actual plan: GrantedMemory is close to MaxUsedMemory.
insight.memory_grant.rule: A memory grant far larger than what the query uses, or a wait for one
insight.memory_grant.wait.detail: Other queries held the memory it needed. The run was slow before it did any work.
insight.memory_grant.wait.fix: Find the queries with oversized grants (they show up with this same insight) and shrink them; adding memory only postpones it.
insight.memory_grant.wait.title: Waited {time} for memory before it could start
insight.memory_grant.wait.verify: Run with an actual plan: GrantWaitTime is 0.
insight.misestimate.detail.correlated: The filter combines {columns}; databases assume such columns are independent, which is wrong when they move together.
insight.misestimate.detail.expression: The filter compares an expression, not a plain column, so the column's statistics can't predict it.
insight.misestimate.detail.planned: Everything above this operator was planned for the wrong number of rows: join types, memory grants and parallelism.
insight.misestimate.detail.planned_spill: Everything above this operator was planned for the wrong number of rows: join types, memory grants and parallelism (here a sort or hash above it ran out of memory as a result).
insight.misestimate.detail.unused: Nothing above it in this plan was sized from that estimate, but the same statistics decide every plan that reads this table.
insight.misestimate.fix.below: Refresh statistics on the tables below this operator.
insight.misestimate.fix.mariadb_columns: Refresh the statistics on {table}, with column statistics (histograms) on {columns}.
insight.misestimate.fix.mssql: Refresh the statistics on {table} with a full scan.
insight.misestimate.fix.mssql_columns: Refresh the statistics on {table} with a full scan, and create statistics on the filtered columns together.
insight.misestimate.fix.mysql_columns: Refresh the statistics on {table} and add a histogram on {columns}.
insight.misestimate.fix.postgres_columns: Analyze {table}, and tell PostgreSQL the filtered columns are related with extended statistics.
insight.misestimate.fix.postgres_express: Analyze {table}; on PostgreSQL 14+ statistics on the expression itself help (CREATE STATISTICS … ON (expression) FROM table).
insight.misestimate.fix.table_variable: {table} is a table variable, so it has no statistics: use a temporary table instead, or add OPTION (RECOMPILE) so the row count at run time is used.
insight.misestimate.fix.temporary_table: {table} is a temporary table: update its statistics in the session that fills it, after loading it, or add OPTION (RECOMPILE) to the query that reads it.
insight.misestimate.fix.yugabyte: Refresh YSQL optimizer statistics on {table} and compare a measured plan with representative values.
insight.misestimate.rule: Actual rows far from the estimate
insight.misestimate.title_fewer: {n, plural, one {Expected {count} row from {table}, got {got} ({factor}× fewer)} other {Expected {count} rows from {table}, got {got} ({factor}× fewer)}}
insight.misestimate.title_more: {n, plural, one {Expected {count} row from {table}, got {got} ({factor}× more)} other {Expected {count} rows from {table}, got {got} ({factor}× more)}}
insight.misestimate.verify: Run with actual rows again: the estimate is within about 10× of the actual count.
insight.missing_index_hint.detail: The optimizer noticed it had to read {table} without a fitting index. Its estimate is a guide, not a promise: check the columns against the other queries on {leaf}.
insight.missing_index_hint.detail_read: {n, plural, other {The optimizer noticed it had to read {table} without a fitting index ({rows} rows read by {op}). Its estimate is a guide, not a promise: check the columns against the other queries on {leaf}.}}
insight.missing_index_hint.fix_include: Create the index on {keys} and include {include}.
insight.missing_index_hint.title: SQL Server estimates an index on {table} ({keys}) would make this {share} cheaper
insight.missing_index_hint.verify: Explain again: the suggestion is gone and the read of {table} becomes a seek.
insight.missing_statistics.detail: SQL Server reported ColumnsWithNoStatistics when this plan was compiled. This is a compilation-time warning, not a measurement of current statistics or proof of a slow plan. Query Store can retain the original plan XML after statistics change.
insight.missing_statistics.fix: Inspect the current column and index statistics and AUTO_CREATE_STATISTICS before choosing a change. An index histogram describes only its first key, so a column appearing in a seek does not prove that it has a usable histogram. Refresh or create statistics only where current evidence supports it; compare actual rows with estimates if the query is costly.
insight.missing_statistics.seek_keys: SQL Server reported no usable statistics on {columns} when this plan was compiled. These columns appear in seek keys of {indexes}. An index has statistics, but its histogram describes only the first key; the seek alone does not establish that each named column has a histogram or that the statistics are out of date. Query Store can retain the original warning after statistics change.
insight.missing_statistics.title: The captured plan reported no usable statistics on {named, select, true {{columns}} other {some columns}}
insight.missing_statistics.verify: Capture a newly compiled plan after any justified statistics change and compare its warning and row estimates with representative runs. Reopening Query Store's original saved XML alone cannot verify that the warning is still current or has cleared.
insight.nested_loops.detail.misjudged: {n, plural, other {The optimizer expected {expected} rows from {outer} and chose a nested loop; it got {got}.}}
insight.nested_loops.detail.misjudged_ha: At that size one pass with a hash join is usually much cheaper, and the optimizer would have weighed one.
insight.nested_loops.detail.misjudged_my: MySQL joins through an index whenever one fits; the estimate decides the join order, so a wrong one can start from the bigger side.
insight.nested_loops.detail.replays: {n, plural, other {The {op} reads {inner} once and replays its {rows} rows for each row of {outer}; the join then checks `{predicate}` on every pair.}}
insight.nested_loops.detail.rereads: {n, plural, other {Each run reads about {rows} rows of {inner}, so the loop reads it {times} times over.}}
insight.nested_loops.detail.rereads_shar: {n, plural, other {Each run reads about {rows} rows of {inner} ({share} of the table), so the loop reads it {times} times over.}}
insight.nested_loops.fix.condition: Give the join a condition it can seek or hash on: compare stored columns with = (no functions or computed values around them), indexed on the inner side, or filter {outer} earlier so fewer rows reach the loop.
insight.nested_loops.fix.estimate: Fix the estimate for {outer}: update its statistics. With the right row count the optimizer can choose a hash join by itself.
insight.nested_loops.fix.estimate_mysql: Fix the estimate for {outer}: ANALYZE TABLE, and a histogram on its filtered columns, so MySQL plans the join for the real row count; filtering {outer} earlier means fewer rows reach the loop.
insight.nested_loops.fix.hint: The query forces a loop join (LOOP JOIN / OPTION (LOOP JOIN)); remove the hint and let the optimizer choose.
insight.nested_loops.fix.index: Index {inner} on the join column so each run reads only its matching rows, or filter {outer} earlier so fewer rows reach the loop.
insight.nested_loops.fix.narrower_index: Give {inner} an index that leads with the join column and the columns the inner side filters on, so each run reads only its matching rows; or filter {outer} earlier so fewer rows reach the loop.
insight.nested_loops.forced: The query forces a loop join, so the optimizer didn't weigh a hash or merge join.
insight.nested_loops.rule: A nested loop rereading its inner side thousands of times
insight.nested_loops.title.pairs: {n, plural, other {Compares each of {rows} rows of {outer} with {replayed} rows the {op} replays ({pairs} pairs)}}
insight.nested_loops.title.repeats: {n, plural, other {Repeats its read of {inner} {times} times, once per row of {outer}}}
insight.nested_loops.verify.hint: Explain again without the hint: a hash or merge join instead of the loop.
insight.nested_loops.verify.mysql: Explain again: {inner} is read with ref or eq_ref access, and far fewer rows reach the loop.
insight.nested_loops.verify.pairs: Explain again: no {op} under the join, or a join that seeks its matches.
insight.nested_loops.verify.repeats: Run with actual rows: a hash join, or far fewer rows read per execution of {inner}.
insight.no_join_predicate.detail: {n, plural, other {{op} has no join condition, so its output is the product of both inputs ({rows} rows planned). That's almost always a missing ON clause.}}
insight.no_join_predicate.fix: Add the missing join condition; if you really want every combination, write CROSS JOIN so the intent is clear.
insight.no_join_predicate.rule: Two inputs joined without a condition
insight.no_join_predicate.title: Two inputs are joined without a condition: every row with every row
insight.no_join_predicate.title_sides: {first} and {second} are joined without a condition: every row with every row
insight.no_join_predicate.verify: Explain again: the join has a condition and its row count is reasonable.
insight.non_sargable.detail: {n, plural, other {Each row's {column} is computed before it can be compared (`{filter}`), so an index on {column} can't narrow the search: {op} reads {rows} rows to keep {kept}.}}
insight.non_sargable.fix.cast: Compare {column} with a value of its own type, so nothing has to be converted per row.
insight.non_sargable.fix.date_range: Where it preserves the original date, time-zone and NULL rules, compare {column} itself with a range, e.g. `{column} >= '2026-03-01' AND {column} < '2026-04-01'`. Test representative values: an index can then narrow that range when the optimizer finds it cheaper.
insight.non_sargable.fix.mariadb: Store {column} in the form you search for, or define a generated column for {function}({column}) and index that column. MariaDB uses indexed generated columns rather than MySQL's direct expression-index syntax; whether the original expression can use that index depends on the server version. Test the query against the generated column and preserve its collation and NULL behavior.
insight.non_sargable.fix.mssql: Store {column} in the form you search for, or add a computed column with {function}({column}) and index it.
insight.non_sargable.fix.mysql: Store {column} in the form you search for, or add a functional index, e.g. `CREATE INDEX ... ON {table} (({function}({column})))` (MySQL 8.0.13+).
insight.non_sargable.fix.null_replacemen: Preserve the replacement value and NULL behavior when rewriting this condition. For example, `COALESCE({column}, fallback) = wanted` includes NULL rows only when `fallback = wanted`; adding `OR {column} IS NULL` unconditionally changes the result. Compare the original and rewritten results, including NULLs and parameter types, before measuring performance.
insight.non_sargable.fix.postgres: Store {column} in the form you search for, or index the expression itself, e.g. `CREATE INDEX ON {table} (({function}({column})))`.
insight.non_sargable.fix.sqlite: Store {column} in the form you search for, or index the expression itself, e.g. `CREATE INDEX ... ON {table} ({function}({column}))`.
insight.non_sargable.fix.yugabyte: Store {column} in the form you search for, or index the expression with explicit ordered keys, e.g. `CREATE INDEX ON {table} (({function}({column})) ASC)`. Review its tablet distribution and preserve collation and NULL behavior.
insight.non_sargable.rule: A function or cast around a filtered column
insight.non_sargable.title: {function}() around {column} keeps the database from using an index on {table}
insight.non_sargable.title_cast: A cast on {column} keeps the database from using an index on {table}
insight.non_sargable.verify: Compare identical results, including NULLs and boundary values, then obtain a fresh plan for {table} with representative parameters. Compare rows read and execution time; an index condition on {column} can help, but the optimizer may correctly retain a scan.
insight.not_in.detail.mssql: The plan includes repeated work and a Row Count Spool under {op}. NULL handling can require extra checks for NOT IN, but this shape alone does not establish which constraints or values apply. A rewrite must preserve the query's NULL semantics.
insight.not_in.detail.mysql: NOT IN has to treat a NULL from the subquery specially, and here MySQL could neither turn it into an antijoin nor materialize the subquery once, so it runs the subquery for each row.
insight.not_in.detail.postgres: The plan searches the subquery repeatedly instead of using a hashed membership test. Cost, correlation and NULL semantics can affect that choice; the plan alone does not establish that a larger work_mem or a rewrite would improve it. A NULL in a nonempty subquery prevents a nonmatching value from passing NOT IN.
insight.not_in.detail.sqlite: If the subquery ever returns NULL, NOT IN returns nothing at all.
insight.not_in.fix: First establish the intended NULL behavior: NOT IN and NOT EXISTS are not interchangeable when either comparison value can be NULL (an empty subquery is another boundary case). If both compared expressions are guaranteed NOT NULL and the subquery's conditions and correlations stay the same, test an equivalent NOT EXISTS rewrite. Otherwise preserve the original three-valued logic explicitly; do not remove NULL handling or add a NOT NULL constraint merely to change the plan.
insight.not_in.rule: NOT IN that checks the subquery row by row
insight.not_in.title.mssql: NOT IN adds repeated subquery work; preserve NULL behavior when testing a rewrite
insight.not_in.title.mysql: NOT IN (subquery) makes MySQL run the subquery once per row
insight.not_in.title.postgres: NOT IN tests rows against a repeatedly searched subquery
insight.not_in.title.sqlite: NOT IN against a subquery whose column can be NULL returns no rows once it meets a NULL
insight.not_in.verify: Compare original and rewritten results with NULLs on either side, an empty subquery, duplicates and representative values. Then compare repeated subquery executions, reads and execution time in a fresh measured plan. An anti-join is one possible improvement, not a required operator.
insight.note.changes_schema: This plan builds an index or changes the schema: reading and sorting the table is the work it's for, so no advice is read from it.
insight.note.generic: This generic plan was obtained without the application's parameter values. Its estimates and connection settings may differ from an application's run, and partitions listed here may be skipped at runtime. It does not identify the plan used by historical executions. Actual rows and timing require a measured plan with representative values.
insight.note.generic_sqlite: Planned with Culprit's SQLite library and unknown parameter values. The application's version, modules and build options may differ. This plan shows access paths, without row counts, costs or timings. Compare application-log durations and a plan from the application's connection with representative values.
insight.note.mariadb_actual: MariaDB plans don't record memory grants or parallel threads, so those checks don't apply.
insight.note.mariadb_estimated: MariaDB's EXPLAIN has no actual rows or timings; ANALYZE adds them, with pages read and sort spills.
insight.note.mssql_estimated: Estimated plan: misestimates, spills, unused memory grants and uneven threads need an actual plan.
insight.note.mysql_actual: MySQL plans don't record spills, memory grants or parallel threads, so those checks don't apply.
insight.note.mysql_cannot_analyze: MySQL's EXPLAIN has no actual rows, spills, memory or threads, and this version can't measure a run (EXPLAIN ANALYZE arrived in MySQL 8.0.18).
insight.note.mysql_estimated: MySQL's EXPLAIN has no actual rows, spills, memory or threads; EXPLAIN ANALYZE adds actual rows.
insight.note.postgres_actual: PostgreSQL plans carry no index suggestions or memory grants; index advice comes from the filters.
insight.note.postgres_estimated: Without EXPLAIN ANALYZE there are no actual rows, spills or timings to check. PostgreSQL plans never carry index suggestions; Culprit reads filters instead.
insight.note.sqlite: SQLite's EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN shows the access path only: no estimated or actual rows, costs or timings.
insight.note.statistics_maintenance: This plan updates optimizer statistics. Reading and sorting samples is maintenance work, so ordinary query index, ORDER BY and parallelism advice does not apply. Review its frequency and sampling only if measured maintenance cost warrants it.
insight.note.yugabyte_actual: DocDB storage RPCs and rows scanned are distinct from PostgreSQL buffer pages. RPC timings may overlap and are not exclusive shares of execution time.
insight.note.yugabyte_estimated: Without EXPLAIN ANALYZE DIST, actual DocDB RPCs, storage rows scanned and execution timings are unknown.
insight.optimizer_timeout.detail: SQL Server reports StatementOptmEarlyAbortReason = {reason}: the query is complex enough that the plan in use is the best one found in the time allowed, not necessarily the best one.
insight.optimizer_timeout.fix: Make it simpler to optimize: split it into steps with a temporary table, remove joins the result doesn't need, or replace nested views with direct table references.
insight.optimizer_timeout.rule: The optimizer stopped before finding the best plan
insight.optimizer_timeout.title: The optimizer stopped searching before it found the best plan (timeout)
insight.optimizer_timeout.title_memory: The optimizer ran out of memory before it finished choosing a plan
insight.parallel_skew.detail_process: Parallel work is only as fast as its busiest process; the others finished early and waited.
insight.parallel_skew.detail_thread: Parallel work is only as fast as its busiest thread; the others finished early and waited.
insight.parallel_skew.fix: Uneven work usually means one key value holds most of the rows (check the distribution of the join or filter column) or a parallel scan over a small range; update statistics and consider filtering that value separately.
insight.parallel_skew.rule: One thread or worker doing most of the work
insight.parallel_skew.title_process: One process of {workers} handled {share} of the rows in {op}
insight.parallel_skew.title_thread: One thread of {workers} handled {share} of the rows in {op}
insight.parallel_skew.verify_process: Run with actual rows: each process handles a similar share.
insight.parallel_skew.verify_thread: Run with actual rows: each thread handles a similar share.
insight.parallelism_blocked.detail.defau: Its estimated cost is {cost}, above this server's cost threshold for parallelism ({threshold}) and the {common} it's commonly raised to, so SQL Server would consider a parallel plan for it either way; the whole run happens on a single core instead.
insight.parallelism_blocked.detail.thres: Its estimated cost is {cost}, above this server's cost threshold for parallelism ({threshold}), so SQL Server would consider a parallel plan for it; the whole run happens on a single core instead.
insight.parallelism_blocked.detail.unkno: SQL Server considers a parallel plan above the server's cost threshold for parallelism (5 by default, often raised to 50), so whether it would split depends on that setting; the whole run happens on a single core instead.

SQL Server considers a parallel plan above the server's cost threshold for parallelism (5 by default, often raised to 50), which this plan passes either way; the whole run happens on a single core instead.
insight.parallelism_blocked.fix.maxdop_d: Raise the database's MAXDOP (ALTER DATABASE SCOPED CONFIGURATION SET MAXDOP), or give this statement OPTION (MAXDOP n) where it should run in parallel.
insight.parallelism_blocked.fix.maxdop_e: Look for what sets it: a Query Store hint on this query (sys.query_store_query_hints), or the workload group its session runs in (MAX_DOP).
insight.parallelism_blocked.fix.maxdop_h: Remove OPTION (MAXDOP 1) from the statement, unless something needs it to run on one CPU.
insight.parallelism_blocked.fix.maxdop_s: Raise the server's max degree of parallelism, or set the database's MAXDOP (ALTER DATABASE SCOPED CONFIGURATION SET MAXDOP), which overrides it for this database.
insight.parallelism_blocked.fix.maxdop_u: Remove OPTION (MAXDOP 1) if the query has it; otherwise check MAXDOP for the database (ALTER DATABASE SCOPED CONFIGURATION) and the server.
insight.parallelism_blocked.fix.other: Remove what prevents parallelism if the query allows it; otherwise make the single-threaded run cheaper (indexes, fewer rows).
insight.parallelism_blocked.rule: An expensive plan that can't go parallel
insight.parallelism_blocked.title.clr_fu: This plan runs on one CPU because it calls a CLR function that reads data
insight.parallelism_blocked.title.editio: This plan runs on one CPU because this SQL Server edition doesn't run parallel plans
insight.parallelism_blocked.title.intrin: This plan runs on one CPU because the query calls a built-in function that can't run in parallel
insight.parallelism_blocked.title.maxdop: This plan runs on one CPU because the database's MAXDOP setting is 1

This plan runs on one CPU because MAXDOP is 1, though neither its statement nor the database's or server's setting says so now (a Query Store hint, a Resource Governor workload group, or a setting changed since it was compiled)
This plan runs on one CPU because its statement says OPTION (MAXDOP 1)
This plan runs on one CPU because the server's max degree of parallelism is 1
This plan runs on one CPU because MAXDOP is 1 (a query hint, or the database or server setting)
insight.parallelism_blocked.title.memory: This plan runs on one CPU because it touches memory-optimized tables
insight.parallelism_blocked.title.no_val: This plan runs on one CPU because SQL Server couldn't build a valid parallel plan for it
insight.parallelism_blocked.title.one_cp: This plan runs on one CPU because only one CPU is available to it
insight.parallelism_blocked.title.report: This plan runs on one CPU: SQL Server reports {reason}
insight.parallelism_blocked.title.table_: This plan runs on one CPU because it writes to a table variable
insight.parallelism_blocked.title.writeb: This plan runs on one CPU because it assigns to a variable
insight.parallelism_blocked.verify: Explain again: no NonParallelPlanReason, and Parallelism operators appear.
insight.partition_filtering.detail: {n, plural, other {Measured partition scans read {read} rows and returned {returned} after their filters. This establishes broad partition access in this run, not failed pruning: the filter may intentionally span these partitions or use a different key.}}
insight.partition_filtering.fix: Check the partition key and whether the query's intended range can constrain it directly. Review casts, functions and parameter types only where they prevent that constraint. Do not add a narrower range that changes results; some reports correctly need every partition. Check per-partition indexes separately.
insight.partition_filtering.rule: A measured run visits many partitions and filters most rows afterwards; inspect intended pruning
insight.partition_filtering.title: {n, plural, other {This run visits {count} partitions of {table} and filters most rows afterwards}}
insight.partition_filtering.verify: Compare equivalent results, actual partitions executed, rows read and execution time for representative values. Runtime pruning can skip partitions listed in a generic plan, so compare measured executions rather than counting planned branches.
insight.remote_query.reads.detail: Rows from another server travel over the network, and filters that can't be sent along are applied locally after the transfer.
insight.remote_query.reads.fix: Filter on the remote side (OPENQUERY with the WHERE clause inside), or copy the data you need locally on a schedule.
insight.remote_query.reads.title: {n, plural, one {Pulls {count} row from a linked server} other {Pulls {count} rows from a linked server}}
insight.remote_query.reads.verify: Explain again: far fewer rows come back from the Remote operator.
insight.remote_query.rule: Rows pulled from a linked server
insight.remote_query.writes.detail: Each row written through a linked server crosses the network, usually one statement per row on the other side.
insight.remote_query.writes.fix: Run the change on the remote server itself (EXEC (…) AT the linked server, or a procedure there) with the rows it needs, rather than row by row from here.
insight.remote_query.writes.title: {n, plural, one {Sends {count} row to a linked server ({op})} other {Sends {count} rows to a linked server ({op})}}
insight.remote_query.writes.verify: Explain again: no Remote Insert, Update or Delete over many rows.
insight.scalar_udf.detail.measured: This run spent {time} in it, {share} of the statement's time.
insight.scalar_udf.detail.per_row: A scalar function runs like a small separate query for each row.
insight.scalar_udf.detail.per_row_serial: A scalar function runs like a small separate query for each row, and it keeps the whole plan on one CPU.
insight.scalar_udf.detail.unmeasured: Its cost doesn't show in the plan's numbers, which makes it easy to miss.
insight.scalar_udf.fix: Inline it: rewrite the function as an inline table-valued function or a plain expression in the query. SQL Server 2019+ inlines scalar functions automatically unless they use things like GETDATE(), table variables or loops.
insight.scalar_udf.rule: A scalar function called once per row
insight.scalar_udf.serial.detail: SQL Server reports TSQLUserDefinedFunctionsNotParallelizable: a T-SQL scalar function in the query can't run in parallel, and it's called for each row.
insight.scalar_udf.serial.fix: Inline the function as an inline table-valued function or an expression; on SQL Server 2019+ remove what prevents automatic inlining (GETDATE(), table variables, loops).
insight.scalar_udf.serial.title: A scalar function keeps this plan on one CPU and runs once per row
insight.scalar_udf.title.per_row: {n, plural, other {{names} runs once for every row (about {calls} calls per run)}}
insight.scalar_udf.title.per_seek: {n, plural, other {{names} runs once for every seek (about {calls} calls per run)}}
insight.scalar_udf.verify: Explain again: no UserDefinedFunction in the plan, and no NonParallelPlanReason.
insight.scan_filter.detail.actual: The {op} reads the rows and checks `{filter}` on each one, so most of the reading is thrown away.
insight.scan_filter.detail.measured: As the statement's runs measured, the {op} reads the rows and checks `{filter}` on each one, so most of the reading is thrown away.
insight.scan_filter.detail.planned: As planned, the {op} reads the rows and checks `{filter}` on each one, so most of the reading is thrown away.
insight.scan_filter.fix.has_index: {index} already starts with {key}, yet this plan reads {table} instead: refresh {table}'s statistics first, then check that the filter compares the column as it is (no function or conversion on it).
insight.scan_filter.fix.index: An index on {columns} lets the database go straight to the matching rows; if one already exists, the optimizer didn't use it, so refresh the table's statistics first.
insight.scan_filter.fix.no_index: No index on {table} starts with {starts_with}: one on {columns} lets the database go straight to the matching rows.
insight.scan_filter.order.any: {columns} can go in any order, and the SQL below takes the filter's ({first} first).
insight.scan_filter.order.instead: Put {pair, select, true {{second}} other {another one}} first instead if it has more distinct values, or if another index you add on {table} leads with it: then that one index serves this query too.
insight.scan_filter.rule: A scan reads far more rows than its filter keeps
insight.scan_filter.title: {n, plural, one {Reads {count} row of {table} to keep {kept}} other {Reads {count} rows of {table} to keep {kept}}}
insight.scan_filter.verify: Explain again: {table} reads about as many rows as it keeps.
insight.slow_compile.detail: When the plan isn't reused, every run pays this again. Many joins, many partitions or long IN lists make planning expensive.
insight.slow_compile.detail_cold: This is one measurement, and the first planning on a new connection also reads the tables' metadata: explain it twice in one session to see the time a warm connection pays.
insight.slow_compile.fix: Make sure the plan is reused: send the query parameterized rather than with literal values, and avoid OPTION (RECOMPILE) on frequent queries.
insight.slow_compile.fix_prepared: Reuse the plan with prepared statements, keep IN lists short (use = ANY($1) with an array), and make sure partition pruning can happen at plan time.
insight.slow_compile.rule: Planning takes long, or longer than running
insight.slow_compile.title: Compiling this plan took {planning}
insight.slow_compile.title_slower: Planning takes {planning}, longer than running it ({running})
insight.slow_compile.verify: Explain again: compile/planning time is a small fraction of the run.
insight.spill.exchange.detail: SQL Server spills an exchange's buffers to tempdb when its parallel threads would otherwise wait on each other for good, usually at an exchange that keeps rows in order (merging streams) fed unevenly. It isn't a memory grant problem.
insight.spill.exchange.fix: Remove the need for order at that exchange (an ORDER BY or merge join above it that an index or a hash join could serve), and check whether one value holds most of the rows; comparing a run with OPTION (MAXDOP 1) shows what parallelism costs here.
insight.spill.exchange.title: The {op} exchange wrote to tempdb to keep its threads from waiting on each other
insight.spill.exchange.title_size: The {op} exchange wrote {size} to tempdb to keep its threads from waiting on each other
insight.spill.exchange.verify: Run with an actual plan: no ExchangeSpillDetails on the Parallelism operator.
insight.spill.rule: A sort or hash that ran out of memory and wrote to disk, or an exchange that spilled
insight.spill.sort_buffer.detail: Each merge pass writes the sorted runs to a temporary file and reads them back.
insight.spill.sort_buffer.fix: Raise sort_buffer_size for the session that runs it rather than server-wide (it's allocated per sort), or add an index that returns rows already in order so the sort disappears.
insight.spill.sort_buffer.title: {n, plural, one {The sort needed {count} merge pass through temporary files because it didn't fit in sort_buffer_size} other {The sort needed {count} merge passes through temporary files because it didn't fit in sort_buffer_size}}
insight.spill.sort_buffer.underestimated: The rows feeding it were badly underestimated.
insight.spill.tempdb.detail: The memory granted to {op} was too small for the rows it got, so part of the work went to disk in tempdb.
insight.spill.tempdb.fix: Fix the row estimate first (update statistics on the tables feeding it); an index that returns rows in the needed order removes the sort altogether. SQL Server 2019+ also grows the grant on later runs (memory grant feedback, compatibility level 150).
insight.spill.tempdb.title: {op} ran out of memory and wrote to tempdb
insight.spill.tempdb.title_size: {op} ran out of memory and wrote {size} to tempdb
insight.spill.tempdb.underestimated: The rows feeding it were badly underestimated; the grant was sized for the estimate.
insight.spill.tempdb.verify: Run with an actual plan: no spill warning on that operator.
insight.spill.work_mem.detail: Disk is many times slower than memory for sorting and hashing.
insight.spill.work_mem.fix: Give this workload more memory for sorts and hashes, per role or per session rather than server-wide, or add an index that returns rows already ordered so the sort disappears.
insight.spill.work_mem.title: {op} wrote temporary files because it didn't fit in work_mem
insight.spill.work_mem.title_files: {op} writes {size} of temporary files because it didn't fit in work_mem
insight.spill.work_mem.title_groups: {n, plural, other {{op} split its groups into {batches} batches on disk because they didn't fit in work_mem}}
insight.spill.work_mem.title_hash: {n, plural, other {The hash split its input into {batches} batches on disk because it didn't fit in work_mem}}
insight.spill.work_mem.title_sort: The sort writes {size} to disk because it didn't fit in work_mem
insight.spill.work_mem.underestimated: The rows feeding it were badly underestimated, so it was planned with too little memory.
insight.spill.work_mem.verify: Explain analyze again: Sort Method is quicksort/top-N (in memory) and Hash Batches is 1.
insight.table_gone.fix: Nothing to create: {table} isn't in the database's catalog any more, so it was dropped or renamed since this plan was captured.
insight.table_gone.verify: Nothing to check while the table is gone.
insight.table_variable.detail: Table variables have no statistics, so everything joined to it is planned as if it held a single row. That's fine for a handful of rows and badly wrong for thousands.
insight.table_variable.fix: If {name} can hold more than a few hundred rows, use a temporary table (#{temporary}) instead; it gets statistics. Compatibility level 150+ also defers its compilation so the first run's row count is used.
insight.table_variable.rule: A table variable estimated at one row
insight.table_variable.title: SQL Server plans for 1 row in table variable {name}
insight.table_variable.title_held: SQL Server planned for 1 row in table variable {name}, which held {held}
insight.table_variable.verify: Run with an actual plan: the estimate for that table matches its actual rows.
insight.temp_table_sort.group.detail: The rows don't arrive in the order the GROUP BY / DISTINCT needs, so {server} builds a temporary table (on disk once it outgrows tmp_table_size) and sorts the result.
insight.temp_table_sort.group.fix: An index whose leading columns match the GROUP BY may let {server} group in index order and reduce grouping work. An ORDER BY that differs from the grouping, especially an aggregate such as COUNT(*) DESC, can still need a temporary table and sort. Filter rows before grouping, or keep a pre-aggregated result, to reduce that work.
insight.temp_table_sort.group.title: {n, plural, other {Collects {count} rows in an internal temporary table}}
insight.temp_table_sort.group.title_sort: {n, plural, other {Groups {count} rows in an internal temporary table, then sorts them (filesort)}}
insight.temp_table_sort.group.verify: Explain again: look for grouping in index order or fewer rows entering the temporary table. A temporary table and sort for a different ORDER BY can remain; compare on-disk temporary tables on new runs to check the spill itself.
insight.temp_table_sort.groups.detail: Grouping already reads an index in order; {server} then sorts the grouped result, because the query orders by an aggregate or by columns the index doesn't provide.
insight.temp_table_sort.groups.fix: Ordering by an aggregate (COUNT(*) DESC) always needs this sort: keep the grouped set small with a selective WHERE, or add a LIMIT so only the top groups are kept.
insight.temp_table_sort.groups.title: Sorts the groups in a temporary table (filesort)
insight.temp_table_sort.groups.verify: Explain again: the sort's input is the groups you expect, not every row.
insight.temp_table_sort.order.detail: The ORDER BY isn't on the table the join reads first, so {server} collects the joined rows in a temporary table (on disk once it outgrows tmp_table_size) and sorts them.
insight.temp_table_sort.order.fix: Order by columns of the table the join reads first, with an index that returns them in that order; or sort fewer rows with a more selective WHERE or a LIMIT.
insight.temp_table_sort.order.title: {n, plural, other {Collects {count} rows in an internal temporary table to sort them (filesort)}}
insight.temp_table_sort.order.verify: Explain again: no "using temporary" on the sort.
insight.temp_table_sort.rule: Grouping in a temporary table, then a filesort
insight.workers_short.detail: The server had no free parallel workers when this ran (max_parallel_workers / max_worker_processes), so it ran with less help than it was planned for.
insight.workers_short.fix: If the server has idle CPUs, raise max_parallel_workers (and max_worker_processes, which needs a restart); otherwise reduce how many queries run in parallel at once.
insight.workers_short.rule: Fewer parallel workers started than planned
insight.workers_short.title: {n, plural, other {Planned {planned} parallel workers, only {launched} started}}
insight.workers_short.verify: Explain analyze again: Workers Launched equals Workers Planned.

provider.yugabyte.coverage.identities_hi: Some statement identities are hidden by this login's permissions.

provider.yugabyte.coverage.index_usage_p: Some indexes did not supply usage from every current node; those counts remain unknown.

provider.yugabyte.coverage.statements_bu: Statement text and counters reached the shared 8 MiB retention budget. Only a contiguous prefix is retained; source totals still cover every statement when a retained row supplies them.

provider.yugabyte.coverage.terminations_: Termination records reached the 1,000-row/8 MiB retention limit, a contributor warned or changed, or some records could not be decoded.

provider.yugabyte.coverage.visibility_ch: Statement visibility changed during collection; hidden identities cannot establish query counts or safely owned plans.

provider.yugabyte.plan_history.note: Retained plan-cache entries have their own first/last-use dates, resets and evictions. Their calls and timings are independent of this statement's statistics window; a cache entry's first use does not prove when its plan was introduced.
provider.yugabyte.plan_history.partial: This read was partial; no complete plan history is established.
provider.yugabyte.plan_history.unreadabl: Retained plan history could not be read with this connection. See the scan's source coverage; the Plan tab can still estimate safely owned statements.
provider.yugabyte.progress.analyze_note: ANALYZE reports its current native phase. PostgreSQL heap-block counters do not measure DocDB progress.
provider.yugabyte.progress.backend_gone: The YSQL backend ended, changed identity, belongs to another node, or is hidden from this login. Refresh Live.
provider.yugabyte.progress.copy_note: Native row counters follow the source's transaction mode. Batched COPY FROM can leave completed transactions persisted after a later error. A zero or missing file size is unknown; counters do not prove whole-command completion or commit.
provider.yugabyte.progress.copy_rows: {n, plural, one {{count} row reported processed} other {{count} rows reported processed}}
provider.yugabyte.progress.index_note: Index backfill counts describe table rows, including for partial indexes. The total comes from an estimate; it is not a measured completion percentage.
provider.yugabyte.progress.not_authorize: Current activity was read; this backend's ownership or visibility could not authorize planning its text with this login's privileges.
provider.yugabyte.progress.note: YSQL reports current activity and supported command phases; it does not expose completed-work percentages or live rows for every operator. Requested plans are estimates and never execute the statement.
provider.yugabyte.progress.partial: Some activity was hidden or a node was skipped; this observation cannot establish complete progress.
provider.yugabyte.progress.pooled_worker: This is a reusable Connection Manager worker, not a stable logical-client identity. Its latest observed statement can change between reads; automatic planning is withheld.
provider.yugabyte.progress.rows_estimate: about {n, plural, one {{count} table row estimated} other {{count} table rows estimated}}
provider.yugabyte.progress.rows_processe: {n, plural, one {{count} table row processed} other {{count} table rows processed}}
provider.yugabyte.progress.unplanned: Current activity was read, but this login could not safely plan the statement. No estimated operator progress is presented as measured work.
provider.yugabyte.progress.view_unavaila: Current activity was read, but the native command-progress view was unavailable or skipped a node. No completion percentage is inferred.
provider.yugabyte.resources.cpu: CPU fields are user/system fractions from a short native sample. Exact per-node sample timestamps and duration are not returned; the observation interval bounds this read, not a workload history.
provider.yugabyte.resources.memory: Host memory can describe the VM or host rather than a container's allocation. The TServer root tracker is neither process RSS nor total YSQL-backend memory; its own limits stay separate from host capacity.
provider.yugabyte.resources.shared: Host CPU and memory are shared with other databases and processes; these measurements do not grade the selected database's pressure or identify which queries caused load.
provider.yugabyte.sessions.actions_produ: Production connection: Culprit does not cancel or end sessions here.
provider.yugabyte.sessions.actions_rules: Actions require this node, the same backend start time, and a direct client backend. Pooled Connection Manager workers are not logical clients.
provider.yugabyte.sessions.hidden: Some active statements are hidden by this login's permissions.
provider.yugabyte.sessions.lock_limits: DocDB lock collection follows transaction heartbeats and has transaction/per-tablet limits; missing chains do not establish that no session is blocked.
provider.yugabyte.sessions.locks_unavail: DocDB lock metadata is unavailable; PostgreSQL heap lock views are not substituted.
provider.yugabyte.sessions.no_backend: A YSQL session had no usable backend identity.
provider.yugabyte.sessions.node_scope: Sessions cover connected YB-TServer {node} only. Enable and authorize cluster views to observe other nodes.
provider.yugabyte.sessions.node_skipped: A YSQL node was skipped or raised a warning while reading sessions; cluster activity is incomplete.
provider.yugabyte.sessions.truncated: Only the first 1,000 YSQL sessions are retained; activity and blocking totals are partial.
provider.yugabyte.sessions.unknown_node: A YSQL session's node identity is unknown; it cannot be signaled safely.
provider.yugabyte.sessions.unknown_node_: Sessions cover only the connected YB-TServer, whose identity is unknown. Enable and authorize cluster views to observe other nodes.
provider.yugabyte.sessions.young_locks: Short-lived DocDB locks may be omitted by the server's minimum transaction-age filter.

provider.yugabyte.terminations.complete_: Complete monitoring privilege for this database
provider.yugabyte.terminations.dates: Records have their own dates and retention, independent of statement-statistics resets. They do not establish a failure rate, failed business requests, or an ongoing incident.
provider.yugabyte.terminations.local: Global termination reads require effective pg_read_all_stats. This read retains connected-node records under native login visibility, without changing global-view configuration.
provider.yugabyte.terminations.role_visi: Native visibility for login role {role}; inherited privileges may expose other roles' records
provider.yugabyte.terminations.scope: This evictable buffer records unexpected backend terminations and temporary-file-limit failures, not all SQL errors, timeouts, cancellations or deadlocks. Empty history does not prove that no queries failed.
provider.yugabyte.terminations.sigkill: SIGKILL alone does not prove an out-of-memory kill; inspect the node's logs. Raw SQL and free-form termination messages were not collected.
provider.yugabyte.waits.method_cluster: YSQL active sessions sampled at a one-second target cadence for {seconds} s (configured cluster views)
provider.yugabyte.waits.method_node: YSQL active sessions sampled at a one-second target cadence for {seconds} s (connected node)
provider.yugabyte.waits.node_scope: Connected YB-TServer {node} only; this is not whole-cluster activity.
provider.yugabyte.waits.partial: Visibility changed, permissions hid sessions, or a node was skipped. Observed categories are partial and no complete active-session count is asserted.
provider.yugabyte.waits.unknown_node_sco: Only the connected YB-TServer is observed, and its identity is unknown; this is not whole-cluster activity.
provider.yugabyte.waits.weighted: Session observations are weighted over the measured duration. They describe active YSQL backends, not CPU utilization or the time spent by internal DocDB tasks. Short operations can fall between samples.

service.cli.about: Run a background collector with durable recovery and independent delivery.
service.cli.delivery_only: Deliver archived telemetry without connecting to a source database or changing its ownership.
service.cli.init: Initialize the remote recovery namespace. Provision cloud resources separately.
service.cli.initialized: The remote recovery namespace is initialized.
service.cli.quiescent: Confirm that the previous source owner and its SQL requests have stopped. Storage fencing alone does not prove this.
service.cli.run: Collect and deliver telemetry using a static shard assignment.
service.cli.valid: The collector configuration is valid. No database or Azure connections were opened.
service.cli.validate: Validate the collector configuration without connecting to a database or Azure.

support.lock_holder.logged_instead: Have the next ones logged instead.
support.lock_holder.mssql: Have the next ones reported instead: SQL Server's blocked process report names the session holding the lock, with its statement, for each wait longer than the server's blocked process threshold (s) (0, off, by default; sp_configure sets it). Capture sqlserver.blocked_process_report in an event session to keep them.
support.lock_holder.mysql.keeps: The slow query log {logging, select, already {already keeps} other {then keeps}} each statement slower than {bar} s with its lock time and when it ran; {server} keeps no record of who held the lock, so match those times with what the application ran then.
support.lock_holder.mysql.look: Look for the next ones in the slow query log.
support.lock_holder.postgres.logs: {on, select, yes {log_lock_waits is on already, and logs} other {log_lock_waits then logs}} each lock wait longer than deadlock_timeout ({deadlock}) with the process holding the lock.
support.lock_holder.postgres.logs_slow: {on, select, yes {log_lock_waits is on already, and logs} other {log_lock_waits then logs}} each lock wait longer than deadlock_timeout ({deadlock}) with the process holding the lock, and log_min_duration_statement each statement slower than {threshold} (any statement, not only this one) with its duration.
support.lock_holder.postgres.on_already: Log_lock_waits is on already, and logs each lock wait longer than deadlock_timeout ({deadlock}) with the process holding the lock: the server log has the next ones, with the process holding the lock.
support.lock_holder.ran_once: It ran once in {window}, so there is no wait to catch now; if it runs again, have its lock waits logged ({log}) to see what holds them.
support.lock_holder.sqlite: SQLite keeps no record of what held the file's write lock: the application's own logs of its writes at those times say which one it was.
support.lock_holder.stopped: It no longer runs, so there is no wait to catch now; if it comes back, find what holds the locks while it waits (Live shows the blocking chain).
support.lock_holder.stopped_rare: It no longer runs, so there is no wait to catch now; if it comes back, have its lock waits logged ({log}): its runs are too few to catch one while it waits.
support.lock_holder.yugabyte: Correlate YSQL statement logs and DocDB wait-queue evidence by transaction, node and time. Configure supported logging through YugabyteDB administration.

view.advisor.cleanup.duplicate: Same keys as {other}: the same index twice, both maintained on every write.
view.advisor.cleanup.foreign_key_caveat: It supports the foreign key {key}; deletes on the parent scan without it.
view.advisor.cleanup.invalid: Marked invalid after an unfinished concurrent build; the planner never reads it.
view.advisor.cleanup.invalid_maintained: Marked invalid after an unfinished concurrent build; the planner never reads it, yet every write to {table} still updates it.
view.advisor.cleanup.overlap: Read {reads} times next to {other}'s {other_reads}; both start with {key}, so its queries can almost always seek on {other} instead.
view.advisor.cleanup.overlap_caveat: Check the plans of the queries that read {index} before hiding it.
view.advisor.cleanup.prefix: Its keys are the start of {other}'s, so any seek it serves {other} serves too.
view.advisor.cleanup.prefix_caveat: {index} is narrower; keep it if a hot query scans it rather than seeking.
view.advisor.cleanup.unused: Not read once {since}, yet updated with every write to {table}.
view.advisor.cleanup.unused_maintained: Not read once {since} while maintained {writes} times, yet updated with every write to {table}.
view.advisor.cleanup.unused_prefix: Not read once {since}, and its keys are the start of {other} (which isn't read either).
view.advisor.cleanup.unused_same_keys: Not read once {since}, and it has the same keys as {other} (which isn't read either).
view.advisor.engine_built.reason: {n, plural, one {{engine} builds an index on {keys} of {table} for itself every time one query runs, because none fits, and drops it after. Created once, it saves that work on every run.} other {{engine} builds an index on {keys} of {table} for itself every time one of {count} queries runs, because none fits, and drops it after. Created once, it saves that work on every run.}}
view.advisor.engine_built.share: {n, plural, one {It takes {share} of database time.} other {They take {share} of database time.}}
view.advisor.engine_built.verify_explain: Explain one of the queries again: no automatic index on {table}, and a search using the new one.
view.advisor.engine_built.verify_rescan: Re-scan after the workload has run: the queries' share of database time drops.
view.advisor.foreign_key.also: {n, plural, one {It is also the foreign key to {parent}, which {count} more query filter or join on.} other {It is also the foreign key to {parent}, which {count} more queries filter or join on.}}
view.advisor.foreign_key.also_share: {n, plural, one {It is also the foreign key to {parent}, which {count} more query filter or join on: together they take {share} of database time.} other {It is also the foreign key to {parent}, which {count} more queries filter or join on: together they take {share} of database time.}}
view.advisor.foreign_key.reason: {columns} is the foreign key to {parent}. Without an index, deleting or re-keying a row in {parent} reads all {rows} rows of {child} looking for matches, and joins from {parent} can't seek.
view.advisor.note.catalog_incomplete: Current index and schema definitions were incomplete: {reason}. No index changes can be chosen safely from this scan.
view.advisor.note.counted: Index usage counters have counted for {span}; an index has to go unread for a week before it's listed to clean up.
view.advisor.note.counted_maybe_reset: Index usage counters may have started over with performance_schema's statements, which have counted for {span}; an index has to go unread for a week of them before it's listed to clean up.
view.advisor.note.counted_maybe_reset_un: Index usage counters may have started over with performance_schema's statements, which have counted for an unknown time; an index has to go unread for a week of them before it's listed to clean up.
view.advisor.note.counted_unknown: Index usage counters have counted for an unknown time; an index has to go unread for a week before it's listed to clean up.
view.advisor.note.no_index_usage: Index usage counters aren't readable: unused indexes and the runtime impact of overlaps are unknown. Duplicate and prefix coverage checks use the recorded definitions.
view.advisor.note.no_plans: No plans were captured, so plan-based candidates are missing.
view.advisor.note.partition_copies: {n, plural, one {{count} index on partitions is left out of the clean-ups: each is a partition's copy of its partitioned table's index, a cold partition reads as unused because queries skip it, and a copy can't be dropped on its own.} other {{count} indexes on partitions are left out of the clean-ups: each is a partition's copy of its partitioned table's index, a cold partition reads as unused because queries skip it, and a copy can't be dropped on its own.}}
view.advisor.note.rewrites: Query rewrites to evaluate before adding indexes: {queries}. Their plans filter an OR across tables after a scan. Compare equivalent UNION or EXISTS forms and representative branch plans first; these are structural observations, not indexes to create.
view.advisor.note.skipped: {n, plural, one {Left out {count} candidate without sufficient current measured workload, or for a table that is gone or queries that are history.} other {Left out {count} candidates without sufficient current measured workload, or for tables that are gone or queries that are history.}}
view.advisor.note.small_foreign_keys: {count} more foreign keys on tables under {rows} rows have no usable index; the finding “{finding}” lists them with the SQL.
view.advisor.optimizer.asked: SQL Server's optimizer asked for it {lookups} times {since} and estimates those lookups would be about {improvement} cheaper.
view.advisor.optimizer.parameter_finds: {n, plural, one {The query passes {columns} as a parameter, which keeps SQL Server off {index}, filtered to {literals}; written as a literal, it finds the rows by {keys}, not by {range}.} other {The queries pass {columns} as a parameter, which keeps SQL Server off {index}, filtered to {literals}; written as a literal, it finds the rows by {keys}, not by {range}.}}
view.advisor.optimizer.parameter_serves: {n, plural, one {The query passes {columns} as a parameter, which keeps SQL Server off {index}, filtered to {literals}; written as a literal, it serves them, reading {missing} from the table for each row.} other {The queries pass {columns} as a parameter, which keeps SQL Server off {index}, filtered to {literals}; written as a literal, it serves them, reading {missing} from the table for each row.}}
view.advisor.optimizer.rest_filtered: This index is the rest of the request, filtered the same way.
view.advisor.optimizer.rest_included: {n, plural, one {Including it is the rest of the request.} other {Including them is the rest of the request.}}
view.advisor.optimizer.share: {n, plural, one {The query behind it accounts for {share} of database time.} other {The {count} queries behind it account for {share} of database time.}}
view.advisor.optimizer.too_many_includes: SQL Server also wanted {count} more columns included; the statement keeps the keys only, so add INCLUDE columns just for what the hot queries select.
view.advisor.optimizer.verify_literal: Write {literals} as a literal in the queries first, then re-scan: the request either disappears or asks for this.
view.advisor.optimizer.verify_plan: Obtain a newly compiled plan after representative runs; an old stored request need not disappear.
view.advisor.optimizer.verify_seek: The queries listed seek on {index} and read far fewer pages per run.
view.advisor.optimizer.verify_seek_new: The queries listed seek on the new index and read far fewer pages per run.
view.advisor.optimizer.verify_uses: Check whether the queries listed use {index} and compare reads and time per run under equivalent parameters and load.
view.advisor.optimizer.verify_uses_new: Check whether the queries listed use the new index and compare reads and time per run under equivalent parameters and load.
view.advisor.plan_scan.reason: {n, plural, one {One captured query plan scans {table} and keeps only those matching {predicate}; no enabled index starts with {keys}. {rows}} other {{count} captured query plans scan {table} and keep only those matching {predicate}; no enabled index starts with {keys}. {rows}}}
view.advisor.plan_scan.verify_compare: Compare reads and time per run after equivalent workload, including storage and write cost. Old saved plans and a changing share of database time alone do not verify improvement.
view.advisor.plan_scan.verify_plan: Obtain a newly compiled plan and check whether {table} uses the candidate index to read fewer rows; a scan can still be appropriate for some parameters.
view.advisor.table.forwarded: A heap: reads followed a forwarding pointer to another page {count} times {since}. A clustered index ends that.
view.advisor.table.over_indexed: {count} secondary indexes and {how_many}: every insert updates all of them.
view.advisor.table.scan_heavy: Read in full {how_many} ({rows} rows without an index).
view.advisor.table.scan_heavy_explain_ma: Explain the statements listed with it to check their access paths, then measure rows kept in representative runs.
view.advisor.table.scan_heavy_explain_on: Explain the statement listed with it to check its access path, then measure rows kept in representative runs.
view.advisor.table.scan_heavy_unexplaine: None of the captured statements explains these full reads: they come from statements outside the top of the workload.

view.plan_advice.context.history: This statement ran once or stopped running in the selected workload. These are observations about its captured plan, not a current incident. Recheck if the workload returns.
view.plan_advice.context.not_material: The selected workload does not establish material execution cost. Structural concerns remain relevant as table size or call volume grows; compare reads and time under representative load before changing an index.
view.plan_advice.growth: A filtered scan of a small table can be appropriate today. Track rows read and execution time as the table grows; low current cost does not establish that the access path will scale.
view.plan_advice.index.definitions_unava: Current index definitions were unavailable in this scan. Inspect the current keys, filters and included columns before choosing an index change; the captured structure can still pose a scaling risk.

view.plan_advice.index.no_keys: Inspect the complete predicate and current index definitions; these conditions do not establish a safe choice of index keys.
view.plan_advice.index.predicate_unknown: Check the complete predicate and current index definitions before choosing index keys.
view.plan_advice.index.table_gone: The captured table is absent from this scan's catalog. Confirm the current schema before acting on this historical plan.
view.plan_advice.index.verify: Obtain a newly compiled plan and compare reads and execution time with equivalent parameters and load. Check index usage and write cost; a retained scan or old stored suggestion alone does not establish success or failure.
view.plan_advice.index.wide_include: The wide INCLUDE list is omitted. Select fewer columns and test a narrow index before copying the payload into an index.
view.plan_advice.lookup.fix: Select fewer columns where possible. Test adding only the narrow columns needed by frequent reads as included columns, balancing saved lookups against index size and write cost.
view.plan_advice.lookup.unknown_columns: Confirm the projection against current column definitions before choosing INCLUDE columns.
view.plan_advice.lookup.verify: Compare a newly compiled plan, lookup counts, reads and time under equivalent parameters and load. Retain a covering index only if its read benefit justifies its storage and write cost.
view.plan_advice.lookup.wide: The remaining projection is also wide; a covering index is not automatically worthwhile.

view.sql_lint.blocking_unique.fix: Build the unique index first with `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, then attach it with `{attach}`.
view.sql_lint.blocking_unique.summary: The statement `{sql}` adds a {kind} constraint on {table} ({size}) directly. PostgreSQL builds the backing unique index while holding an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock on {name}, blocking all reads and writes until the index build finishes.
view.sql_lint.blocking_unique.title: ADD {kind} constraint on {table} ({size}) without USING INDEX builds the index under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock
view.sql_lint.blocking_unique.verify: Re-run `culprit lint-sql` after switching to `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` + `ADD CONSTRAINT ... USING INDEX`.
view.sql_lint.cluster.fix: Use `pg_repack` to reorder a large production table online without holding an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock.
view.sql_lint.cluster.summary: The statement `{sql}` runs `CLUSTER` on {table} ({size}). `CLUSTER` physically reorders and rewrites the table while holding an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock, blocking all concurrent reads and writes.
view.sql_lint.cluster.title: CLUSTER on {table} ({size}) rewrites the table under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock
view.sql_lint.cluster.verify: Avoid running `CLUSTER` directly on large production tables during traffic.
view.sql_lint.concurrent_in_tx.fix: Run the `CONCURRENTLY` statement outside `BEGIN ... COMMIT` (for example `disable_ddl_transaction!` in Rails, `atomic = False` in Django, or `-- migrate:no-transaction`).
view.sql_lint.concurrent_in_tx.summary: The statement `{sql}` uses `CONCURRENTLY` inside an explicit `BEGIN ... COMMIT` transaction block. PostgreSQL immediately aborts `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, `DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY` and `REINDEX CONCURRENTLY` when executed inside a transaction block.
view.sql_lint.concurrent_in_tx.title: {statement} ({target}) cannot run inside a transaction block
view.sql_lint.concurrent_in_tx.verify: Remove the surrounding `BEGIN`/`COMMIT` and re-run `culprit lint-sql`.
view.sql_lint.create_index.mssql.cost: Online index builds use additional tempdb version store space while running.
view.sql_lint.create_index.mssql.fix: Add `WITH (ONLINE = ON)` to the `CREATE INDEX` statement so concurrent reads and writes continue.
view.sql_lint.create_index.mssql.summary: The statement `{sql}` builds an index on {table} ({size}) without `WITH (ONLINE = ON)`, which this SQL Server edition supports. Offline index builds hold shared or schema-modification locks that block writers.
view.sql_lint.create_index.mssql.title: CREATE INDEX on {table} ({size}) without ONLINE = ON blocks writes during the build
view.sql_lint.create_index.mysql.cost: Online InnoDB index builds buffer concurrent DML in innodb_online_alter_log_max_size while running.
view.sql_lint.create_index.mysql.fix: Add `ALGORITHM=INPLACE LOCK=NONE` so the server guarantees an online build and fails immediately instead of locking the table.
view.sql_lint.create_index.mysql.summary: The statement `{sql}` builds an index on {table} ({size}) without `ALGORITHM=INPLACE LOCK=NONE`. Without explicit `LOCK=NONE`, MySQL/MariaDB can fall back to `LOCK=SHARED` or `ALGORITHM=COPY` if an online build is not supported, blocking concurrent writes until the build finishes.
view.sql_lint.create_index.mysql.title: CREATE INDEX on {table} ({size}) without LOCK=NONE can fall back to a table lock
view.sql_lint.create_index.postgres.cost: CONCURRENTLY performs two table scans and cannot run inside a transaction block.
view.sql_lint.create_index.postgres.fix: Use `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` (outside a transaction block) so writes continue while the index builds.
view.sql_lint.create_index.postgres.summ: The statement `{sql}` builds an index on {table} ({size}) without `CONCURRENTLY`. Standard `CREATE INDEX` in PostgreSQL acquires a `SHARE` lock on the table for the entire index build, blocking all `INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE` statements.
view.sql_lint.create_index.postgres.titl: CREATE INDEX on {table} ({size}) without CONCURRENTLY blocks writes until the build finishes
view.sql_lint.create_index.verify: Re-run `culprit lint-sql` on the updated migration to confirm no blocking index builds remain.
view.sql_lint.drop_index.mysql.fix: Drop the index with `ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE` so concurrent reads and writes are not blocked.
view.sql_lint.drop_index.mysql.summary: The statement `{sql}` drops `{index}` on {table} ({size}) without `ALGORITHM=INPLACE LOCK=NONE`. Specifying `ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE` guarantees an online drop that never falls back to a blocking table lock.
view.sql_lint.drop_index.mysql.title: DROP INDEX {index} on {table} ({size}) without LOCK=NONE can block concurrent writes
view.sql_lint.drop_index.postgres.cost: DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY waits for active transactions using the index and cannot run inside a transaction block.
view.sql_lint.drop_index.postgres.fix: Use `DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY` (outside a transaction block) so concurrent reads and writes are not blocked.
view.sql_lint.drop_index.postgres.summar: The statement `{sql}` drops `{index}` on {table} ({size}) without `CONCURRENTLY`. Standard `DROP INDEX` in PostgreSQL acquires an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock on the table, blocking all concurrent reads and writes until in-flight queries finish.
view.sql_lint.drop_index.postgres.title: DROP INDEX {index} on {table} ({size}) without CONCURRENTLY acquires an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock
view.sql_lint.drop_index.postgres.verify: Re-run `culprit lint-sql` after switching to `DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY`.
view.sql_lint.fk_type_mismatch.summary: The statement `{sql}` references {parent} (`{parent_type}`) from {child} (`{child_type}`). Mismatched foreign key types either fail DDL validation or force implicit conversions during joins and referential integrity checks.
view.sql_lint.fk_type_mismatch.title: Foreign key {child} ({child_type}) does not match {parent} ({parent_type})
view.sql_lint.fk_type_mismatch.verify: Confirm both columns share the same data type before adding the constraint.
view.sql_lint.mysql_online_ddl.fix: Append `ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE` (or `ALGORITHM=INSTANT` for compatible column additions on MySQL 8.0+) so the database rejects any blocking table copy immediately.
view.sql_lint.mysql_online_ddl.summary: The statement `{sql}` alters {table} ({size}) without specifying `ALGORITHM=INSTANT` or `ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE`. Without an explicit online DDL clause, MySQL/MariaDB can fall back to `ALGORITHM=COPY` or `LOCK=SHARED`, blocking concurrent writes while rebuilding the table.
view.sql_lint.mysql_online_ddl.title: ALTER TABLE on {table} ({size}) without LOCK=NONE or ALGORITHM=INSTANT can lock the table
view.sql_lint.mysql_online_ddl.verify: Re-run `culprit lint-sql` after adding `ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE` or `ALGORITHM=INSTANT`.
view.sql_lint.not_null_without_default.f: Either supply a non-volatile `DEFAULT` value, or add `{column}` as nullable first, backfill existing rows, and then enforce `NOT NULL`.
view.sql_lint.not_null_without_default.s: The statement `{sql}` adds `{column}` as `NOT NULL` without a `DEFAULT` clause to {table} ({size}). Because existing rows would receive `NULL` for `{column}`, the database rejects the statement immediately at runtime.
view.sql_lint.not_null_without_default.t: ADD COLUMN {column} NOT NULL without DEFAULT fails on non-empty table ({size})
view.sql_lint.not_null_without_default.v: Re-run `culprit lint-sql` after adding a `DEFAULT` or making the initial column nullable.
view.sql_lint.reindex.cost: REINDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction block.
view.sql_lint.reindex_index.fix: Use `REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY` (outside a transaction block) so concurrent reads and writes can continue.
view.sql_lint.reindex_index.summary: The statement `{sql}` rebuilds `{index}` on {table} ({size}) without `CONCURRENTLY`. Standard `REINDEX INDEX` blocks writes on the parent table and reads of the index until the rebuild finishes.
view.sql_lint.reindex_index.title: REINDEX INDEX {index} on {table} ({size}) without CONCURRENTLY blocks writes
view.sql_lint.reindex_index.verify: Re-run `culprit lint-sql` after switching to `REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY`.
view.sql_lint.reindex_table.fix: Use `REINDEX TABLE CONCURRENTLY` (outside a transaction block) so concurrent reads and writes can continue.
view.sql_lint.reindex_table.summary: The statement `{sql}` rebuilds all indexes on {table} ({size}) without `CONCURRENTLY`. Standard `REINDEX TABLE` holds `SHARE` and `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` locks that block concurrent writes and reads.
view.sql_lint.reindex_table.title: REINDEX TABLE {table} ({size}) without CONCURRENTLY blocks reads and writes
view.sql_lint.reindex_table.verify: Re-run `culprit lint-sql` after switching to `REINDEX TABLE CONCURRENTLY`.
view.sql_lint.set_not_null.fix: Add `CHECK (col IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID`, run `ALTER TABLE ... VALIDATE CONSTRAINT ...` (which only takes `SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE`), and then run `SET NOT NULL`.
view.sql_lint.set_not_null.summary: The statement `{sql}` runs `SET NOT NULL` on {table} ({size}). Without an existing validated `CHECK (col IS NOT NULL)` constraint, PostgreSQL scans the entire table while holding an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock.
view.sql_lint.set_not_null.title: SET NOT NULL on {table} ({size}) scans the table under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock unless backed by a valid constraint
view.sql_lint.set_not_null.verify: Re-run `culprit lint-sql` after splitting the constraint validation step.
view.sql_lint.table_rewrite.fix: Prefer an expand-and-contract migration (add a new column, backfill in small batches, swap reads/writes) unless the engine guarantees a metadata-only cast.
view.sql_lint.table_rewrite.summary: The statement `{sql}` alters a column type on {table} ({size}). Changing a column's representation rewrites every row and index while holding an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` / schema-modification lock, blocking all reads and writes on {name}.
view.sql_lint.table_rewrite.title: Column type change on {table} ({size}) can rewrite the table under an exclusive lock
view.sql_lint.truncate.summary: The statement `{sql}` truncates {table} ({size}). `TRUNCATE` acquires an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` / schema-modification lock on the table, blocking all concurrent queries while deallocating its storage.
view.sql_lint.truncate.title: TRUNCATE on {table} ({size}) acquires an exclusive table lock and deletes all rows
view.sql_lint.truncate.verify: Confirm `TRUNCATE` is intended for this environment before running.
view.sql_lint.unindexed_fk.fix: Create an index on {table} ({columns}) before or alongside the foreign key.
view.sql_lint.unindexed_fk.summary: The statement `{sql}` adds a foreign key on {table}.({columns}) referencing {parent}, but neither the snapshot nor the migration defines an index with ({columns}) as its leading key. Deletes or key updates on the referenced parent table will scan {name} on every check.
view.sql_lint.unindexed_fk.title: New foreign key on {table}.({columns}) has no supporting index
view.sql_lint.unindexed_fk.verify: Add the supporting `CREATE INDEX` to the migration and re-run `culprit lint-sql`.
view.sql_lint.unvalidated_constraint.fix: Add the {kind} constraint with `NOT VALID` first, then run `{validate}` in a separate step (which only holds `SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE` and allows concurrent reads and writes).
view.sql_lint.unvalidated_constraint.sum: The statement `{sql}` adds a {kind} constraint on {table} ({size}) without `NOT VALID`. PostgreSQL validates every existing row immediately while holding a `SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE` / `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock that blocks writes on {name}.
view.sql_lint.unvalidated_constraint.tit: ADD {kind} constraint on {table} ({size}) without NOT VALID scans the table under a lock
view.sql_lint.unvalidated_constraint.ver: Re-run `culprit lint-sql` after adding `NOT VALID` to the constraint definition.
view.sql_lint.vacuum_full.fix: Run standard `VACUUM (ANALYZE)` (which reclaims dead tuples online without blocking reads or writes), or use `pg_repack` if physical table compaction is required.
view.sql_lint.vacuum_full.summary: The statement `{sql}` runs `VACUUM FULL` on {table} ({size}). Unlike standard `VACUUM`, `VACUUM FULL` rewrites every row and index into new disk files while holding an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock, blocking all concurrent reads and writes.
view.sql_lint.vacuum_full.title: VACUUM FULL on {table} ({size}) rewrites the entire table under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock
view.sql_lint.verify.lock_timeout: Verify in staging with `SET lock_timeout = '2s'` before running on production.
view.sql_lint.volatile_default.fix: Add `{column}` without a default, backfill existing rows in batches, and then set `{set_default}`.
view.sql_lint.volatile_default.summary: The statement `{sql}` adds `{column}` to {table} ({size}) with volatile `DEFAULT {function}()`, which cannot use metadata-only fast defaults because every existing row requires a newly evaluated value. The engine rewrites every row and index while holding an exclusive table lock.
view.sql_lint.volatile_default.title: ADD COLUMN {column} with volatile DEFAULT {function}() rewrites the table ({size})
view.sql_lint.workload_break.fix: Stop reading/writing `{target}` in application code and deploy that change before running `{action}` in a later migration.
view.sql_lint.workload_break.impact: {n, plural, one {{count} active query} other {{count} active queries}}
view.sql_lint.workload_break.summary: The migration statement `{sql}` runs `{action}` on `{target}`, which is referenced by {n, plural, one {{count} active statement} other {{count} active statements}} in the captured workload. Deploying this DDL while the current application code is running will cause immediate query errors.
view.sql_lint.workload_break.title: {action} on {target} breaks {n, plural, one {{count} active workload query} other {{count} active workload queries}}
view.sql_lint.workload_break.verify: Verify no active queries in `culprit top` reference `{target}` before applying `{action}`.

view.waits.note.mysql: {server} counts waits since it started, only for enabled performance_schema instruments. Lock time is attributed to statements; the rest is a server-wide total.
view.waits.note.mysql_no_performance_sch: performance_schema is off, so {server} times no waits; the slow query log keeps each statement's lock time. {now} samples what sessions are doing.
view.waits.note.postgres: PostgreSQL keeps no history of what sessions waited on. These totals come from per-statement timing; use {now} to sample what sessions wait on at this moment.
view.waits.note.track_io_timing: Turn on track_io_timing so time spent reading from disk is measured per statement. {how}
view.waits.note.track_io_timing_sql: Turn on track_io_timing so time spent reading from disk is measured per statement. {how} ({sql})
view.waits.note.yugabyte: DocDB storage timings and RPC times can overlap; they are not exclusive shares of statement time. Use native metrics or sample YSQL sessions.

view.waits.query_store.off: Query Store is off; with it on (and recording waits, the default from SQL Server 2017), Culprit can tie waits to queries: {sql}
view.waits.query_store.old_version: Query Store on {product} doesn't record waits per query; SQL Server 2017 and later do.
view.waits.query_store.totals: These are server totals since startup and can't be tied to queries.
